  2. Hirak and Hosha : Modalities of Collective Action in Jordan in the Wake of the Arab Spring
    Frederick Sefton Jenkins Wojnarowski · pp. 718-744 · online 2026-01-12
    摘要

    This essay considers how the rural and tribal have been obscured from prevailing scholarly accounts of unrest and protest in the years since the Arab Uprisings of 2010–2012, and what this might mean for wider scholarly theorizations of protest and revolution. It draws on fieldwork in central Jordan, especially with Hirak Dhiban, where historical circumstances render visible dynamics also significant elsewhere. It takes as a heuristic binary two broad discursive modalities of seemingly dissimilar collective action that in fact reference and relate to each other in various revealing ways: on the one hand the politically populist and self-consciously leftist Hirak protest movements, prominent in the waves of protest since 2011, and on the other hosha —"tribal clashes.” It considers how contestations over the legitimacy, revolutionary potential, and moral valence of protests often hinge on discursive claims that, in a sense, Hirak is hosha , or hosha , Hirak. It engages with anthropological theories to interpret protest as a generative and affective process, rooted in local histories and imaginaries, even while responding to wider events. It calls for a broader reappraisal of where revolutionary potential is located and how it is recognized in anthropological and historical scholarship.

  3. Post-imperial Reckoning: Transitional Injustice and the Unmaking of the Japanese Empire in East Asia
    Yukiko Koga · pp. 745-768 · online 2026-05-06
    摘要

    This essay explores what it means to reckon with imperial violence decades after the Japanese Empire’s demise in 1945. Through legal, historical, and ethnographic analyses of civil lawsuits filed in courts across Japan since the 1990s by Chinese and South Korean victims seeking apologies and monetary compensation from the Japanese government and corporations involved in enslavement, I explore how the lawsuits exposed a politics of abandonment that left victims of imperial violence unredressable for decades. This evasion of imperial accountability, I argue, was etched into the legal, economic, and diplomatic structures of what I call the unmaking of empire—the entwined processes of de-imperialization and de-colonization. The move from empire to nation-state thus produced transitional injustice which calls for post-imperial reckoning: a double task of accounting for both the original imperial violence and the politics of abandonment after empire in perpetrator and victim nations. I show how new legal and moral landscapes for imperial reckoning are expanding the scope and agency of accountability, challenging accepted models of redress and raising the stakes for current generations to reckon with unaccounted-for pasts.

  4. “The Word of the State against Ours”: The Right to Know and State Terror in 1970s Mexico
    Vanessa Freije · pp. 769-797 · online 2026-04-23
    摘要

    This article brings together two stories of 1970s Mexico that are often narrated separately: the story of the PRI’s attempts to reform itself, specifically through the right to know, and the story of activists’ mobilizations against disappearances. Epistemic struggles surrounding the right to know and disappearances created a shared discursive arena in which activists and state officials contested the nature of information, the authority to produce it, and the seemingly unbridgeable gap between evidence and the state’s recognition of wrongdoing. Debates in the legislative and activist realms often occurred in parallel without necessarily intersecting. Nonetheless, they engaged similar questions: What would it mean to entrust the public and media with sensitive information? What strategies could move state actors to produce information and what effects would doing so have on public life? This article contends that the struggle over information and recognition became the central battlefield for negotiating state violence and opening in Mexico.

  5. Spiraling out in the Circular Economy: Movement and Belonging at a Malaysian Rare Earth Elements Refinery
    Tom Özden-Schilling · pp. 798-824 · online 2026-05-20
    摘要

    The rise of “circular economy” discourse in the extractive industries has altered how researchers, laborers, activists, and consumers conceptualize movements of materials. To proponents, building a circular economy around rare earth elements (REE) production will “close the loop” around extraction, processing, design, manufacturing, and disposal practices to minimize and eventually eliminate all “waste” produced through technology development. Articulated through utopian imaginaries projecting environmental and technological futures far beyond mining, however, these conceptualizations of movement also carry far-ranging entailments for the movements of specific groups of people, including their place in future social and political orders and their capacity to plan for multi-generational futures. This article follows activists and university researchers brought into conflict through a REE processing facility in Malaysia, where research on commercial applications for post-processing wastes has been treated alternately as pathways to economic diversification and as threats to minoritized communities’ welfare and senses of national belonging. Both groups correlate “responsible” waste management to mismanaged flows of people: prospective experts drawn overseas for more sophisticated work; children emigrating for university education or middle-class jobs after struggling to find positions in Malaysia. While explicitly offering future stability and a broadened ethics of responsible attention, the visions of circularity undergirding these debates effectively collapse the many forms of movement at stake in industrial transition into a promise of transcendence, obscuring the racialized patterns of exclusion and migration that invariably accompany the extractive industries.

  6. Constructing a Colonial State: The Land Rights Debate in Eighteenth-Century Bengal
    Tirthankar Roy · pp. 825-846 · online 2026-06-17
    摘要

    The paper reinterprets the East India Company’s state-building effort in late eighteenth‑century Bengal by foregrounding the intertwined evolution of fiscal capacity and institutional reform. It argues that the Permanent Settlement of 1793 emerged not from a desire to follow Indian or English precedent, but from the Company’s struggle to concentrate fiscal powers. A debate on the need to obtain information on taxpayers, which delayed the reform, reveals this struggle. Repeated failures in data collection pushed the state to anchor the reform in an expanding judicial system capable of producing actionable information. The Settlement strengthened revenue flows, enabling the financing of a centrally controlled army and contributing to Britain’s wider imperial expansion. However, its long-term rigidity limited fiscal flexibility and impeded broader developmental outcomes.

  7. Money on Trial: Performances of Value and Authority in Ottoman Istanbul during the Age of Global Silver
    Ellen M. Nye · pp. 847-873 · online 2026-05-07
    摘要

    Flows of Spanish American silver have long been bound up in narratives of early modernity, the growth of globalization, and the coming of capitalism. This article reconsiders these narratives through a trial held in seventeenth-century Ottoman Istanbul of imported lion dollar coins that were suspected of being false. The trial shows the different ways groups—both within and outside the state and transacting on different scales from local to interstate—sought to impose criteria of evaluation on coins as they crossed oceans and empires in an era of incomplete state power and growing interstate trade. The trial worked to align competing understandings of money and restored confidence through a performance of measurement. In reckoning with competing understandings of money before multiple monetary authorities, social relations, as much as the physical coins, were on trial. By moving past a traditional divide between thinking globally about money as a trade commodity and thinking comparatively about money as a creature of the state in distinct polities, the trial of the lion dollars shows how early modern money was made and remade through a process of global circulation and far-reaching interactions with competing authorities.

  8. Two Journeys into Diaspora: Qing and British Imperial Investigations in the Dutch East Indies and Australia
    Nicholas McGee · pp. 874-899 · online 2026-05-19
    摘要

    This paper compares the experiences and conclusions of two imperial investigations into diasporic Chinese communities of the Asia-Pacific in the 1880s. These were the official investigations undertaken by the specially appointed Qing Commissioners Wang Ronghe and Yu Qiong, and the unofficial mission carried out by the British translator, orientalist, and diplomat Edward Harper Parker. At a crucial moment in the history of Chinese immigration, these two parties undertook almost simultaneous expeditions to investigate the conditions of the vast Chinese diaspora across Southeast Asia and Oceania. Both missions engaged with some of the most contentious issues surrounding Chinese migration of the era. In particular, I focus on their documentation of the brutal exploitation of trafficked Chinese workers on the tobacco plantations of Deli, in the Dutch East Indies, as well as the rising tide of white supremacist efforts to exclude Chinese migrants from British Australia. Arguing for bold new approaches to imperial engagement with Chinese diaspora, both parties faced significant resistance to their work. Using Chinese, British, Dutch, and Australian sources, this paper traces these journeys to reveal unexpected commonalities between two very different imperial systems, demonstrating the surprisingly global reach of the late Qing state. Moreover, it uses the materials created by these missions to paint in-depth portraits of two Chinese communities and situate the period’s “Chinese Question” of migration to white settler colonies in its broader diasporic context.

  9. Stars, Kings, Pirates: The Nine Emperor Gods Festival and the Making of a Diasporic Religious Ecology in Postcolonial Southeast Asia
    Esmond Chuah Meng Soh, Keng We Koh · pp. 900-925 · online 2026-07-06
    摘要

    This article examines the Nine Emperor Gods Festival as a site of religious transformation among Chinese communities in Southeast Asia, offering a lens through which to theorize how migration, memory, and marginality reshape ritual life. While the festival originated in Qing-era China, it was reconfigured across the nineteenth and twentieth centuries through colonial labor migration, local ritual innovation, and the institutional life of overseas Chinese organizations. Adopting a longue durée perspective, we trace the shifting identities of the Nine Emperors, also known in the diaspora as the Nine Emperor Gods, and their mother, the Dipper Matriarch, alongside the transformation of the festival’s ritual structure. We propose the concept of diasporic religious ecology to theorize how Southeast Asian Chinese communities reconstituted religious authority outside East Asia. These communities invoked China as a cultural origin while simultaneously rejecting its political legitimacy. The Nine Emperor Gods, often recognized as exiles, martyrs, or liminal figures, mediated these tensions: their ritual features became metaphors for the diaspora’s tenuous but enduring relationship with China. By treating the festival not as evidence of survival but as a method of reckoning with displacement, this study positions religious transformation as a medium through which exile, rupture, and authority are not merely remembered but actively reconceptualized.

  10. A History of Clamor: Historical Time and the Late Ottoman Surreal
    Kabir Tambar · pp. 926-949 · online 2026-03-24
    摘要

    This essay examines a scene of late Ottoman parliamentary politics characterized by verbal disruption, raucous applause, and strident indignation: in short, clamor. Centered on the brief period in late 1918 following the empire’s exit from World War I but prior to the rise of the Turkish nationalist movement, the essay focuses on a moment shaped by remarkable uncertainty about how to narrate the political present—what aspects of the historical past remained relevant to defining a possible political future? It looks at the efforts of a Greek Orthodox deputy of parliament, Emmanouil Emmanouilidis, to rebuke the promise of the nearly century-long process of reform ( ıslahat ). As part of this effort, he also historicized the interruption of his own speech, identifying the traces of his own frailty of voice in the stenographic records from prior parliamentary sessions. Attention to noise requires a careful unpacking of seemingly contingent moments of communicative misfire, places where denotational discourse is disrupted and therefore unheard, or what speech act theorists have referred to as infelicities. I offer a critical reimagining of the concept of infelicity, attentive to Emmanouilidis’ own preoccupation with the historical weight assumed by the fact of being persistently drowned out by his colleagues. I contend that Emmanouilidis was challenging regnant assumptions about the historical unfolding of freedom in Ottoman political life. The essay argues for the importance of interrogating the labile and contested character of historical temporality at the end of empire.

  11. Piracy as Political Prism: Sea Raiders and the Rise of the International Atlantic
    Lauren Benton · pp. 950-977 · online 2026-09-28
    摘要

    This article places maritime violence at the center of the history of international ordering. It views the transformation of the nineteenth-century Atlantic from the deck of one ship, a Baltimore-built privateer called the Irresistible. The ship’s captain seized Spanish and Portuguese shipping under a privateering commission from the Oriental Republic. Sponsorship of privateers by the Oriental Republic and other new Latin American governments reflected an open-ended Atlantic constitutionalism that recognized sovereignty at multiple scales. That constitutional context formed the background to three cases involving the Irresistible and its crew that reached the U.S. Supreme Court. The cases show how privateering politics opened to wide-ranging debates about the definition of states, war, and piracy, while preserving the indeterminacies of sovereignty in the new Atlantic system. That system, closing as it formed, was composed of new states pressured to align with powerful empires. Privateering disputes featured sharpening rhetoric about piracy as a crime under the law of nations while at the same time preserving a regime that protected low-level maritime violence. Situating the politics of piracy at the nexus of domestic and international orders, the article highlights the political uses and legal limits of the discourse of pirates as enemies of all and connects this history to an understanding of terrorism and states in the international order.

    Nathan Perl-Rosenthal · pp. 978-986 · online 2026-10-08

  13. Booty into Property: The View from the Desert
    Judith Scheele · pp. 987-995 · online 2026-09-28
    摘要

    Lauren Benton’s paper invites a comparison between deserts and oceans, camels and ships. This is a comparison that I have always resisted, partly because it is somewhat trite; partly because it directs attention away from the desert—the Sahara, in this case—not merely as a space to be crossed, but as a space of life in its own right. Much of the recent renewal in Saharan studies stems from the rejection of this analogy (McDougall 2007): people live in the Sahara in a way that they do not live in the in-between spaces of the ocean, which is something I will return to later. But if, just for once, we set these misgivings aside, a few interesting parallels do emerge.

  14. The Protection of Refusal: On Disavowal in the Indian Ocean
    Jatin Dua · pp. 996-1001 · online 2026-10-16
    摘要

    Lauren Benton reminds us that to write about piracy as historians (and anthropologists) is to engage in projects of “myth-making and myth-busting.” As she notes, pirates are either imagined as “colorful rogues…inherently anti-authoritarian actors who possessed a penchant for experimenting with alternative forms of political solidarity,” or they are depicted in a less renegade fashion, one that shows “their integration in established, if fluid, networks of patronage and power.” Instead of colorful outlaws, Benton (2014) argues that pirates are more akin to lawyers engaged in “legal posturing,” converting “booty into property.” As political actors, their politics are often far from revolutionary. Benton’s scholarship has been at the forefront of this latter school of myth-busting, and her work has been inspirational in rethinking the relationship between piracy, politics, and maritime space in order to tell a different kind of sea yarn. As she wrote in her 2005 CSSH essay, “[i]n my sea yarn, the oceans have a quality of lumpiness about them, pirates strain not to break the law, and international norms take shape not at Westphalia but at the edges of the Indian Ocean” (Benton 2005: 701–2).

  15. On Capture
    Lauren Benton · pp. 1002-1008 · online 2026-10-14
    摘要

    Drawing on the articles in this forum, the essay considers continuities in the relation of raiding to regional reordering and reflects on capture as a sociolegal phenomenon. It comments on three dimensions of capture: the moment of capture, the transformation of booty into property, and the wider legal and institutional context of capture, from protection arrangements to jurisdictional politics.

  1. On Friendship’s Mystic Affordances (Also, On Universalism, Particularism, and the Generic)
    Ashley Lebner · pp. 1-24 · online 2026-10-21
    摘要

    Four recent monographs have inspired me to reflect on studying friendship across contexts and disciplines. I write from the perspective of an anthropologist, however, whose discipline has long had trouble being truly interested in friendship. Part of the problem comes from relative perceptions of friendship’s universality: friendship has been seen as either not universal, too universal, or not universal(ly important) enough to merit much sustained attention. The works under consideration here show that even beyond anthropology, scholarship on friendship and other topics is always affected by questions of universalism. Specifically, these works indicate that relatively unreflective positions on universalist modes of description (including the reaction to them, what it means to seek particulars) can curtail understandings. This is not a blanket rejection of universalizing orientations. Rather, I argue that, instead of ignoring the problem of the universal—simply assuming that universalizing is not what particularists do—we need to understand how universalism appears in our scholarship, which means understanding what the limits of particularism are, too. Ultimately, if we can admit that elements of universalism always shadow how scholars think, we can then also concede that what some scholars have called generics can sometimes help us to be better, more measured particularists. To this end, I offer the generic of friendship’s mystic affordances, to improve our empirical studies of friendship and even our coming politics. And with regard to our politics, I note in conclusion that we might also consider embracing “a” (though not “the”) mystic of friendship.

  2. Ibn Khaldûn as a Colonial Archive: Toward an Epistemic Decolonization
    Abdelmajid Hannoum · pp. 1-25 · online 2026-10-16
    摘要

    This article examines Ibn Khaldûn not as a stable, timeless precursor of modern social science but as a figure constituted through colonial translation and reception. Focusing on nineteenth- and twentieth-century French and English translations of the Muqaddimah , it argues that Ibn Khaldûn emerged in modern scholarship as a colonial archive—a site where translation, race, and epistemic authority intersected to produce new forms of historical and sociological knowledge. Through close comparison of Arabic originals and their European translations, the article shows how colonial epistemologies reconfigured Ibn Khaldûn’s analytical categories—particularly those concerning tribe, generation, civilization, and climate—into racialized frameworks foreign to his medieval context. It further demonstrates how this translated Ibn Khaldûn became selectively relevant to European social science while remaining excluded from its canonical genealogies. Finally, the article critically reassesses the enduring claim that Ibn Khaldûn articulated racist views about Black populations, showing that this attribution itself belongs to the colonial archive generated through translation rather than to the epistemic logic of the original text. The article thus contributes to comparative histories of knowledge, colonial epistemology, and the global formation of the social sciences.

  3. Borrowed Time: Sovereign Debt and Temporal Disorder In Socialist Yugoslavia
    James M Robertson · pp. 1-22 · online 2026-10-15
    摘要

    When Francis Fukuyama described the collapse of state socialism as marking the “end of history,” he captured the imagination of the post-Cold War moment, rendering the fall of the Berlin Wall a metonym for the definitive eclipse of communism and the advent of a new era of liberal capitalist hegemony. For Europe’s Left, the term became associated with a moment of profound demoralization. Fukuyama’s end of history, however, was only one moment of a longer and more expansive crisis in the socialist order of time. This crisis can be traced back to the global economic upheavals of the 1970s that impacted both social democracy in the West and state socialism in the East. A decade before crowds forced their way across a divided Berlin, socialism on both sides of the Iron Curtain had entered an existential decline. This article argues that the sovereign debt crises that beset European states in the final decade of the Cold War disrupted socialism’s regime of historicity. It develops this argument with reference to late-socialist Yugoslavia and demonstrates how the temporal conditions of sovereign indebtedness shaped popular culture. Through a reading of the films Balkanski špijun (1984) and Već viđeno (1987), the article argues that the erosion of socialism’s horizons of expectation fostered a new experience of historical time in which the past returned in uncanny, troubling, and ultimately destructive ways.

  4. Nazi Views on Race and Genocide in Australia: A Comparative and Contrastive Approach
    Matthew P. Fitzpatrick · pp. 1-26 · online 2026-10-15
    摘要

    Via an examination of comparative approaches to radically violent societies such as Nazi Germany and colonial Australia, this article investigates how German representations of Australian state racism shed light on the similarities and differences between the Holocaust and frontier violence in Australia. Indicative of these German views, it suggests, were those of government officials like Rudolf Asmis, who frequently wrote and spoke on the question of radical violence against Indigenous people in Australia against the backdrop of increasing antisemitic violence in Germany that culminated in the Holocaust. Assessing the position of Australia in Nazi views on the racial state, it suggests that there are important differences between settler colonial violence and the Holocaust that can only be uncovered through comparative historical method.

  5. Culture and Contradiction Before the End of History: From Socialist Legacies to Market Logics
    Petrică Mogoș · pp. 1-27 · online 2026-10-14
    摘要

    In late-socialist Romania, the state sought to govern economic crisis by demanding market-like conduct from cultural institutions while continuing to bind them to the political structures of socialism. Drawing on archival planning reports, media accounts, and post-socialist recollections, this article traces the emergence of a “self-financing regime” that reorganized cultural production around revenue generation, entrepreneurial conduct, and managerial accountability. I argue that self-financing constituted neither a retreat of socialism nor an incipient transition to capitalism, but an experiment in governing crisis by relocating the burdens of economic survival onto institutions themselves. This shift generated a contradictory institutional world: cultural actors were compelled to pursue economic self-sufficiency and become self-optimizing subjects even as markets remained ideologically repudiated, socialist obligations endured, and nominal decentralization extended bureaucratic oversight. Yet contradiction did not simply signal the incoherence of late socialism. As these tensions became embedded in everyday institutional practice, contradiction provided the very means through which austerity was rendered governable. The Romanian case thus shows how market-like rationalities could emerge from within socialist crisis management and crystallize into historically distinct forms of governance. By situating these entanglements before the so-called “end of history,” the article unsettles teleological narratives of socialist-capitalist rupture and reconsiders crisis as a historically contingent site where seemingly opposed political-economic logics can be made and remade in practice.

  6. A View from the Italian Side: Transit Migrants from the Soviet Union in Italy during the 1970s and 1980s
    Denis Kozlov · pp. 1-25 · online 2026-10-02
    摘要

    During the 1970s and 1980s, thousands of migrants from the Soviet Union transited through Italian territory. Awaiting Western immigrant visas, people spent weeks or months in the maritime periphery of Rome. Based on Italian archival evidence, the article discusses how this migration was perceived in Italy. The article interprets the ex-Soviet transit as an integral part of the broader migrations that crossed Europe during the second half of the twentieth century. Within the Italian context, I inscribe the transit in the tectonic shift from emigration to immigration that Italy underwent from the 1970s onward. Scholars have commented on how slowly Italian government policies and legislation came to appreciate the country’s changing migration landscape. This article goes further by connecting high-level politics to the situation on the ground—in the localities where people from the Soviet Union stayed—and shows how ordinary Italians confronted the new migratory reality face to face. Although the former Soviet citizens were transit migrants rather than immigrants proper, the challenges they faced had much in common with those encountered by many immigrants from other countries. In that sense, the reception of the ex-Soviets not only revealed the extent to which Italian society was (un)prepared for these new population dynamics but also offered an instructive preview of the larger, more bitterly contested migrations that awaited Italy and the rest of the Western world.

  1. Ideology, Memory, and Silence: Thai Studies under Cold War Historiography in China
    Cui Feng · pp. 369-388 · online 2026-02-04
    摘要

    Between the 1950s and 1970s, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) maintained contact and cooperation with the Communist Party of Thailand (CPT) through multiple channels. The CPT received material support, political training, and ideological guidance from China, particularly from bases in Yunnan Province. Using the development of Thai Studies in China as a case study, this article examines how Chinese academia has engaged with—or avoided—the Cold War history of Thailand. Through a critical review of the field, it identifies structural tensions shaped by political sensitivity and institutional constraints, situating these dynamics within the broader context of Southeast Asian studies. Such constraints influence topic selection, access to sources, and publication practices, resulting in a field characterized by narrowed perspectives, uneven critical engagement, and structurally constrained academic autonomy. In this sense, Thai Studies in China reflects a paradoxical trajectory in which the field has been repeatedly shaped, disrupted, and revived by shifting political imperatives rather than by autonomous scholarly inquiry.

  2. Learning in (Re)Production: Spare-time Learning and the Reproduction of Gendered Labor in Socialist China
    Changwen Chen · pp. 389-414 · online 2026-03-15
    摘要

    This article examines spare-time learning (yèyú xuéxí) in socialist China as a form of labor-mediated pedagogical governance that expanded women’s access to education while simultaneously reproducing gendered divisions of labor. Drawing on archival materials from Shaanxi Province, I trace how spare-time learning was organized across urban industrial and rural agricultural settings, showing that it constituted an ambitious effort to democratize intellectual authority by locating knowledge production within collective labor practice. Yet the capacity of spare-time learning to serve as an equalizing institution was unevenly structured across institutional contexts. I introduce the concept of a “gendered mobility loop” to specify the mechanisms through which the gendered division of labor was continually reconstituted within socialist pedagogy. By tracing shifts from early literacy campaigns to increasingly moralized political training, I argue that women’s double burden was not merely a residual legacy of tradition or an effect of incomplete implementation but was continually reconstituted through pedagogical arrangements embedded in production regimes. Reconceptualizing spare-time learning as a site of ideological reproduction embedded in production, this article contributes to feminist scholarship on social reproduction under socialism and to Marxist cultural studies of the education–labor nexus.

  3. Hidden Smoke: Air Pollution, Agrarian Change, and Governance Gaps in Luang Prabang, Laos
    Danny Marks, Ian G. Baird · pp. 415-437 · online 2026-04-21
    摘要

    Air pollution has emerged as a major public health and economic threat in Southeast Asia, yet Laos has received limited attention in scholarly and policy debates despite significant mortality and economic losses. This article analyses the drivers, lived experiences, and governance of air pollution in Luang Prabang, Laos’ premier tourist destination and a UNESCO World Heritage city. Drawing on semi-structured interviews, field observations, and satellite data, our findings challenge dominant policy narratives that attribute haze primarily to traditional swidden cultivation. Instead, commercial agrarian change, particularly cassava expansion, grass cultivation, and cattle pasture expansion linked to regional and Chinese cattle demand and a prolonged urban landfill fire, drove air pollution in 2023. These sources stem from labor shortages, economic insecurity, poor urban waste planning, and a reliance on fire as a low-cost management tool. Despite significant health, livelihood, and tourism impacts, haze remains underappreciated and underfunded. Weak monitoring infrastructure, fragmented institutional responsibilities, and the absence of disaggregated health data render air pollution uncertain and socially normalized. The article argues that air pollution in Luang Prabang represents a form of slow violence, maintained by epistemic gaps and administrative silence within a development model that prioritizes expanded agriculture and tourism over environmental protection.

  4. Telling What was not Told: Acehnese Women’s Narratives of Conflict and the Tsunami
    Alfi Rahman, Rizanna Rosemary, Safrina, Norma Susanti, Syahrul Ridha, Siti Ghaisani Mastura et al. · pp. 438-458 · online 2026-04-24
    摘要

    This study investigates how Acehnese women experience, remember, and transmit narratives about prolonged armed conflict and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. In-depth interviews were conducted with women across two generational categories: those who had directly experienced these events (experiential narrators) and those who have learned the stories through familial or community transmission (post-memory narrators). The study situates narratives as a social practice, exploring how women’s experiences, survival, and resilience are interpreted, negotiated, and passed on. The study reveals a striking divergence in how these two crises are remembered and narrated. The tsunami, often seen as a divine test, has been spiritualized, moralized, and publicly commemorated through museums, school drills, and religious discourse. This structured and didactic form of storytelling fosters intergenerational compassion and preparedness. In contrast, conflict memories are fraught with moral complexity, silence, and fear. These narratives, often fragmented, emotionally restrained, and selectively told, have been shaped by past surveillance, suspicion, and unresolved trauma. The study underscores the importance of integrating women-centered approaches into post-disaster and post-conflict recovery. It also shows how the recognition and protection of women’s voices is vital to understanding long-term resilience, collective memory, and processes of social repair.

  5. Technocratic Turn: Authoritarianism, Global Capitalism, and Cambodia’s State Transformation since 2013
    Kimhean Hok · pp. 459-479 · online 2026-04-15
    摘要

    Scholars have characterized Cambodia as a weak state, strong party governance system in which administrative institutions are subordinated to the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP). This article argues that since 2013 Cambodian governance has taken a significant technocratic turn, as party rule has become increasingly dependent on a stronger and more capable administrative state. It traces a reform pattern involving selective creation and upgrading of institutional nodes that expand overall state administrative capacity without disrupting the party-political order. Through three cases — the transformation of the National Bank of Cambodia through the Bakong digital payment system, the restructuring of public–private partnership frameworks to fund the Techo International Airport, and the creation of executive-linked agencies such as the Techo Startup Center — the article shows how new centers of administrative capacity have emerged and been positioned at the core of the state’s developmental agenda. These institutions have enhanced the party-state’s capacity to mobilize revenue, coordinate and develop mega infrastructures, and formalize the economy, producing a more capable but still party-embedded state. The Cambodian case illustrates a particular trajectory within broader contemporary developmental state-making under global capitalism, in which strengthened administrative states and political authoritarianism are mutually reinforcing.

  6. The Making of an Indian Company Town: Manufactured Cosmopolitanism, Communal Violence, and Urban Memory in Jamshedpur, India
    Isha Dubey · pp. 480-504 · online 2026-06-13
    摘要

    In 1907, after months of prospecting across India, the little-known and remote hamlet of Sakchi in Singhbhum was chosen by Jamshetji Nusserwanji Tata (1839-1904), founder of the Tata Group, as the location for India’s first indigenously owned iron and steel works. This paper examines the construction of an institutional cultural memory of what would become the planned city of Jamshedpur as an integral part of India’s industrial heritage, steeped in ideas of progress, modernity and cosmopolitanism. The article juxtaposes this cultural memory with the lived experiences and memories of Jamshedpur inhabitants who have witnessed its transformation in response to and beyond the institutional narrative of the ideal steel city. Finally, the article discusses the immediate and long-term impacts of communal riots in 1964 and 1979 and the ways in which this violence is remembered or forgotten. In doing so, the article argues that public and private histories and memories of Jamshedpur intersect, overlap, and negotiate with each other in ways that complicate and contradict a carefully cultivated discourse of model industrial urbanism that has been erected on a foundation of manufactured cosmopolitanism.

    This article examines how Pakistan's local government gender quota policy, aimed at improving women's political representation, has been undermined by entrenched patriarchal structures in rural Punjab. Based on longitudinal ethnographic research, including fieldwork conducted in 2005-2006 and 2019, with follow-up observations in 2024, the study highlights the problem of proxy representation. In this scenario, elected women often act as figurehead councilors while their male relatives wield actual decision-making power. The analysis indicates that the apparent increase in female representation often amounts to mere symbolic inclusion, offering little genuine empowerment for women. By drawing on feminist theories of representation and agency, along with concepts of patriarchal bargains and a governmentality perspective, the article argues that state-led “empowerment” reforms can be co-opted and reshaped by local kinship norms concerning honor and authority. In practice, rather than fundamentally disrupting male dominance, Pakistan’s gender quota has largely been transformed into a new form of patriarchy—one that maintains male control while creating a façade of female representation. These findings contribute to discussions on feminist governance by illustrating that efforts to democratize gender relations must confront deeply entrenched social structures.

    Unang Uday · pp. 529-551 · online 2026-05-18
    摘要

    When I applied for Truku Indigenous status in 2022, I discovered that my mother had never been officially registered as Indigenous in Taiwan and my application was therefore denied. Only through an arduous bureaucratic process was I able to obtain state recognition of my Truku Indigenous identity. This experience led me to ask what epistemic and ideological foundations structure Taiwan’s Indigenous Peoples Status Act (IPSA). Drawing on narrative inquiry and combining autoethnographic reflection with legal and policy analysis, this article identifies two ideologies underlying the Act: post-colonial dossierism and patriarchal governance. Taiwan’s recognition regime privileges colonial archives over Indigenous self-determination while operating through patriarchal norms of descent and identity transmission. This study contributes to the literature on postcolonialism in two ways. First, it identifies dossierism and patriarchal governance as mechanisms through which colonial epistemology is reproduced in law. Second, it shows that once colonially produced documents are codified as mandatory state law, it legitimized the colonial way of seeing and, in turn, shapes how colonized subjects come to understand themselves.

  1. Indigenous Communities and Development: The Mising People and Dam Construction in Assam, India
    Pranab Kumar Pegu, Vasundhara Jairath · pp. 1-19 · online 2026-10-17
    摘要

    Much of the early literature on dams and Indigenous peoples focused on resistance and organized opposition to the projects, with an emphasis on threats to Indigenous life ways, sustainability, and their roles as custodians of nature. This article examines how Indigenous people in one community in Northeast India engage with a development project that dispossesses them, provoking opposition to the project, while also offering opportunities to enter the market economy and earn higher incomes. It discusses the case of the Subansiri Lower Hydro Electric Project (SLHEP) in Assam. The article argues that what appears to be a contradiction in how people respond to this project reflects a more complex response to the set of changes brought about by a growing neoliberal order and the place that Indigenous working people find themselves in. This is marked by the rapid erosion of the material life worlds of Indigenous peoples and a growing dependence on market interactions for meeting most basic needs, alongside growing aspirations and the precarity brought on by a crisis of social reproduction.

  2. Under Construction: Frontier Infrastructure in Northeast India
    Debasish Hazarika · pp. 1-21 · online 2026-10-17
    摘要

    This article investigates encounters between infrastructure projects and Indigenous communities in Northeast India. Focusing on two projects by the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation in the Dollungmukh region of Arunachal Pradesh, namely the Subansiri Lower Hydroelectric Project (SLHEP) and a Nyder Namlo (prayer hall), it shows how a large-scale, long-drawn-out construction process has become the turf for intense encounters between local communities, the state, and infrastructural technologies. Based on ethnographic fieldwork, the article demonstrates how the construction of the SLHEP, one of India’s largest dams, has reshaped the local political economy, aspirations, and social relations. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in 2012–2013 and 2024 in parts of the Amdo region of Tibet (now part of Qinghai and Gansu Provinces), this article examines how education policies and practices are mobilized discursively as technical, practical, and non-political, while simultaneously extending state power into the everyday lives of rural Tibetans with cross-generational disciplinary effects.     This article examines the Esperanto movement within the Thai Chinese community during the 1930s as a prism through which to explore the early formation of leftist internationalism in Thailand. Drawing on a diverse corpus of primary sources, this study reconstructs how a small but committed group of intellectuals mobilized Esperanto as both a practical tool for transnational communication and a symbolic vehicle for articulating a vision of leftist internationalism grounded in the specific realities of China’s anti-Japanese resistance. The article argues that the Esperanto movement was a transnational leftist cultural network that mediated the interplay between internationalism, nationalism, and communism—three forces that collectively shaped the political consciousness of Thai Chinese. While ultimately crushed by the rise of Thai state nationalism under the Phibun Songkhram regime, the movement’s radical ideas and networks survived through clandestine channels.     Mohamad Muzammil · pp. 1-26 · online 2026-08-10
    摘要

    This article examines how Malaysia’s Democratic Action Party (DAP) has been discursively constructed as a political adversary by rival Malay-Muslim political parties and nationalist actors in post-2018 Malaysia. Moving beyond static narratives of ethnic politics, it argues that portrayals of the DAP as a threat to Malay-Muslim interests do not reflect a fixed ideological order, but rather emerge from ongoing struggles over meaning, legitimacy, and political power. Drawing on a qualitative analysis of political speeches, media narratives, and digital discourse between 2018 and 2025, the article demonstrates how fear operates as a central mechanism in shaping political perceptions and mobilizing support. Rather than indicating a unified Malay response, these narratives are received unevenly across class, generational, and ideological lines, thereby revealing significant internal contestations. By focusing on political discourse, the article examines how political fear operates in practice. Focusing especially on the Cultural Revolution period, it traces the emergence of Maoism in the city-state to texts and ideas from the People’s Republic of China that circulated widely within left-wing circles in Singapore starting in the 1950s, as well as to the three years after Coldstore, when Maoism came to dominate public leftist discourse and practice in Singapore. The article intervenes in the historiography of global Maoism by triangulating between the work of orthodox scholars such as Yinghong Cheng and recent, left-historical interpretations by the likes of Matthew Galway and Fabio Lanza. By focusing on the increasingly extremist Barisan and its Maoist critics such as the student activist Li Xiquan, it shows, contrary to orthodox analyses, that Maoism in Singapore cannot be reduced to a purely foreign ideology, and was, rather, underpinned by the Barisan and its critics’ shared commitment to Malaya as an anticolonial project and adaptation of Maoism to fit local circumstances. Maoists were likewise capable of critical self-reflection, as left-historical scholarship contends and the example of Li Xiquan suggests. Yet, such scholarship fails to capture how fanaticism, mimicry, and emotion were constitutive of Maoist experiences in Singapore, and indeed how ideological commitments evolved over time in ways that underscore these aspects of Singapore Maoism.

  4. Toward Divergence: Social Trends in Tomb Epitaphs During Liao, Song, and Jin China
    Ya-Hwei Hsu 許雅惠 · pp. 1-42
    摘要

    This study presents a comprehensive view of middle-period China by focusing on excavated epitaphs from Liao, Song, and Jin tombs. It systematically examines the social backgrounds of epitaph users, compares their compositions across dynasties, and delineates societal trends in North and South China. Although the stratum of officials dominated the use of epitaphs across all dynasties, the overall social composition of epitaph users reveals divergences between northern and southern dynasties. The Liao displayed the strongest aristocratic traits, with a remarkable proportion of epitaphs belonging to upper-level Khitan nobles. The Northern Song exhibited meritocratic characteristics, with a considerable number of epitaphs belonging to scholar-officials and shi 士 literati. It also featured the most diverse backgrounds among non-literati elite users, some of whom were expressive in their epitaphs, suggesting a lively local society. The destructive wars of the early twelfth century deepened the North-South divide. In the North, under the Jin, Jurchen and Han Chinese elites turned away from the use of epitaphs. In the Southern Song, the literati predominated among burials with epitaphs, while non-literati elites became more silent compared to their Northern Song predecessors. Many new types of epitaphs emerged in the southeastern region, where Neo-Confucianism flourished. These may have served as a means for Neo-Confucians to express their intellectual identity. The variety of these epitaphs further signaled growing internal differentiation among literati users. This macro-level comparative research of excavated epitaphs illuminates the distinctive characteristics of each society, traces long-term developments, and offers explanations for these changes. 摘要: 南北對峙的遼、宋、金是中古向近世中國轉變的關鍵時期。本研究全 面收集遼、宋、金出土墓誌，以統計方法分析其使用者，宏觀呈現各朝上層 菁英在「死後世界」的組成與差異。本文發現，各朝墓誌的主要使用者都是官 吏，但整體的使用者身份組成有明顯南、北差異。遼代集中於契丹貴族，北 宋多為地方菁英。南、北差異隨宋金戰爭而擴大。金代隨葬墓誌的上層菁英遽 減，女真貴族亦罕用墓誌。南宋墓誌的隨葬增加，且更集中在官吏與士人， 東南地區亦出現許多新型態的墓誌，推測與理學興起有關。從跨越朝代與 國別的出土墓誌可見南、北社會的特點與發展。

  5. Slavery and Zhang Dai’s Aesthetics
    Tina Lu 呂立亭 · pp. 43-70
    摘要

    This article argues that the celebrated aesthetics of Tao’an mengyi 陶庵夢憶 by Zhang Dai 張岱 (1597–1689) are inseparable from the system of bonded labor that structured late-imperial Chinese elite culture. Often read as exemplary memory writing, the collection constructs an aesthetic centered on spectacle, surface, and perceptual disorientation. I argue that this aesthetic both depends on and obscures a pervasive system of human commodification, which I approach through the analytic lens of slavery. Drawing on recent scholarship that emphasizes the ubiquity of trafficking, the article shifts focus from defining enslaved populations to examining a broader system of social transactionality. Readings of essays on theater, visual display, and elite sociability show how aesthetic effects rely on the precise coordination—and erasure—of labor. Zhang Dai’s fascination with illusion and perfect staging reflects and reproduces a world structured by mastery over others. At moments, especially in depictions of sex work, this aesthetic distance becomes unstable, revealing underlying tensions. Ultimately, Tao’an mengyi not only represents but enacts an aesthetics of control, inviting readers to participate in transforming domination into aesthetic pleasure. 摘要: 本文主張，張岱之《陶庵夢憶》的美學與晚期帝制中國之依附性勞動體 制密不可分。其審美以奇觀、表面與感知錯置為核心，既奠基於亦遮蔽人身 商品化，本文以「奴隸制」作為分析概念。透過細讀戲曲、展示與社交場景，指 出審美效果依賴對勞動的精密調度並將其抹除，從而再生產支配他人的社 會結構。部分涉及性交易之描寫亦顯露出內在張力。總之，《陶庵夢憶》不 僅再現，亦實踐一種將支配轉化為審美愉悅的控制美學。

  6. Learning to Hear: Evidential Scholarship and the Ancient Song in High Qing China
    Matthew Wild 韋邁 · pp. 71-108
    摘要

    This article examines the power of song within the High Qing phil-ological movement known as evidential scholarship ( kaozheng xue 考證學). Focusing on the celebrated poet Huang Jingren 黃景仁 (1749–1783) and his association with the influential evidential scholar Zhu Yun 朱筠 (1729–1781) during Zhu’s tenure as education commissioner of Anhui Province, it challenges modern accounts that oppose lyric subjectivity to philological inquiry. I argue that prevailing understandings of both High Qing literature and scholarship fail to apprehend the integral connection between poetic and evidentiary practices in the period. For Qing writers such as Huang and Zhu, the idea of song afforded not merely aesthetic expression but a medium of self-evident, apodictic proof. Close readings of key episodes show how this claim to truth functioned as a nexus of shared immanence wherein writing presents itself as singing and reading unfolds as an act of present listening. By attending to this regime of “notional song,” the study reframes evidential scholarship not as a protoscientific divergence from the poetic but as a culture in which sound, citation, and proof were mutually constitutive. 摘要: 本文探討「歌」在清代盛世考證學語境中的作用。以詩人黃景仁 (1749–1783)及其與朱筠(1729–1781)在安徽學政任內的交往為線索，本 文重新審視近 現代將抒情的內在性對立與考證學術的敘述框架。作者指出，廣為流傳的 對清代文學與學術實踐的論述，往往忽略了詩歌作與考證學之間的內在聯 繫。對黃景仁與朱筠等人而言，「歌」不僅用於審美表達,更發揮著一種自證 自明的媒介作用。本文透過對「歌」的若干關鍵場景的細讀來說明，詩歌的 真理主張是在一種共享的臨在經驗中展開的——書寫在此呈現為歌唱，閱 讀則成為當下的聆聽。從「意念之歌」的角度出發，本文主張考證學不應被 理解為與詩性深具分歧的前科學，而應被納入一種能使聲音、引證與證成彼 此交織、相互生成的文化框架之中。

Vol. 63, No. 3 · 2026-09 · 8 篇 · SAGE · South Asian history · Peer-reviewed
  1. Viewing the world from the Karnatak: Place and caste in Kannada and Persian warrior narratives in the long eighteenth century
    Subah Dayal, Naveen Kanalu · pp. 301-328 · online 2026-07-19
    摘要

    To commemorate the 25th anniversary of the publication of Textures of Time (2001), this article returns to the question of ‘history’ in South Asia. It counterposes two unlikely suspects: textual traditions in Persian and Kannada—tārīkh and campū kāvya, respectively—from the Karnatak region of southern India to show how caste concerns, specifically of warrior groups, shaped literary production in the late eighteenth century. It puts into dialogue genres from the literary cultures of these two languages that had a continuous set of conventions and themes since at least the medieval period. The two texts we analyse are Munshi Muhammad ‘Azimuddin’s Tārīkh-i Dilīrjangī (The Chronicle of Dilir Jang, completed ca. 1839), which was produced for the Miyana Afghan Nawabs of Savanur at the time when many such little kingdoms were increasingly beholden to the authority of the English East India Company, and Linganna’s Keḷadinṛpavijayaṃ (The Victory of the Kings of Keladi, ca. 1762–1804), written during or after the dissolution of the nāyaka kingdom of Keladi. Written from geographic zones located at the interstices of multiple political formations, both texts offer sites for intertextual readings of the intersecting social domains of elite martial groups and the literary cultures they fostered. Specifically, we pay close attention to parallel ways of narration and modes of recording contemporary politics, and build upon previous attempts to compare a regional vernacular like Kannada with transregional, imperial Persian. The article demonstrates how texts from two putatively different literary traditions show features of continuity in their respective genres while sharing concerns about the region, political genealogy and caste. The article makes the case for why the two texts—and by extension, the two literary traditions they are thought to be representing—should be seen as intertextually related, rather than dissimilar. In doing so, it opens up fresh avenues for historicising the region by questioning the long-standing practice of associating a region with a monolingual literary tradition.

  2. Reading the realm: Divination, warfare and political authority in the Ahom kingdom
    Ronit Konch · pp. 329-367 · online 2026-07-12
    摘要

    This article analyses the impact of divination on political decision-making and warfare in the Ahom kingdom of Northeastern India. It identifies two principal state-sponsored mantic specialists: Ahom priests who relied on osteomancy (bone-divination), a practice traceable to Chinese cultural traditions; and daivajnas, a caste group in the Ahom kingdom, who utilised astrological knowledge derived from northern India. The Brahmaputra Valley became a site of ritual contestation as these traditions vied for royal patronage. The article traces the brahmanisation of Ahom polity reflected in the ascendancy of the daivajnas at the Ahom court. The study contributes to the scholarship on ritual power and state formation in pre-modern South Asia. Drawing on mythological, historical and ethnographic data, the article argues that divinatory praxis held greater importance in the kingdom’s political and social processes than hitherto recognised. The study situates dreams and omens within their socio-religious milieu, while emphasising their centrality in political decision-making. In military contexts, diviners were integrated into the army hierarchy, advising on strategic appointments and battlefield tactics. Their pronouncements could induce shifts in political allegiance, compelling the state to regulate their activities. Given the weight attached to and high stakes associated with the divinations, mantic practitioners faced risks of punishment as well as the lure of rewards, intensifying the contestations between mantic and religious traditions.

  3. Regimental prostitution in provincial cantonment: A case study of chaklas, lock hospitals and colonial governance in Faizabad
    Richa Singh, Preeti Sharma · pp. 369-390 · online 2026-07-31
    摘要

    The article studies the regulation of regimental prostitution during the nineteenth century in Faizabad, a small provincial cantonment town in northern India that has garnered little attention in the existing scholarship. While the literature on colonial prostitution stressed the centrality of medical surveillance, spatial segregation and moral discipline in major colonial port towns, this article employs Michel Foucault’s concept of governmentality, Radhika Singha’s notion of delegated authority, and Mark Condos’ view of uncertain sovereignty to examine the everyday administrative practices rather than the legislative intent. Drawing on cantonment correspondence, annual lock hospital reports, statistical returns and medical officers’ observations, the article reconstructs how prostitution was organised, supervised and rendered administratively visible in Faizabad. The study foregrounds the primary role of native intermediaries like mahaldarnis, dhais and darogas, whose indigenous knowledge and labour translated legislative intent into practice. Additionally, the article illustrates the negotiated, uneven and eventually fragile aspects of colonial regulation of regimental prostitution in the small cantonment town of Faizabad, challenging historiographical assumptions about coherence and efficiency of colonial regulatory governance.

  4. Faraway futures: Life insurance and the human lifespan as a commercial time-horizon in colonial India
    Poorva Rajaram · pp. 391-415 · online 2026-07-27
    摘要

    This article focuses on the processes, practices and discourses that led to the creation of the uneven and unstable market for life insurance from the 1880s to 1950 in India. It is particularly interested in the concrete ways in which commercial futures had to be lengthened to almost unthinkably long spans of time to make life insurance for Indians seem plausible and viable to both subscribers and companies. The lengthening of commercial futures to approximate better to the human lifespan was a complex and, in some ways, difficult process, heavily influenced by its location in a colonial setting where credible information on subscribers was scarce. This article argues that life insurance could overcome the shorter timescales of commercial life in colonial India only by placing very careful restrictions on who or what could be designated as a legitimate subscriber or insurance company. In effect, urban professionals became the de facto subjects of life insurance in colonial India. The peculiar tension of life insurance in colonial India was the extended futurity embedded in the financial form along with the lack of desire shown in the same futurity by many potential subscribers and smaller companies. This meant that the macro-historical processes of ‘taming chance’ or ‘disciplining the future’ in colonial India were effectively restricted to small pockets of the economy and society.

    Charu Gupta · pp. 420-422 · online 2026-07-06
    摘要

    Aakriti Mandhwani's Everyday Reading is an elegantly written contribution to a growing scholarship on print culture, reading practices and social history of Hindi in twentieth-century India.Focusing on the two decades after independence, Mandhwani reconstructs the vibrant world of Hindi middlebrow magazines and paperback publishing through a close study of Sarita, Dharmyug, Hind Pocket Books and genre magazines such as Maya and Manohar Kahaniyan.The result is not merely a history of publishing.It is also a history of aspiration, consumption, domesticity and the changing textures of middle-class life in north India.The 1950s and 1960s in India were marked by contradictory energies: trauma of Partition, shortages and inflation, building of democratic institutions and emergence of new middle-class aspirations.Historiography on this period has largely focused on nationalism, Nehruvian planning, constitutional debates and Partition.Mandhwani intervenes by shifting attention to everyday reading practices.Her central argument is persuasive, that is, commercially successful Hindi magazines and paperbacks fostered new forms of reading, pleasure and selfhood that cannot be understood solely through the framework of nationalist austerity and developmentalism.One of the book's strengths lies in the seriousness with which Mandhwani treats pleasure in post-independence Hindi print culture.She argues that magazines and paperbacks opened spaces where readers could imagine themselves not merely as citizens obligated to the nation, but also as consumers, desiring individuals and members of aspirational families.This is especially visible in her nuanced reading of Sarita, which fashioned itself as a magazine for the entire family, while simultaneously cultivating women as active readers and contributors through letters, adviceThe Indian Economic and Social History Review, (2026): 1-3 Sage Los Angeles/London/New Delhi/Singapore/Washington DC/Melbourne

  7. Book review: Divya Cherian, Merchants of Virtue: Hindus, Muslims, and Untouchables in Eighteenth-Century South Asia
    Akhila Mathew · pp. 422-424 · online 2026-07-06
    摘要

    Divya Cherian's bookMerchants of Virtue is a micro study of the precolonial state of Marwar in western Rajasthan.Through a detailed study of the legal archives, Cherian examines how law and state power were deployed to shape the category of 'Hindu', a process that was inextricably linked to the shaping of the 'Other', that is, groups labelled as untouchable.The book challenges the notion that the labels 'Hindu', 'Muslim' and 'Untouchable' were products of colonial modernity and makes the compelling argument that these categories can only be understood by investigating how caste shaped them.The book's strength lies in the rich eighteenth-century legal archives that it uses, which effectively display the fraught, everyday disputes and experiences that created the boundary between 'Hindu' and others.Cherian argues, in line with current scholarship on western India, that caste practices were repeatedly negotiated and altered using law.The book demonstrates the juridical jockeying by elite communities-Vaishnavs, Jains and Brahmans, in particular-to alter customary practices and reshape social and ethical norms.The author repeatedly asserts that mercantile groups leveraged their economic and political clout to achieve their objectives.They had a willing partner in this in the ruler Vijai Singh (r.1752-93).The latter took initiation into the Vallabh sampradaya in 1765, which, according to Cherian, brought him into the 'same spiritual and moral community as many merchants of Marwar' (p.27).However, the author acknowledges that the pursuit of a new ethical orientation witnessed in this period may be an exception.This requires further study, especially since later rulers shifted their patronage away from Vaishnavism. The Indian Economic and Social History Review, (2026): 1-3Sage Los Angeles/London/New Delhi/Singapore/Washington DC/Melbourne

  8. Book review: Prem Poddar and Lisa Lindkvist Zhang, Through the India–China Border: Kalimpong in the Himalayas
    Shubhanga Pandey · pp. 424-427 · online 2026-07-06
    摘要

    Two distinct, although related, portrayals have dominated the historical imagination of the eastern Himalayan town of Kalimpong.In the mid-1950s, everyone, it seemed-from Jawaharlal Nehru to his Chinese counterpart Zhou Enlai, to a French ethnologist-agreed that Kalimpong was a hotbed of espionage.Spawned in the years between Tibet's 1949 annexation and 1959 rebellion, Nehru's description of the hill station as a 'nest of spies' has indelibly coloured how Kalimpong is remembered.The other trope is that of the frontier town as a site of intercultural, inter-imperial and international encounters, a Himalayan 'contact zone' tucked between Tibet, Sikkim, Bengal and Nepal, and conveniently close to the relatively mild Jelep La pass heading to Lhasa.Kalimpong was, after all, home not just to covert operatives and 'foreign Kautilyas' (p.125), but also to merchants, missionaries, war-torn refugees and wandering émigrés.In Through the India-China Border, Prem Poddar and Lisa Lindkvist Zhang subordinate these admittedly powerful notions under the rubric of Kalimpong as an 'interface' and a 'metonym'.Drawing on Alexander Galloway's definition, the authors argue that Kalimpong is an interface, which is not simply a political or geographical zone along a transimperial and later a transnational frontier.Instead, it is a dynamic object, in this case, a threshold in the Himalayas from where to view the effects of larger international forces, which also becomes a catalyst informing such forces.One such effect is Kalimpong's emergence as a metonym: it was a convenient index for Chinese political elites to strategically assess late-colonial and independent India, as well as a measure of the China-IndiaThe Indian Economic and Social History Review, (2026): 1-3 Sage Los Angeles/London/New Delhi/Singapore/Washington DC/Melbourne

  1. Kingship and the language of ecology in early medieval Tamil̄akam, 500–800 ce
    Nishant Singh · online 2026-10-22
    摘要

    This essay studies the manner in which the Pallavas of Kān͂cīpuram, the dominant ruling power in the Tamil region from the seventh to ninth centuries ce, engaged with nature, ecology and the surrounding physical world to fashion a meta-language to articulate their political ideology. The eco-poetic contexts (tiṇai) in the Caṅkam poems show rich emotional and semantic associations that the early Tamils had with the natural world and landscapes. However, the physical environment was also a key point of political interest in the early medieval period, especially with the dramatic expansion of agriculture in the river valleys, construction of artificial irrigation apparatuses and the expansion of oceanic and inland trade, which provided a basis for the growing bureaucratic monarchical systems through the revenue generated. Aside from economic and military dominance, legitimation of power was a significant concern for the evolving monarchies, and this took different forms. Appropriation of semantic and cultural connotations associated with nature and ecology and their deployment in their epigraphic, literary and artistic rhetoric was one of the methods adopted by the Pallavas of Kān͂cīpuram to legitimise their rulership over the Tamil region, especially from the time of Mahendravarman I (580–630 ce ) to Nandivarman II, Pallavamalla (731–96 ce ). This essay will examine the beliefs and ideas associated with the natural world and their use in Pallava political rhetoric.

  2. Hindustan–Tibet Road and colonial interventions in Shimla Hill States
    Rakesh Kumar, Ankush Bhardwaj · online 2026-10-22
    摘要

    This article argues that the construction of the Hindustan–Tibet Road (from the 1850s) functioned not only as infrastructure but also as a strategic tool of colonial governance. It transformed the western Himalayan frontier from a flexible trans-regional exchange zone into a controlled imperial corridor. Focusing on the Shimla Hill States, the article illustrates how colonial intervention reconfigured existing trade networks, increased labour extraction through the system of begar and facilitated the appropriation of forest resources to serve imperial economic and geopolitical goals. The article demonstrates that the road was an example of colonial infrastructural power that served simultaneously as a commercial route, a military corridor and an instrument of colonial administration, enabling the British colonial state to reorganise trade, mobilise labour and consolidate frontier governance in the western Himalayas. Rather than establishing new economic structures, colonial infrastructure reorganised and regulated existing networks, thereby integrating the region into the empire’s political economy.

    Tara Puri · online 2026-10-21
    摘要

    Priyasha Mukhopadhyay'sRequired Reading asks us to reconsider both what we understand as an archive as well as what we understand as reading.Focusing on the writing that was circulated in the British Empire, the author argues that it is impossible to separate the book-as-object and the book-as-text (p.3), or indeed differentiate between a literary text and a more mundane, official, officious, bureaucratic document.Both are so deeply embedded in colonial networks of production and circulation that they are equally part of what she terms the 'functional archive'.This is an inventive, capacious term that allows the book to contain close studies of military handbooks, account books, petitions, letters, governmental records, panjika (a Bengali Hindu almanac) and a women's magazine, alongside writing by Rudyard Kipling, Leonard Woolf, Krupabai Satthianadhan and Rabindranath Tagore.This functional archive highlights how the 'contact zone' between the British and South Asians was instituted through everyday forms of writing that were not just produced by agents of colonial power but also by their subjects who composed their own reading material as printing technologies became cheaper and more widely available in this period (Mary Louise Pratt, Imperial Eyes: Travel Writing and Transculturation, London, 1992).What holds this archive together is not the genre, or the target audience, or the intention of this material, but rather the opposite: 'the functional archive was always an archive-in-process, expanding and buckling-but never collapsing-under the weight of added texts' (p.10).The 'functional' here is tentacular, suggesting the practical, the operational, the mobile and flexible, the often incompetent but still serviceable aspects of this assortment of texts.In this, Mukhopadhyay's approach and methodology build on recent scholarship that has highlighted the uneven and contingent nature of the imperial

  7. An appraisal of the lallup system in pre-colonial Manipur
    Yaruipam Muivah · online 2026-10-19
    摘要

    This article re-examines the lallup system of compulsory labour in Manipur before the establishment of British colonial administration (1892), challenging its conventional portrayal as both an ancient institution originating under King Pakhangba or King Loiyumba and as the backbone of the state economy. While not dismissing the possibility of its earlier origins (before the seventeenth century), the article argues that the textual and archival evidence commonly cited in support of these claims remains inconclusive. It further contends that framing lallup as the backbone of the pre-colonial economy obscures the contributions of women, ‘lower’ caste and class groups, and hill communities. By foregrounding the exclusions, the article shows how post-colonial historiography has reproduced caste, gendered and spatial hierarchies in the interpretation of Manipur’s past. It concludes by calling for a more inclusive and empirically grounded framework for understanding labour and state formation in pre-colonial Northeast India.

  8. The Scheduled Castes, late colonial constitutional reform and the ghost of the ‘Gait Circular’
    Ian Duncan · online 2026-10-15
    摘要

    The Gait Circular, issued as part of the preparations for the Census of India in 1911, was an enquiry into the possibility of determining the numbers belonging to caste groups who were not considered ‘proper’ Hindus. It caused a commotion and, following widespread protests, it was abruptly withdrawn. However, it left a deep and enduring apprehension in the administration about attempts to categorise caste groups according to their degree of adherence to Hindu social norms or religious practices. Representatives of potentially affected caste groups also became vigilant about any moves the colonial power was perceived to be making towards the use of ‘untouchability’ as a determining factor in the schema of official classification. The reform enquiries of the late 1920s and 1930s revived concerns about the categorisation of individual caste groups. The authorities went to great lengths to present proposals exclusively as a matter of administrative convenience intended to assist franchise reform and electoral organisation. They denied any recourse to Hinduism as the basis for decisions about the classification of castes. However, caste groups refused to accept the terms under which the reforms were presented and suspected that the ghost of Gait was haunting the proceedings. They challenged the narrative being deployed by government and insisted that untouchability was being used once again as a criterion for decisions.

  2. Popular Nanyang: re-thinking Chinese cultures in post-war Singapore and Malaya/Malaysia
    Lanjun Xu, Cheow Thia Chan · pp. 526-538 · online 2026-08-13
    摘要

    This special issue aims to rethink the significance of “popular culture” for Singapore and Malayan/Malaysian Chinese studies, and more broadly, for modern Chinese cultural studies. Located in the heart of Nanyang, Singapore and Malaya/Malaysia are well-known sites of vibrant Chinese cultural production. After World War Two, besides literature written by intellectuals, cultural forms with wider appeal have enriched the everyday lives of Chinese in the region. From large-scale publishing, to theatre, to radio broadcast, to film and television, the mix of old and new media technologies enlivened by multiple languages and Chinese dialects were entangled with complex commercial and ideological concerns. This special issue frames the resultant sociocultural formation as “Popular Nanyang,” offering a conceptual framework as well that analyse how people’s leisure preferences and ideas about regionality associated with Singapore, Malaya/Malaysia—and beyond—were animated by quotidian and translocal practices of cultural production and consumption. Collectively, the articles demonstrate how the “popular” in its varied senses of extensive reach, non-state positionality, substantial profitability, content accessibility, and contemporary resonance enabled “Nanyang” as a regional imaginary and a cultural sensibility to survive, travel, and reinvent itself across shifting political and historical contexts from the 1950s till the 1990s despite the rise of “Southeast Asia” as the favoured alternative. Advocating for a cultural history of Chinese communities composed from a grassroots perspective, the special issue harnesses the internal diversity of “Popular Nanyang” to point towards a future mode of historical analysis that recognizes the non-Chinese and non-Sinophone dimensions of mass-oriented Nanyang culture.

  3. Transborder malleability: examining popular Nanyang through film stardom
    Min Hui Yeo · pp. 539-559 · online 2026-08-05
    摘要

    What does it mean to characterise someone, something or somewhere as “Nanyang”? Whether in studies of Nanyang elite or popular cultures, the term is today frequently invoked as a shorthand for a place-based Southeast Asian Chinese identity formed predominantly through acclimatisation to, and interaction with, local cultures and environments, especially in the context of Singapore. This paper rethinks the notion of “popular Nanyang” beyond this usual paradigm through an examination of Singaporean film star Chong Sit Fong’s regional stardom in the 1950s and 1960s. Uncovering how Chong simultaneously embodied different kinds of Chinese national, local and translocal identities, this paper illustrates how the characteristic of transborder malleability, which refers to the capacity to simultaneously embody seemingly contradictory ideologies across borders, enabled Chong to attain regional film stardom during a time of geopolitical flux. This gestures towards an understanding of Nanyang Chineseness not only as place-based, but also inherently translocal and transnational, suggesting how “Nanyang” indexes a flexible modality of identity that functions across geopolitical borders during the 1950s and 1960s.

  4. Popular crossings: Lin Chen and his bifurcated editorial practice in 1950s Singapore and Malaya
    Cheow Thia Chan · pp. 560-582 · online 2026-08-14
    摘要

    This article reframes the Singapore Chinese dramatist Lin Chen’s cultural practice by explicating discrepant modes of popular cultural production and circulation in 1950s Singapore and Malaya through commercial printing. Today, Lin Chen (1919–2004) is remembered primarily as the pioneering playwright-director who shaped Singapore’s Mandarin theatre scene after the second World War. Alongside his amateur theatrical engagements, he served vocationally as an editor at the World Book Company (Shijie Shuju), one of the five major localised Chinese-language publishing houses. It is now revealed that Lin helmed both Linglong (Smart) and Wenyu Shenghuo (Culture and Amusement), two leisure magazines published contemporaneously around the mid-1950s. Whereas Smart carried salacious content, Culture and Amusement promoted “healthy arts and entertainment,” focusing on collective performing art forms. The two publications’ conflicting stances on nurturing readers’ interests placed them on opposing sides of the anti-yellow culture campaign in Singapore, which criticised the widespread societal access to prurient material. Examining the two periodicals in tandem as well as the content within Smart, this article outlines how Lin negotiated fluid ideas about the landscape of mass market publishing that spans the nature of the content, his non-state positionality as a cultural actor, the journals’ audience constituencies, and the contents’ varying degrees of contemporary resonance with the decolonising ethos in Singapore and Malaya. The inter-journal and intra-journal analyses reveal the intransparency of Chinese culture labelled as “yellow” and how the idea of the “popular”—represented through overlapping vernacular senses in Chinese—index an internally dissonant landscape of grassroots culture.

    Ying Xin Show · pp. 583-601 · online 2026-07-22
    摘要

    During the peak of the anti-yellow cultural movement in Singapore (1953–1956), Yao Zi—now recognised as a pioneering figure in postwar Sinophone Malayan literature—was criticised as a pornographic “yellow” writer. This article explores the cultural debates and phenomena of 1950s Malaya, a period of social transformation in the late colonial era shaped by ideological polarisation during the Cold War and anti-colonial nationalism. It focuses on the moral panic surrounding “yellow”—a term in which concerns surrounding sexuality and Chinese ethnicity intersect—through a historical and cultural analysis of the author Yao Zi’s literary and editorial works. It situates them within broader debates about yellow literature, demonstrating the ways sexuality, ethnicity, and womanhood were constructed as moral categories of social engagement within the Cold War-era battlegrounds of modernity and decolonisation. The first section of this article reexamines the anti-yellow cultural movement and its associated moral discourse by introducing Yao and his conceptualisation of popular literature in Nanyang, showing how they challenged ideological binaries and gender norms during the cultural Cold War. The second section shifts to another dimension of yellow panic: its intersections with Chinese identity and gender. Focusing on the romance genre that secured Yao’s literary prominence, it analyses his lesser-known novella The Storm (1954) for its depiction of women's narrative presence and the Chinese experience of gendered modernity in Malaya, an experience conditioned by a cultural nationalism uneasy with hybridity.

    Li Wen Jessica Tan · pp. 602-617 · online 2026-08-10
