Existing scholarship has largely focused on his editorial advocacy for Malayanisation and modern Mahua literature within a Cold War framework, while less attention has been paid to his fiction, which draws more heavily on melodramatic than modernist aesthetics. This article examines Huang’s best-selling romance Wisteria (1960) through the lens of the “Cold War middlebrow,” understood here as a contingent literary formation that served sociocultural, sentimental, and pedagogical functions during a period of polarised ideologies. By analysing Wisteria’s adaptation of the melodramatic mode for a local readership, this article offers a reassessment of what constitutes the “popular” in Mahua literature, showing how Huang’s fiction engaged questions of taste, value, and affect within a rapidly changing decolonising milieu. Through the subversion of melodrama’s Manichean binaries and the reconfiguration of the relationship between modernism and the middlebrow, Huang demonstrates a self-conscious effort to balance accessibility with aesthetic ambition. Situating Wisteria within the intersecting contexts of Cold War cultural politics and inter-Asian literary networks connecting Hong Kong and Malaya, this article highlights how popular Mahua literature participated in the circulation of cultural influences and the forging of new national identities, thereby expanding critical understandings of both “literary value” and the “popular” within the Mahua canon.

Revisiting a canonical text by Miao Xiu, Singapore under the Roofs (1951), which is set in Singapore on the cusp of decolonisation, this article examines the left-leaning realist camp’s engagement with a plurilingual and transnational public sphere where different forms of popular culture—some profit-driven, others politically oriented—competed for resources and audiences. The story’s incorporation of non-Mandarin Chinese languages and non-standard linguistic registers draws attention to how linguistic variations associated with the subaltern class mediate access to their subjectivity. In seeking to broaden the scope of current discussions of the language question beyond the conventional framing of the state’s ideology of language in Singapore, the analysis here refutes the technological determinism inherent in excluding literature in print from popular culture simply because its medium of production has been overtaken by “newer” technologies.

  8. Nanyang popular culture on Singapore television (1963–1979)

    This essay explores the film-to-television evolution of the Nanyang popular cultural imaginary between Hong Kong and Singapore in the 1960s and 1970s. Not having the capacity to produce films or television serials, Singapore was heavily reliant on Hong Kong films to fill its airtime, and in so doing, gave the diasporic imaginary projected by films a second lease of life on television. Television was a more capacious medium than film—a wider range of popular cultural performances were featured on its variety shows. The more literary and artistic (wenyi) songs surprisingly sold as well if not better than their liuxing counterparts. Combined, television and popular music remade the Nanyang popular cultural imaginary for Singapore, as the radical left’s Malayanisation cultural vision became increasingly marginalised from the reality of Singapore’s independence and its development in the capitalistic world.

    Originating in the UK in 1928 and introduced to Singapore in 1949, the cable radio service Rediffusion gained popularity for its affordable, multi-ethnic programming. In addition to a channel featuring Tamil, Malay, and English content, Rediffusion offered a dedicated Chinese channel that included not only Mandarin programmes but also broadcasts in various Sinitic dialects such as Hokkien, Cantonese, and Teochew. This article examines Rediffusion’s role from the 1950s to the 1970s in fostering a pluralistic Sinophone community in Singapore, collaborating closely with Chinese clan associations organized around Sinitic dialect affiliations. However, this linguistic diversity diminished with the implementation of the “Speak More Mandarin, Less Dialect” policy in 1979. In compliance with the policy, Rediffusion gradually reduced and eventually phased out its dialect programmes. I interpret this shift in Rediffusion’s programming as indicative of Singapore’s increasing linguistic homogenization, despite the People’s Action Party (PAP) government’s efforts to present the nation as multicultural and multilingual. The post-independence rhetoric of fostering a multicultural society with four official languages—English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil—ironically streamlined the diverse Sinophone community into a monolithic one, with Mandarin imposed as the “official” mother tongue for all Sinophone subjects, regardless of their dialect heritage.

Emerging from networks around the anti-yellow culture movement and earlier left-leaning cultural and entertainment circles, Chong Gay recast progressive cultural ideals through the discourse of “healthy films” within an increasingly regulated media environment. Drawing on archival sources, media reports, and oral interviews, I trace how “healthy films” were redefined through the interaction of ideological commitment and commercial pressure during a period of cultural transition in Singapore. By examining film delegations and festivals in the 1980s, hybrid genres, and youth reception, I argue that Singapore became a key node in late Cold War transregional exchange, where films from Taiwan, Hong Kong, and mainland China converged and were reinterpreted. Intermediaries such as Lim promoted PRC cinema as an edifying alternative to commercial culture while sustaining cultural ties with reform-era China. Singapore thus functioned as a distribution hub and testing ground where PRC films were evaluated and adapted for Southeast Asian audiences. Although officially-sanctioned healthy films were associated with discipline and social harmony, their ambivalent reception reveals unease over the commercialisation of PRC cinema and the persistence of residual leftist sensibilities.

Historically, ethnic Chinese played an important role in the creation of “the popular,” albeit often dismissed as commercial or of low cultural value, in the plurilingual settings of their respective domiciles. Their networked production, distribution, circulation, consumption, and (e)valuation of popular culture helped substantiate the reach and bounds of “Nanyang” as geography, market, and regional imaginary. This article reclaims and repurposes the term “Greater Nanyang” to give weight to Southeast Asia, Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Macao as hubs for the multi-sited co-creation of the Popular Nanyang from the Cold War era to the end of the twentieth century. The Greater Nanyang concept highlights the historicity, materiality, politics, economies, ecologies, and cultures of localisation, meaning-making, and value creation that underpin place-, identity-, and claim-making in, across, and beyond the region. The temporal depth of Popular Nanyang also raises questions about Sinophone assumptions of the convergence of language, audience, cultural literacy, and ethnicity in the production, circulation, and consumption of popular culture.

  1. Perverted normalcy: on the cultural durability of authoritarianism
    Hilmar Farid · pp. 1-19 · online 2026-10-15
    摘要

    Authoritarianism in Indonesia persists not only through institutions and coercion, but through everyday understandings of what constitutes normal life. This article develops the concept of perverted normalcy to explain that persistence. Following a historical trajectory from Dutch colonialism through the New Order to the post-Reformasi present, it argues that unresolved violence has accumulated within social relations, shaping expectations, habits, and the limits of political imagination. Violence does not simply leave wounds in the past. It helps establish the terms on which the present is lived. The article examines how this condition took shape, survived democratic transition, and found renewed expression through digital governance. It then traces its reproduction across generations through family, education, media, and silence. These are the everyday settings in which domination becomes familiar, and its historical origins disappear from view. Perverted normalcy thus directs attention to a problem that institutional reform alone cannot resolve. Understanding authoritarian persistence across the region requires examining how histories of violence become ordinary social life, and how democratic transformation might interrupt their reproduction within the relationships and practices that organize everyday existence.

  2. “Asia” in the making: friction, relational authorship, and the pedagogy of productive discomfort in the Asia Documentary Co-Production Network: A critical autoethnography of transnational Zoom workshops, 2021–2026
    Chul Heo · pp. 1-16 · online 2026-10-06
    摘要

    This article argues that “Asia,” as a category of regional belonging, is not a precondition of transnational collaboration but a relation produced within it—assembled, incrementally and unevenly, in the friction of cross-border documentary co-production. Drawing on the Asia Documentary Co-Production Network (ADCN), a hybrid pedagogical project linking film schools across East and Southeast Asia, it reads the transcripts of monthly online meetings, rather than the finished films, as its primary text. Through a critical autoethnography written from the position of a faculty mentor and former chair, it traces friction in two directions: outward, where students raised in mutual national hostility come to reference one another laterally and so constitute the region in real time; and inward, where an encounter with another nation’s history estranges students from their own. Building a single conceptual chain from Tsing’s friction through platform mediation and radical listening to Chen’s inter-Asian referencing and critical syncretism, the article shows these concepts being enacted at the smallest scale—by undergraduates, over poor connections—and, crucially, where they fail. Against celebratory accounts of frictionless online collaboration, it insists on asymmetry: of resource, of language, and of the mentor’s power to redirect. “Asia” so understood is closer to a verb than a noun—permanently unfinished, and real in the measure of that unfinishedness.

    Fekadu Malede Abitew · pp. 1-20 · online 2026-09-28
    摘要

    This article introduces the concept of racial unlearning to examine how racism is deconstructed within micro-level Afro-Chinese interactions. Drawing on longitudinal data generated among Ethiopian traders who travel between Ethiopia and China, I situate Ethio-Chinese encounters within Bhabha’s [Bhabha, Homi K. [1994] 2004. The Location of Culture. London: Routledge] “in-between spaces”—interstitial zones of fractured hegemony in which African agency produces not merely epistemic articulation but ontological consequence, carving out deracialised social realities. In these spaces, blackness and Chineseness emerge as liminal identities that evolve towards mutual recognition through iterative processes of racial unlearning. I argue that, within localised Afro-Chinese interactions, racialisation and racial unlearning unfold as concomitant processes—a dynamic that dominant global racial discourses have failed to anticipate. This reorientation shifts analytical attention away from macro- and meso-level scholarship preoccupied with the formation of racial hierarchies, and towards blackness and Chineseness as active, lived, and relationally constituted experiences.

International Journal of Taiwan Studies

Vol. 9, No. 2 · 2026-02-04 · 11 篇 · Brill · Taiwan · Peer-reviewed
  1. Why Do We Need Taiwan Studies in the Twenty-First Century?
    Wen-chi Li · pp. 255-283
    摘要

    This article reviews scholarly literature related to Taiwan from the 1950s to the present to depict the development of Taiwan studies, its fraught relationship with China studies, and Taiwan scholars’ search for a home of their own. I explore the expansion in research focus from anthropology in the 1950s and 1960s, to political science in the 1970s, to economics in the 1980s, and to literary and culture studies in the 1990s and describe how scholars established associations, research centres, programmes, and a journal devoted to Taiwan studies. This institutionalisation has created a feeling among scholars of being ‘at home’ and led me to the question of which routes should be taken for the future development of the field: the ‘ Sinocentric ’ (strikethrough intentional) route of working with China studies, or the alternative, ‘oceanic’ route of seeking alliances with other marginalised countries that also believe in freedom, democracy, and resistance to hegemony.

  2. Going Weigen: Animal Advocacy and Sustainability Intersections under Taiwan’s New Vegan Movement
    Gina Song Lopez · pp. 284-317

This article examines the emergence of Taiwan’s new vegan movement during the socially receptive period that followed the Sunflower Movement. It introduces the actors involved in vegan advocacy, noting its distinct routes of diffusion, and where new vegan identities and alternative advocacy spaces play a key role. It shows that while animal rights rationales informed the inception of the contemporary vegan movement, some actors have shifted their attention to policy processes by reconnecting their discourses to matters of dietary sustainability, thus bringing the local movement into closer alignment with global vegan mainstreaming through engagement with sustainability regimes.

  3. Save the Children: Youth Narratives and Historical Learning in Three Taiwanese Horror Video Games

It offers a comparative study of these games, focusing on their shared ‘save the children’ theme, which reimagines Taiwan’s traumatic past through nightmarish settings tied to the February 28 Incident and the White Terror. Additionally, the article explores how youth narratives shape and mobilise players through interactive digital gameplay. By blending historical memory with horror aesthetics, these meticulously crafted games serve as immersive portals, allowing players to engage with Taiwan’s past in a deeply interactive and affective manner.

  4. Entanglement in an Endangered Situation: Paiwan Society and the Conservation of the Mountain Hawk-Eagle
    Agathe Lemaitre · pp. 337-362
    摘要

It also addresses the bird’s endangered status and proposed conservation strategies to protect it. Wildlife management collaborations between indigenous communities and conservationists have sparked conflicts in values and worldviews that are challenging to reconcile. While the Paiwan wish to continue using the eagle’s feathers in important cultural rituals, this increased demand exacerbates hunting pressures on the species. This article seeks to find a better balance between preserving cultural practices and ensuring species survival. Drawing on four years of fieldwork among the Paiwan, it demonstrates the complexities of navigating entangled human–animal relationships in the context of species endangerment.

The extracts also reveal fresh aspects to Spanish relationships with Taiwan’s Indigenous people. These descriptions add to arguments that the Indigenous people had a significant influence on the departure of the Spanish from the island. The fragmentary details in these texts give further evidence of the multinational exchange that took place during those years. To analyse these fragments, a thematic analysis places them at the centre of discussions, to explore what they add to existing knowledge about the settlements during those years.

The fact that the series has triggered Taiwan’s belated #MeToo movement showcases the profound impact it has had on Taiwanese audiences, especially regarding conventional narratives surrounding power-based sexual violence, gender inequalities at the workplace, and attitudes towards homosexuality. Using both narrative and discourse analyses, this article unpacks such narratives by providing theoretical readings – both feminist and constructionist – for the series’ various plots and character transformations. Divulged in this process are the hidden social and ideological mechanisms within the Taiwanese context that have perpetuated gender inequalities at the workplace and in the family.

  1. Crisis Communication in a Public Health Emergency: Examining Taiwan and Singapore Government Press Releases through Latent Topic Modelling
    Raphael Duerr, Honeylet Santos, Yvan Ysmael Yonaha · pp. 1-42
    摘要

    The COVID-19 pandemic was an unprecedented public health emergency requiring concerted government action. Government responsibilities included communicating risks, informing the public about hygiene practices, and combating disinformation. Examining government communication strategies is important for improving crisis communication in future emergencies. Using quantitative text analyses, this article examines approximately 3,000 press releases issued by the Taiwanese and Singaporean governments. Topic prevalence was examined in relation to the timing of press releases and COVID-19 case and death counts. We find that both governments employed high-frequency, highly standardised, and detail-rich communication. Their communication strategies correspond closely with the model proposed by the Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC) framework, with their focus shifting from the initial shock of the pandemic through to the resolution stage, when vaccines were deployed. Their communication demonstrated a commitment to being first, being right, and being credible, while their guidelines promoted action by providing the public with concrete measures to reduce risk. Nevertheless, empathy was not prominent in the press releases, which may reflect both the limitations of the format and a division of communicative roles between bureaucratic and executive institutions.

    This article investigates the adaptations made across the Taiwan Strait to sustain popular religious exchanges during the COVID-19 pandemic. Drawing on observations of cross-Strait virtual events and in-depth interviews, it examines the major exchange formats that emerged during this period and assesses their broader implications. The findings reveal that the materiality of divine efficacy in popular religions rendered pilgrimage activities impossible, while formats driven by the ‘United Front’ strategy of the Chinese Communist Party proved more resilient. Previously institutionalised exchange platforms migrated online, and virtual settings facilitated new connections. However, these virtual events also brought unscripted and diverse Taiwanese expressions into direct view, unsettling the carefully choreographed narrative of cross-Strait unity that had previously structured these exchanges. The immediate post-pandemic recovery has been primarily facilitated by the party-state’s United Front objectives. While the pandemic disruptions were temporary, they have ultimately reinforced the political and economic foundations upon which cross-Strait religious networks now rest.

    Ching Kuo Hsieh · pp. 1-30

Drawing on Jacques Derrida’s hauntology and Judith Butler’s theory of grievability, this article argues that the ghost in Li Ang’s fiction functions not merely as a motif but as a structural condition of perception and narration. Across the trilogy, spectrality becomes the medium through which histories are re-entered, not to restore coherence but to expose absence, injury, and unresolved memory. Li Ang does not simply represent the paranormal; she inhabits it. Through increasingly self-referential writing, she stages haunting as a feminist modality of critique and redemption. The paranormal, in this context, is neither superstition nor metaphor—it is the very terrain through which the unspeakable is rendered thinkable, and the unreadable, legible.

  10. Consuming Democracy: Geopolitics, Human Rights, and Tourism in Taiwan
    Hardina Ohlendorf, J. J. Zhang · pp. 1-26

    International tourism has been an area where Taiwan has projected its soft power. Tourism involves constructing an identity for the outside world to see, and tourism as ‘placemaking’ requires the deliberate selection of imagery and rhetoric that will represent and synopsise the history, culture, and environment of a location. This article examines democracy and human rights in Taiwan’s tourism landscape and argues that Taiwan’s experience of political transformation is becoming a vital component of its tourism identity under the Democratic Progressive Party government. Emphasising Taiwan’s democratic achievements helps it to build a collective memory of its democratic citizenry, distinguish itself from the People’s Republic of China, and garner support among Western liberal democracies. Vol. 38, No. 4 · 2026-10-02 · 8 篇 · Routledge (BAJS) · Japan · Peer-reviewed
  1. BCOF at eighty: new perspectives on the British commonwealth occupation force in the occupation of Japan
    Jonathan Bull, Steven Ivings · pp. 489-501 · online 2026-10-02
    摘要

    The British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) component of the Allied Occupation of Japan (1945-1952) has often been overlooked by researchers because of its minimal role in policy-making. Taking the opportunity of the 80th anniversary of the arrival of the first BCOF personnel in Japan, this special issue introduces new perspectives about the organisation based on a range of hitherto unused or under-utilised sources. The introduction begins by emphasising how BCOF’s commanding officer sought to draw attention to his troops’ contribution to the Occupation. There follows a brief overview of the existing secondary research about BCOF in English and in Japanese. The latter half of the introduction outlines the contribution that the four articles make to the special issue. Taken as a whole, the purpose of the special issue is to begin to reassess how the occupiers and the occupied understood the role and meaning of BCOF. The introduction concludes with a call for other researchers to take part in the process of making this reassessment.

  2. Japan’s ‘multiple occupations’: ceremonial parades, ritual practices, and the performance of authority in the BCOF
    Toshihiko Kishi · pp. 502-522 · online 2026-03-18
    摘要

    The Allied occupation of Japan is most commonly remembered through the dominant image of General Douglas MacArthur and a largely American-led occupation regime. Such representations, reinforced by political authority, the concentration of media institutions in Tokyo, and post-war commemorative practices, have long framed the occupation as a singular and coherent project. This article challenges that narrative by advancing the concept of ‘multiple occupations’ to capture the uneven, regionally differentiated realities of occupation governance in post-war Japan. Rather than treating regional diversity as a secondary effect of a unified occupation, the concept foregrounds how authority itself was constituted through differentiated practices across space. Focusing on the early activities of the BCOF (British Commonwealth Occupation Force), a multinational and multi-ethnic force operating primarily in the Chūgoku and Shikoku regions between mid-1946 and mid-1948, the article examines how occupation authority was performed, negotiated, and sustained beyond Tokyo. Although formally subordinate to GHQ/SCAP (General Headquarters/Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers), the BCOF exercised a degree of practical autonomy in day-to-day regional administration while facing internal tensions rooted in imperial hierarchies, racialised divisions, and declining morale. The article further argues that ceremonial practices – notably military parades, musical performances, and funeral processions – played a central role in managing these challenges. Rather than treating such rituals as peripheral or purely symbolic, this article conceptualises them as practical mechanisms of governance. These ceremonies functioned simultaneously as outward-facing performances that communicated legitimacy to Japanese audiences and as inward-facing practices that disciplined personnel and reinforced cohesion within a fragmented occupying force. Drawing on military newspapers, Japanese local and national press, and archival photographs, the study foregrounds the regional experience of occupation and the cultural performance of authority in public space. By recovering the overlooked role of the BCOF and situating it within a framework of multiple occupations, this article complicates dominant narratives of post-war Japan and contributes to broader debates on power, representation, and transnational encounter in modern Japanese history.

  3. British veteran reflections on the British Commonwealth Occupation Force and experiences in Japan during the Korean War
    Steven Ivings · pp. 523-544 · online 2025-10-27
    摘要

    British Commonwealth participation in the Allied Occupation of Japan is a largely overlooked episode in post-war history. Yet at peak, the British Commonwealth Occupation Forces (BCOF) stationed in Japan numbered a sizeable 37,000 personnel from Australia, India, New Zealand and Britain, spread across the Chūgoku and Shikoku regions, including Hiroshima and the key naval port of Kure. BCOF’s missions were to pursue the demilitarisation and demobilisation of Japan, and to promote democratisation, but historians have tended to downplay BCOF’s achievements or overlook it entirely. This paper reassesses BCOF by considering its afterlife during the Korean War, as the British Commonwealth Forces Korea (BCFK) overlapped with BCOF and continued to use its facilities beyond BCOF’s disbanding in 1952. Examining approximately 800 reflections of former British BCOF/BCFK service personnel collected in the 1990s and early 2000s, this paper argues that for many former personnel the experience in Japan helped them to reconcile with Britain’s former wartime enemy (Japan) through personal interactions with Japanese people that generated mutual respect and lasting friendships. In this way BCOF was, for British veterans, an important part of facilitating an improvement in Anglo-Japanese relations at a grassroots level.

    This study examines the perceptions by veterans who served in the British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) and the British Commonwealth Forces Korea (BCFK) of the Japanese during their post-war deployment in Japan. Drawing on the recollections of 819 veterans, it explores how such perceptions were shaped by their experiences—ranging from encounters with the devastation of Hiroshima and interactions with local communities to lingering memories of wartime atrocities. While resentment arising from the mistreatment of prisoners of war frequently influenced their attitudes, interactions with Japanese civilians fostered a more nuanced understanding. A comparative analysis with British veterans’ own experiences of the Blitz further contextualizes their views, offering insight into their evolving perspectives. This study also traces a shift in perception—from witnessing the destruction of Hiroshima as an emblem of wartime devastation to recognizing it as a site of historical reflection and learning. Ultimately, it argues that those recollections, despite their fragmentary and sometimes contradictory nature, provide valuable insights into post-war reconciliation and the complexities of cross-cultural relationships.

  5. Writing BCOF as diary, re-writing the occupation as memoir
    Jonathan Bull · pp. 568-589 · online 2026-04-23
    摘要

    This article examines the diaries and memoir written by an Australian soldier who fought in the Second World War (1939-1945) and who served in the British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) in the Occupation of Japan. The diaries from 1938 to 1945 contextualise how the soldier wrote about BCOF as an important time in his military career. His BCOF diaries (1946-1951) indicate that he was torn between pursuing relationships with local women and trying to secure promotion. This tension lessened towards the end of his BCOF service but never entirely disappeared. In his memoir written in the mid-1960s he re-wrote his experience in BCOF so that the organisation had a greater moral coherence. These writings by the same individual therefore reveal the process by which a good occupation narrative was formed by rewriting, omission and substitution from the personal memory of the diary to the intended public memory of the memoir.

    This paper explores the political allegories embedded in Kafka on the Shore (2002) (Murakami Citation2005), arguing that the novel functions as a historical allegory of World War II, urging contemporary Japanese society to confront its wartime responsibilities. While Haruki Murakami’s works have often been perceived as politically disengaged, this study demonstrates how Kafka on the Shore contains hidden political metaphors referencing both Nazi Germany and the Japanese Empire. Employing close reading and historical contextual analysis, this paper examines key figures—Johnnie Walker, Colonel Sanders, and the imagery of the painting ‘Kafka on the Shore’—to reveal how Murakami engages with historical memory. The conflict between Johnnie Walker and Nakata is interpreted as an allegory of British-Japanese imperial rivalry, while Colonel Sanders symbolizes the Americanization of postwar Japan. Moreover, recurring German references, including a Volkswagen car and the ‘Edelweiss’ song from The Sound of Music (Citation1965), serve as reminders of Japan’s wartime alliance with Germany. The study further suggests that Murakami’s later novel, Killing Commendatore (2017) (Murakami Citation2018), adopts a more explicit approach to political allegory, shifting interpretive agency from the reader to the protagonist. By uncovering these layered political metaphors, this paper highlights Murakami’s evolving engagement with historical responsibility in his fiction.

By directly interviewing the refugees – especially mothers and children – Yoshida has provided access to information concerning life at the refugee shelters, underlining the political and economic burdens as well as the psychological and social costs that the post-3.11 disaster (in)justice provoked on the affected communities. After introducing the state of art in disaster journalism in Japan with particular emphasis on the role of women journalists in the media, this study examines the new professional figure of the ‘free writer’ presenting the case of Yoshida Chia and her commitment to aiding public engagement in coping with disaster (in)justice during the process of Tōhoku’s recovery. In order to do so, the focus of this article will be on Yoshida’s Reportage of the evacuation of mothers and children. The nuclear victims will fade (2016) and After Fukushima.   1. The First World War and Japan’s cabinet system: how the conflict changed the perception and reception of foreign constitutional models by Japanese elites (1912–1920)
    Manon Ramos · pp. 1-25 · online 2026-10-23
    摘要

    The modern Japanese state, built on the Meiji Constitution (1889–1947), has long been understood as inspired by a Prussian model. Recent historiography, however, emphasises a paradigm shift in Japanese national identity after the First World War and the development of party politics in the 1920s. How did the experience of this conflict alter the vision of European constitutional frameworks and the choice of foreign models for interpreting Japan’s own political institutions? This article, while focusing on the cabinet system, addresses this question by analysing constitutional commentaries and reform projects by scholars, statesmen, and journalists across three chronological stages. First, it shows that doctrinal debates from 1912 to 1914 were polarised by ideologies favouring the German or British models. Second, it observes essential changes in information pipelines during the war, a detachment from Germany, and increasing praise for Britain’s resilience. Third, it argues that reform projects by influential actors in the war’s immediate aftermath were designed after the United Kingdom’s recent institutional evolutions. These considerations shed light on an early stage of the global dissemination of the Westminster model and suggest its influence went beyond the Dominions and the post-Second World War Commonwealth.

  2. Ambiguously queer: interrogating youth and queerness in Kyoto Animation’s adaptation of Sound! Euphonium
    Callum Hew Sarracino · pp. 1-23 · online 2026-10-11
    摘要

    Found across a wide variety of genres, youth is a popular setting for media in Japan. Often focused on school club activities, narratives set during adolescence feature intense relationships between members of the same sex that toe the line between homoromantic and homosocial. The language used in the texts and by the creators often supports both readings, with the audience left to draw their own conclusions based on how they understand youth. While previous scholarship has looked at queerness in youth-focused texts, less has been written about how the association a text has with youth affects queer readings of the language of the texts. Through a textual and discourse analysis of the anime Sound! Euphonium (2015–2024), as well as published interviews with creators and online fan discussion about it, this article interrogates the relationship between queerness and youth in the Japanese media. I argue that youth has a normative effect in the Japanese media sphere, obfuscating the existence of queer readings by providing a normative explanation for even the queerest of language. I further suggest that Sound! Euphonium more widely reflects the ambiguity that pervades representations of queerness during female adolescence in the Japanese media.

  3. Ministerial Power in Kantei-Led Policymaking: The Case of the Priority Reform Promotion System for National Universities under the Second Abe Administration
    Yutaro Tsuji · pp. 1-20 · online 2026-10-06
    摘要

    This article examines the policymaking process of the Priority Reform Promotion System, a performance-based funding system for Japanese national universities introduced under the second Abe administration. Existing research has largely portrayed this process through the lens of Kantei-led (prime minister’s office-led) policymaking, which sees the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) as following directives set by prime ministerial councils. However, little attention has been paid to whether and how MEXT’s own preferences were incorporated into the policy design. Using policy documents and elite interviews with MEXT civil servants, this article traces the policymaking process from agenda setting to the final budget negotiations, taking seriously the agency of MEXT. The findings show that MEXT held clear preferences from an early stage and shaped the design of the system within the new Kantei-led structure. These findings indicate that the Kantei-led framework does not on its own explain who determines specific policy content and suggest that ministerial agency deserves closer attention in analyses of Japan’s centralised policymaking structure.

  1. Forging a Double Diaspora: Cuban Jewish Migration and Settlement in 1960s Greater Miami
    Mark A. Goldberg · pp. 5-37 · online 2026-09-01
    摘要

    After the 1959 revolution, Jewish migrants joined the waves of emigrants exiting Fidel Castro's Cuba. They developed a close-knit community in Greater Miami as their parents and grandparents had done when they immigrated to Cuba decades earlier. Analyzing oral histories, newspapers, and Cuban and US community records, this article uncovers an often-untold history and reconceptualizes diaspora by exploring the local influences on Cuban Jewish diaspora formation for a population belonging to multiple racialized groups. In the decades after arrival in Greater Miami, Cuban Jews transitioned from Cuban nationals to Cuban exiles to US residents and citizens. They found affordable housing in the white-designated Miami Beach and carved out an enclave, connecting Cuban Jewish newcomers and grounding them in the city. To integrate, the migrants felt they had to prove their worth to the larger society, and they embraced respectability politics to defuse their perceived otherness—which contained a complex combination of racial, ethnic, and religious elements—while maintaining their Cuban identity. Cuban Jews forged a double diaspora rooted in an entangled Cuban Jewish identity born from Jewish life in Cuba, cultural adaptation to the US socio-political environment, and interactions with other Cuban exiles and Miami residents.

  2. Little Guyana in Motion: Belonging, Religion, and Moral Community in Post–1965 Immigrant New York
    Kavita Gawrinauth · pp. 38-60 · online 2026-09-01
    摘要

    This article argues that post-1965 immigrant New York is often analyzed through two largely parallel literatures—migration and community formation, on the one hand, and religion and transnational devotion, on the other—and that reading them together clarifies how belonging in the outer boroughs was made through overlapping material and moral infrastructures. Bringing the urban scholarship of Nancy Foner, Steven Gregory, Madhulika Khandelwal, and Pyong Gap Min into conversation with work on immigrant religion by R. Stephen Warner, Peggy Levitt, Prema Kurien, and R. Scott Hanson, it demonstrates that labor markets, housing corridors, and neighborhood politics frequently intertwined with ritual calendars, congregational institution-building, and everyday ethics of obligation and care. This article, then, uses the relative absence of the Indo-Guyanese community of Richmond Hill, Queens (“Little Guyana”) from both literatures to probe the limits of frameworks that privilege either “settlement” or “transnationalism.” Drawing on Queens-based community and ethnic press coverage of Phagwah/Holi and Diwali, municipal recognitions such as permits, proclamations, and street co-namings, documentation of mandir-building and temple openings, and oral histories with mandir participants and organizers, it traces devotional circulation between Queens and Guyana as a form of neighborhood-making. This Richmond Hill case shows how ritual processions, institutional expansion, and public commemoration make belonging legible through urban space while sustaining obligations and attachments across borders—treating the neighborhood less as an end point of migration than as a node in a wider devotional circuit.

  3. Collective Care Is Essential: Puerto Rican Feminist Activists and Welfare Rights Organizing after 1960
    Emma Amador · pp. 61-88 · online 2026-09-01
    摘要

    In 1970, a Puerto Rican woman named Juanita Serrano was elected to serve as a chair of the National Welfare Rights Organization (NWRO) after spending numerous years organizing poor women in Cleveland, Ohio. In this role Serrano joined welfare rights organizers from across the country as they protested the social, economic, and political conditions faced by poor people. This article provides a history of Puerto Rican women's contributions to welfare rights organizing in the United States. It argues that Puerto Rican women activists within the welfare rights movement articulated a vision of collective care that insisted that working-class people should have control over social welfare institutions and that welfare recipients should dictate the forms that care took in their communities. Their vision also addressed Puerto Ricans’ experience as colonial citizens, migrants, Spanish speakers, and people of color. The article examines how demands for collective care were advanced both in organizing to improve social welfare programs in the United States and Puerto Rico, and in leftist political mobilizations that contested capitalism and colonialism. Thus, one of the particularities of Puerto Rican welfare rights activism was that it was often closely linked to broader struggles for colonial migrants’ rights and for the decolonization of Puerto Rico.

  4. Immigration, Authoritarian Populism, and Donald Trump
    John Bodnar · pp. 89-118 · online 2026-09-01
    摘要

    Donald Trump fueled a political rise by exploiting the issue of immigration. Rejecting the liberal narrative of a “nation of immigrants” that had long portrayed the United States as a land of opportunity for all and a haven for the oppressed, Trump turned the idea of immigration into an existential threat to the nation itself. He dehumanized people crossing American borders with wild abandon, calling them criminals, drug dealers, “dog-eaters,” invaders, rapists, pollutants of the nation's blood supply, and monsters capable of entering the kitchens of citizens to “slit their throat.” In his first run for the presidency in 2016, he promised to build a massive wall on the southern border. In his second inaugural address, in 2025, he declared a national emergency at the border and said he would send military forces to “repel a disastrous invasion.” Why did Trump do this? Why did he turn immigrants—both undocumented and legal—into extreme threats to the nation? Was he simply a radical xenophobe or racist seeking to keep America mostly white or Anglo-Saxon? And where did this extreme form of hostility come from? This essay seeks to probe these issues and offers an interpretation of matters that will be debated for years to come. It argues that in his rhetoric and deeds, Trump's immigration policies need to be understood as more than a resort to traditional forms of American xenophobia and racism. His narrative of immigration as a peril was a means to a larger end that sought to overturn liberal democracy in the United States with a form of authoritarianism.

  34. Lincoln's Peace: The Struggle to End the American Civil War

    摘要

    Most of us have encountered books that in some respects give us serious pause but that we nonetheless admire because they raise significant historical questions and explore them with such intelligence that the books are thought provoking in the best sense. That encapsulates my appraisal of Michael Vorenberg's Lincoln's Peace, which, in addition to its other virtues, has a strong, lucid style—and opens with a vignette that brilliantly sets up the question at the heart of the book: Just when did the Civil War end? The vignette deals with a lawyer who was present as a Union officer at the Appomattox surrender and decades later was tasked by the War Department to deal with all manner of issues calling for legal appraisal. One such issue was a protest lodged by a U.S. army veteran who had been denied a Civil War pension on the grounds that he had enlisted in a New York volunteer regiment—so far, so good—but had done so on April 19, 1866, more than a year after Appomattox and nearly a year after the last Confederate land forces had surrendered. That seemingly made his protest a prime candidate for the circular file.

  57. Between Here and There: Creating the Political Economy of Mexican Migration, 1900–1942
    Avital Bloch · pp. 405-406 · online 2026-09-28
    摘要

    Daniel Morales is an academic historian who studies Mexican migration to the United States, a subject to which he brings a deeply personal connection. As the grandson of a former bracero and the child of migrants who were deported back to Mexico several times before obtaining legal status, he brings insight to this scholarship. Morales uses multiple archival sources in the United States and Mexico, oral histories, and interviews he conducted with migrants. His main argument is that from 1900 to the early 1940s, migration evolved into a “self-constitutive” phenomenon. Driven by work opportunities, family conditions, as well as political and legal impositions, people were on the move back and forth in a pattern of “circular migration” between Mexico and the United States that continually re-creates itself. To enable their northern journeys, migrants relied first on relatives and community networks for support in financing their trips and protecting their families left behind. Additionally, a complex, cross-border system of communications and services developed to help migrants regarding transportation, finding jobs, getting housing, and retaining legal help. This expanding network encompassed an array of people and institutions, including family members, smugglers, labor contractors, recruiters, boarding houses, churches, and Spanish-language publications. As the number of migrants grew, the structure that handled the “business of migration” expanded into a massive, intricate, and permanent phenomenon. While many were drawn to the dream of life in the United States, this desire did contradict migrants’ pride and identification as Mexicans who longed to return home. Deportations, seasonal cycles of unemployment, and rural economic struggles in Mexico further facilitated this circular migrating pattern.

    Jeanne Theoharis, a scholar-activist teaching at Brooklyn College, is a leading chronicler of the Black civil rights movement in American memory and as a force active beyond the South. In this compelling book, Theoharis places Martin Luther King Jr. at the vital center of her analysis, going against the grain of much recent scholarship that has successfully challenged the view that King was the movement's leader. She does so to fashion a usable past. King's intensifying pursuit of racial justice in the urban North, she contends, has important contemporary lessons for those opposed to the enduring structural racism of the United States. Theoharis provides a wealth of evidence, some of it gleaned from King's understudied columns in the Harlem Amsterdam News, to show that the nation's most famous Black minister was passionately interested in the often-difficult lives of African Americans in the industrial North. While conceding that King's civil rights work above the Mason-Dixon line “felt piecemeal” during the 1950s and early 1960s, she argues persuasively that his early efforts to secure northern funding and allies for the southern movement did not cloud his understanding of northern racism (p. 156). This understanding came from a variety of sources: his experiences as a student at northern colleges; the influence of his wife Coretta, a vigorous opponent of militarism, sexism, and racism; and his consciousness-raising encounters with northern activists and low-paid workers whose strikes he publicly supported. Theoharis skillfully documents King's strong interest and active involvement in community struggles against police brutality and school and housing discrimination in New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles before the Watts uprising in August 1965, an event routinely depicted as the trigger for King's decision to shift his Southern Christian Leadership Conference's focus to the North. She observes, for example, his frequent participation in northern protests such as local school strikes against a racist Chicago education official in 1963 as well as his awareness that state and national governments were complicit in “the de facto segregation and injustice of the North” (p. 117).

  3. Becoming Chinese American: The Chin Siblings During China’s War of Resistance
    Jin Feng · pp. 205-232
    摘要

    The Chin siblings, three second-generation Chinese Americans, went to their ancestral land to teach at institutions of higher education during China’s War of Resistance against Japanese Invasion (1931–1945). While there, they availed themselves of opportunities that were denied to Chinese Americans in the U.S. but also faced prejudice and suspicion. Nonetheless, in family and business correspondence they often portrayed themselves as patriotic citizens of both countries and cultural ambassadors who connected the two peoples. They employed such efforts to negotiate competing nationalist demands made by the Chinese and U.S. governments and thus offered invaluable insights into the complex processes of becoming Chinese American. This article shines a light on a significant yet little known body of materials to demonstrate how family dynamics, as well as political, racial, and cultural forces, shaped the identify formation of Chinese Americans in the mid-twentieth century, especially immediately preceding, during, and after World War II. Ultimately, it builds up the archives of Asian American history and amplifies Asian American voices from the unique perspective of a sibling unit’s wartime experiences.

  4. Making the AAPI Perspectives Oral History Project: Remembering a Place-Based Social History of Activism in Santa Clara Valley
    Yvonne Y. Kwan · pp. 233-270
    摘要

    This article examines the AAPI Perspectives: Oral History and Activism Digital Archive and Curriculum Project (2021–2024), which redirected county funding from carceral “hate crime” initiatives to community-based oral history. The article proceeds in three parts: first, it contextualizes the project’s genesis in the early 2020s; second, it analyzes the project’s oral history interviews to show how these AAPI social histories took actual place in Santa Clara Valley (1840s–present); and third, it argues that these overlapping regional histories facilitated an intergenerational, multiethnic spatial politics that catalyzed various activisms, which seeded social movements, advanced Asian American studies, and challenged the model minority myth. Together, these analyses highlight the potential of grassroots organizing and oral history to generate community-centered narratives that echo the founding vision of Asian American studies as a field committed to “serving the people.” AAPI Perspectives reframes AAPI pasts while modeling how communities can reclaim, preserve, and mobilize their histories in the pursuit of justice.

    In 2024, San Francisco voters approved Proposition G, requiring 8th-grade Algebra 1 for public school students and restores “tracked” course sequences that sort students by their perceived intellectual abilities. Proposition G’s proponents mobilized anti-Asian American racist essentialism, and proximity to whiteness, targeting San Francisco’s large Chinese American electorate. We argue, using Asian Critical Race Theory and critical race discourse analysis, that Proposition G proponents’ arguments mobilized covert anti-Asian American essentialism and Sinocentrism to undermine racial justice discourses in educational politics. We consequently propose an analytic of “(De) Tracking Sinocentrism,” which disentangles Sinocentrism from Asian American panethnic racialization processes.

  2. Introduction
    Raja Adal, Christopher Lowy · pp. 777-789 · online 2026-10-01
    摘要

    Before the Unicode Standard, text shared across digital devices was often garbled, a problem that disproportionately affected users of non-Latin scripts. Unicode's emergence in the 1990s resolved this by encoding the world's major scripts into a single global standard that made text interoperable across digital devices—a development especially consequential in Asia, home to more than 90 percent of non-Latin script users. Yet Unicode is not a neutral infrastructure. Each encoding decision—which characters to include, how to handle script boundaries, whether to unify Sinographs across linguistic traditions—was shaped by the competing interests of large technology companies, national governments, user communities, and scholars. And each carried enduring political implications. This introduction argues that it is time for humanities scholars to critically engage with the ways in which Unicode crystallized at the intersection of state power, capital, and culture to become the foundation of a global infrastructure that governs nearly all textual communication today. It situates the four articles in this volume within the existing scholarly literature, provides a glossary of key technical terms, and introduces the closing roundtable in which technical experts and humanities scholars reflect on the field's future directions.

  3. Big Tech, the Big State, and the Battle for Encoding All of the World's Languages
    Raja Adal · pp. 790-812 · online 2026-10-01
    摘要

    For over three decades, the dominant narrative of Unicode has been that it is a technical solution to a technical problem of global communication. This article argues that this narrative has dominated the discourse about Unicode because it is the narrative of the victors. Understanding the social and political interests at stake requires returning to the battle that yielded the Unicode Standard as the sole universal encoding standard: a period from 1988, when a draft proposal of the Unicode Standard was first made public, to 1993, when the Unicode Standard effectively conquered the dominant encoding standard, ISO/IEC 10646. Whereas Unicode was an organization consisting mostly of engineers at large American software companies, ISO was an international standard organization comprising representatives from member nations. Their confrontation over the encoding of Sinographs pitted big tech against the big state, with significant national and financial interests at stake. The last section discusses how a recent attempt by the Chinese state to rapidly encode a large batch of Sinographs used in proper names reveals some of the stakes of this ongoing negotiation between big tech and big states.

  4. ISCII Imperialism
    Anushah Hossain · pp. 813-838 · online 2026-10-01
    摘要

    In 2009, Daniel Pargman and Jacob Palme published an essay titled “ASCII Imperialism,” which discussed how the American text standard, ASCII, was embedded in existing computer protocols and how it marginalized non-English languages. This article hearkens to that concept by calling for the recognition of “ISCII imperialism.” It examines how the little-known Indian Script Code for Information Interchange (ISCII) has been integrated in global communication protocols since 1991 through the Unicode Standard and has created the potential for an uneven digital landscape for different Indian languages and writing systems. Specifically, ISCII has been controversial for seemingly privileging Devanagari, commonly used to write Hindi, at the expense of other scripts. Public outcry against ISCII imperialism has been transformative, however. As this article demonstrates, advocacy by Indic script communities has pushed the Unicode Consortium to reconsider its implementation of ISCII, demonstrating how even rigid technical structures are influenced by regional language politics.

  5. Abstract Code
    Uluğ Kuzuoğlu · pp. 839-861 · online 2026-10-01
    摘要

    Unicode is everywhere and nowhere at once. Since its invention in 1993 by lucrative American companies, including Xerox, Apple, and Microsoft, Unicode has been the global standard for information exchange, enabling the transfer of data across the world by converting more than a hundred and sixty world scripts into standardized bits and bytes. Its spread throughout the world is so expansive, its technical complexity so elaborate, and its integration into daily lives so seamless that Unicode has become a natural part of the world—used everywhere, yet seen nowhere. This article seeks to denaturalize Unicode by examining its origins from a global perspective and situating it within a longer history of script engineering that was deeply intertwined with imperialism, colonialism, and capitalism. It proposes the term “abstract code” to capture a historical process whereby capitalism homogenizes and standardizes diverse cultures of writing to make them exchangeable and commensurable with one another in the market of information. Disclosing the historical links between the nineteenth-century age of script engineering and the birth of Unicode in the 1980s, this article demonstrates that the new information infrastructure sought to abstract all writing systems into a standardized sequence of bits and thus enable the corporate accumulation of capital at a global scale. Unicode, in short, was the critical infrastructure that enabled the birth of a global neoliberal information economy.

  6. Literary Expression at the Ends of Unicode
    Christopher Lowy · pp. 862-887 · online 2026-10-01
    摘要

    This article examines how Unicode reshapes the humanities by asking what happens when a supposedly universal encoding system meets the demands of the Japanese writing system. Focusing on EnJoe Toh's 2018 collection A Whirlpool of Glyphs, it shows how his fiction probes the tension between standardization and expression that underlies script reform from the Qin dynasty to contemporary Unicode debates. EnJoe's stories stage conflicts between inclusion and exclusion—what counts as an encodable character, which graphic forms are discarded, and how these decisions constrain or enable writers working with Sinographs, kana, and their visual and expressive possibilities. By dramatizing everything from Qin-era script reforms to rebellious furigana and proliferating variant characters, EnJoe makes visible the technical infrastructures that underwrite the process of writing. In doing so, the article argues, he exploits the Japanese writing system's capacity for orthographical variation at the limits of possibility. Unicode functions simultaneously as a tool of global standardization and a platform that “standardizes the nonstandard,” with significant consequences for how the humanities preserve, classify, and imagine written forms, and EnJoe's work offers a key case for understanding how script technologies condition literary creativity across languages and periods.

  12. Multiple Diplomatic Centers
    Lina Nie
    摘要

    Diplomatic interactions between Japanese Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu and Ming emperor Zhu Di, together with the Ming-Japanese tally trade, have received lively scholarly discussion. This article examines a period before the tally trade momentarily became the major diplomatic channel in Sino-Japanese exchanges. By cross-referencing and comparing sources from China and Japan, the author highlights how various players such as Zhu Yuanzhang, Buddhist monks, Prince Kaneyoshi, Go-Enyū tennō, and Kyushu warrior leaders participated in overseas exchanges. The author argues that the lively diplomatic exchanges between Kyushu and China confirm the existence of multiple diplomatic centers beyond Kyoto. The author proposes seeing Ming's rulership in this light and rethinking it in a broader East Asian context. In particular, Zhu Yuanzhang's flexible policies and careful examination of overseas envoys demonstrate that early Ming's overseas policies cannot be summarized simply as conservative and inward-looking. Instead, they show a high degree of openness and variation in the conduct of overseas affairs. By comparing diplomatic exchanges written in different languages and from different sides, the author argues for the need to move beyond political and territorial boundaries to consider important concepts such as rulership, empire, and imperial order in a connected and transregional perspective.

    摘要

    Scholars have made clear the impact of colonial governance on modern states’ racial, ethnic, and national identities. Colonial census efforts were a crucial tool in the creation and politicization of such identity categories. This article analyzes “race” definitions and classifications in the colonial censuses of British India from 1872 to 1931 to show how the challenges of defining race in Burma emerged, in part, because of the stepwise colonization of Burma through British India. Specifically, this article asks: What influenced the definitions of race in Burma? How were efforts at developing and understanding a racial schema in Burma shaped by the colonial landscape in which it was embedded? The article argues that colonial ideas about race in Burma developed out of an initial stage of racial classification and knowledge production in India, revealing the complexity of defining race under the influence of both European perceptions of racial difference and local perceptions of social boundaries in India. This article contributes to knowledge of how the creation and implementation of race categories and definitions is a process embedded in a web of colonial structures that extend beyond the colony-colonizer relationship.

  15. Push-Car Railways, Camphor, and Coal in the Imperial Hinterland
    Youjia Li
    摘要

    This article examines the push-car railway industry in colonial Taiwan from 1895 to the 1930s. It argues that this human-powered transportation resolved a colonial dilemma between the colonial government's economic ambition and its limited capacities as shaped by Taiwan's environmental and colonial conditions. The push-car railways effectively connected Taiwan's local economy to the global market. The article rethinks the relationship between the environment, capitalism, and colonialism from three perspectives. First, muscle-powered technology was crucial to the rise of fossil capitalism at the turn of the century. Second, the push-car railway industry revealed a multilayered relationship between the colonizer and the colonized, profoundly reshaping the environment of the imperial hinterland. Third, as an integral part of fossil capitalism, the push-car railway industry amplified and complicated human cost instead of decreasing it. This analysis unravels how local Taiwanese business actors developed networks under colonial constraints, reshaping socioeconomic and environmental relationships in Taiwan's hinterlands.

    As a postscript to the collected articles in this forum, this article first discusses how and why a high-stakes test-based admissions system has historically been established in East Asia, contextualizing meritocratic educational selection within the historical experience of “catch-up modernization.” Second, using a theoretical framework of “compressed” modernity and development, it discusses how broader and more recent societal changes have contributed to the development of a high-stakes admissions system. Third, it discusses the implications of these recent changes in admissions for understanding changes in meritocracy. Finally, it describes the problems these rapid and simultaneous changes in admissions and other social spheres have created and what implications these changes have for our understanding of meritocracy in the region. It concludes by discussing how meritocracy has created a new social divide, representing a duality in meritocratic college admissions consisting of traditional high-stakes tests and newly introduced admissions procedures that are more holistic.

This study, based on sixty-two interviews, examines how educators and students navigate Taiwan's dual-merit admissions system, where traditional test scores intersect with a new holistic screening model. The author finds that students continue to treat test scores as primary markers of success, while professors and teachers increasingly prioritize nontest merit as signals of social distinction. This divergence highlights varying rates of adaptation to Taiwan's dual-merit system, exposing tensions between old and new standards.   3. Introduction: Expanding the History of Chinese Food Culture
    Thomas Mazanec, Wandi Wang · pp. 411-414 · online 2026-06-19
    摘要

    The consumption of food is simultaneously one of humanity’s most basic necessities and one of its greatest luxuries. It has, appropriately, both inspired and reflected cultural activities, from agricultural rituals and ascetic practices to epicurean banquets and poetry. At the present moment, we seem to be living in an era of peak food obsession, fueled by extremely popular food culture, the rapid rise of “foodie” life on social media, and heated debates over the authenticity and identity of cuisine in a multicultural context. Chinese societies have been equally obsessed, with food being a central theme of ancient bronzes, Confucian classics, religious practices, and literary works. For this reason, the study of Chinese food culture naturally brings one through a wide array of disciplines, including cultural studies, history, religion, medicine, and aesthetics. However, with a few notable exceptions, major research in humanistic food studies has tended to emphasize recent time periods, European and American cultures, or both (the “modern west”). The result has been a strong emphasis on “cultural studies” approaches, usually adopting structuralist, culturalist, or Gramscian critiques of power brokers in the past century. 1 This special issue shows how attention to Chinese food history may bring to light many new questions and methods in the study of food culture.

  4. Tummy Troubles: When Chinese Healers Administered Milk
    Miranda Dympna Brown, Yong Yang · pp. 415-433 · online 2026-01-22
    摘要

    Received scholarship by H.T. Huang and others has argued that the high incidence of lactose intolerance in East Asians discouraged the Chinese from adopting dairy on health grounds before the twentieth century. However, such wisdom overlooks Chinese medical literature that prescribes fresh dairy to treat chronic diarrhea. This essay considers what famed healer Sun Simiao (581–682) had to say about the uses of dairy products in treating digestive ailments. Towards this end, we consider the Essential Formulas Worth a Thousand Pieces of Gold for Emergencies ( Beiji qianjin yaofang 備急千金要方) and the Supplemental Formulas Worth a Thousand Pieces of Gold ( Qianjin yifang 千金翼方). We then compare the uses of dairy in the Sun corpus to both contemporary and earlier texts. Our analysis shows that Tang-dynasty (618–907) healers regarded milk products as generally good for the gut, and, in some cases, recommended using fresh dairy for cases of flux.

  6. Poisoned Meals: Toxic Food, Epistemic Standards, and Retributive Justice in Twelfth-Century Judicial Cases and Anecdotal Narratives
    Ari Daniel Levine · pp. 453-472 · online 2026-02-26
    摘要

    This article examines case studies and anecdotal narratives in which murderers used poisoned food as a weapon, and government officials used their epistemic authority to solve these crimes and bring the perpetrators to justice. Drawn from Zheng Ke’s 鄭克 (fl. 1124–1149) legal compendium Tortoise and Mirror for Judging Cases ( Zheyu guijian 折獄龜鑑) and Hong Mai’s 洪邁 (1123–1202) anecdote collection Record of the Listener ( Yijian zhi 夷堅志), these narratives reflected the violent threat that poisoners posed to the preservation of gender, familial, social, and political hierarchies. In the Mirror ’s legal realm, astute officials used abductive reasoning to expose poisoning plots, thereby restoring the moral fabric of society; in Hong Mai’s Record poisoners are punished by imperial judges as well as by retributive mechanisms of cosmic justice. These six selected case narratives illustrate the permeability of the boundaries that divide the conceptual categories of food, medicine, and poison, and the connections amongst medical, legal, and socio-moral systems of knowledge.

  7. Savoring Beauty and Cultivating a Poet’s Spleen: The Plum Blossom as a Delicacy in Southern Song China
    Wandi Wang · pp. 473-489 · online 2026-01-07
    摘要

    For a plant as renowned and beloved in China as the plum blossom ( meihua 梅花), there is conspicuously little written in English about eating it. However, without understanding the historical affection for consuming plum blossoms, our comprehension of it as a cultural icon misses an important dimension. This article explores the intriguing discourse surrounding plum blossom consumption in three sections. The first section introduces the key concept of qing 清 (“purity”) and its relation to the “poet’s spleen” ( shiren pi 詩人脾), which provides a theoretical framework for a relationship between eating it and writing poetry. The second section examines Song-dynasty poems on this eating practice, particularly those by Yang Wanli 楊萬里 (1127–1206) and the Rivers and Lakes poets ( jianghu shiren 江湖詩人). Their poetry was closely tied to new developments in the notion of qi 氣 and “poetic spleen” ( shipi 詩脾). The third section turns to culinary recipes, primarily from the Rivers and Lakes poet Lin Hong 林洪 (fl. 1224–1263), who promotes qing aesthetics in plum blossom dishes. I argue that the discovery of culinary value in a flower long regarded as more symbolic than edible marks a significant development in Song-dynasty (960–1279) literati culture, aesthetics, intellectual history, and medicine.

  8. Seeking a Deadly Delicacy: Pufferfish, Regional Gastronomy, and Pharmacology in Middle Period China

    摘要

    Seafood gained prominence as a southern flavor in middle-period China. Among the southern products that piqued gourmets’ fancy, the pufferfish as a deadly delicacy presented a special case. How did it come to acquire its contentious reputation? This article traces the process that transformed it from a dangerous ancient killer to an alluring treat by the early twelfth century. Its shifting cultural stature was propelled by demographic and geographical reconfigurations, negotiations between northern and southern culinary traditions, and the literati effort to collect and classify natural knowledge. Along the way, diverse encounters and experiences with different pufferfishes were coalesced into one uniform category hetun (“river-piglet”), connoting at once danger and delicacy. The metamorphosis of the pufferfish demonstrated the interplay between literary, medical, geographical, and natural knowledge across genres in middle-period Chinese history.

  9. The Chickpea in Premodern China: A Perpetual Foreigner in the Central Lands
    Ya Zuo · pp. 508-526 · online 2026-01-07
    摘要

    In this paper, I explore the millennium-long presence of the chickpea in premodern China by highlighting three key historical moments. The legume had its first rise to prominence as a cosmopolitan “Muslim Bean” in the Mongol Yuan (1271–1368) imperial diet. It then experienced a phase of obscurity, as the most renowned Chinese herbalist, Li Shizhen 李時珍 (1518–1593), conflated it with the pea. A disparate identity of the legume emerged around the same time, as the bean garnered attention from famine relief specialists, consequently transforming into a source of sustenance. The multiple lives of the chickpea were characterized with a common emphasis on its foreignness, drawing connections to various Eurasian cultures beyond China. The plant’s enduring presence, coupled with ongoing allusions to its alienness, makes it a perpetual foreigner in the broad expanse of the Chinese empire.

  10. Tea and Place: The Evolving Discussion about Terroir in Song China
    Xiaolin Duan · pp. 527-543 · online 2026-04-14
    摘要

    This article employs terroir as an analytical framework to examine how a place-specific tea acquired its reputation and contributed to processes of cultural self-fashioning in Song China. Focusing on Fujian’s Beiyuan 北苑 tea—exceptionally well documented in Song sources—it explores the close connections among tea, landscape appreciation, and place-making. Drawing on tea manuals and connoisseur writings, the article shows how literati linked tea quality to both natural conditions and cultural practices, using such associations to articulate refined taste and produce place-based knowledge. The case of Beiyuan tea reveals the emergence of a distinctly Chinese rhetoric of terroir, one that transformed environmental description into a rhetoric that mediated between local expertise and imperial order. Within this framework, place itself came to embody quality, integrating physical environment, cultural identity, and sensory experience.

  1. From Individual to Lineage Identity: Huizhou Merchants and the Rise of Genealogies in Ming China
    Xin Yu · pp. 1-29 · online 2026-10-20
    摘要

    This article examines how Huizhou merchants shaped their identities during their economic ascent from the fifteenth century onward. Because commerce carried a stigma in Confucian ideology, they shifted the basis of self-presentation from mercantile success to moral excellence. This produced a competition in virtue, where the moral capital accumulated in a single lifetime could not rival that amassed across generations. Merchants therefore redirected identity claims from personal virtue to membership in lineages where virtue had been cultivated over generations. In doing so, they moved the foundation of identity from individual achievement to collective lineage affiliation. This shift provides a new explanation for the rise of lineages and genealogies from the perspective of identity formation. By underscoring the initiative, creativity, and adaptability of merchants in driving these changes, the article also repositions them from the cultural margins to the center of identity-making in late imperial China.

  23. The Sino-Soviet Alliance, the Korean War, and the Predicament of the CCP’s Attack Plans for Taiwan, 1949–50
    Zhihua Shen, Thomas Burnham · pp. 1-24 · online 2026-09-29
    摘要

    Drawing on archival materials from the Republic of China (Taiwan), the People’s Republic of China (PRC), the United States, and the former Soviet Union, this article discusses why the PRC’s 1949–50 strike plans for Taiwan went unfulfilled. What prevented the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) from “liberating” Taiwan was the fact that it lacked sufficient naval and air power to overwhelm the comparatively better equipped Kuomintang (KMT). The only way to overcome this disparity in a timely manner was to call upon Soviet assistance. In early 1949, seeking to incorporate China into the Soviet Union’s sphere of influence, Joseph Stalin resolved to support the CCP’s seizure of power. At the same time, he adopted a policy of indirectly assisting the CCP’s preparations to take Taiwan. This was also when US strategy in Asia became focused on preventing the PRC and the Soviet Union from consolidating an alliance. The United States attempted to do so by using the occasion of Mao Zedong’s first visit to Moscow to publicly announce a policy of non-intervention on the Taiwan issue. To pull the PRC into the Soviet camp and prevent the CCP from turning to the United States and the West, as well as to maintain the Soviet Union’s ports and military bases on the Yellow Sea, Stalin responded by acquiescing to Mao’s demands that Dalian, Port Arthur (Lüshun), and the Changchun Railway be returned to China. However, he simultaneously halted indirect assistance for the CCP’s preparations for attacking Taiwan, instead giving Kim Il Sung the green light to launch an attack against South Korea. With the outbreak of the Korean War providing a legitimate pretext, and in response to the signing of the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, Alliance, and Mutual Assistance , the United States adjusted its policy of non-intervention regarding Taiwan. Thus, while the status of Taiwan and Fujian’s coastal islands was considered by both the CCP and the KMT to be China’s internal affair, by 1950, it had already, in Mao’s words, “turned into a complex and serious international struggle.”
