Late Imperial China

Vol. 47, No. 1 · 2026-06 · 4 篇 · Johns Hopkins UP · Chinese history · Peer-reviewed
  1. Notes from Enlightenment Studio: The Movement and Materiality of Scientific Information in Nineteenth-Century China
    John Alekna · pp. 1-28
    摘要

    Between 1867 and 1872, a scholar-clerk in Jiangxi Province composed an inventory of scientific and mathematical books. The list records not only their contents, but also the paths they had traced into the scholar's possession. Thus, the inventory preserves a record of how scientific information moved through inland China in the years immediately following the Taiping Rebellion. Analyzing both the physical and metaphorical aspects of this movement, this article argues that scientific knowledge and practice were promoted and constrained by material conditions. The inventory suggests the rarity of certain scientific-mathematical volumes, and underlines that foreign books translated in Shanghai did not circulate easily, even to provincial capitals. In addition to this material movement, information also moved through different representational languages in different texts, for instance through the translation of mathematics from physical forms (counting rod, abacus) to symbolic ones (abstract notation). As illustrated by the scholar's commentaries, material conditions informed intellectual trends. Finally, the inventory shows the continued importance of manuscripts, even in the age of woodblock and moveable type print. The methods of replication of scientific texts shaped what could be known, and in what manner.

  2. Concealing and Revealing: Women and Embodied Exemplarity in Late Imperial Chinese Biographies
    Xu Ma · pp. 29-69
    摘要

    This article examines a distinctive subset of Qing-dynasty biographies of exemplary women that foreground forensic-style description alongside supernatural revelation. Tracing this practice to Ming precedents, especially Gui Youguang's writings, the article argues that the combined staging of the maimed female body and miraculous occurrences constituted a deliberate narrative strategy for resolving juridical and moral ambiguity surrounding women killed while resisting sexual violation. Through close textual analysis and contextualization within Qing forensic practice, judicial debates, and religious culture, the article demonstrates that graphic attention to bodily wounds functioned as a form of para-juridical evidence, transforming the injured corpse into legible proof of resistance and moral integrity. Divine dreams and posthumous miracles, meanwhile, operated as supplementary modes of validation, compensating for the perceived insufficiency of formal legal adjudication. In this sense, bodily spectacle and miracle worked in tandem not to undermine Confucian norms prescribed by the nei–wai (inner–outer) divide, but to reaffirm them through their strategic suspension under conditions of inconclusive bureaucratic and judicial judgment. Situated at the intersection of history, law, and literature, the examples studied here reveal the uneasy interweaving of moral judgment, legal reasoning, and narrative sensation in Qing biographical writing.

  3. The Rise of a Mountain King: Geopolitics and the Tributary System on the Fifteenth-Century Sichuan-Tibetan Frontier
    Xiaobai Hu · pp. 71-106
    摘要

    In the fifteenth century, the rise of Dongbuhanhu presented a significant political and military challenge for Ming China along its Sichuan-Tibetan frontier. The tributary system played a pivotal role in Dongbuhanhu's development, functioning in different ways at various stages of the polity's rise. From the 1410s to 1430s, Dongbuhanhu employed the tributary system to gain recognition from the Ming, thus consolidating its secular and religious authority. In the 1440s, control over tributary routes became a central element in the power struggle between Dongbuhanhu and Zagu, transforming the system into a strategic tool for geopolitical competition. During the 1450s, the tributary system not only facilitated Dongbuhanhu's accumulation of material wealth but also provided the polity a political framework to establish a hierarchical order in frontier regions. By examining the practical implications of the tributary system in the frontier region, this article traces specific ways through which frontier societies took advantage of imperial policies to negotiate with state authorities for their own interests.

  4. Zhongshu in the Grand Secretariat and Everyday Administration of the Qing Empire
    Xue Zhang · pp. 107-146
    摘要

    This paper examines the pivotal yet largely invisible role of Han-Chinese secretaries known as zhongshu 中書 (7b) in the everyday administration of the Qing empire. It is generally believed that the influence of the Grand Secretaries significantly waned with the development of the palace memorial ( zouzhe 奏折)system in the eighteenth century, which allowed senior officials to bypass the Grand Secretariat and communicate directly with the emperor. A low-ranking secretary at the Grand Secretariat thus was viewed as a sinecure with dim career prospects. Examining zhongshu's responsibilities and activities, I argue that despite their obscurity they were actually the backbone of the Qing central administration, indispensable to the daily operation of the imperial bureaucracy. Moreover, zhongshu were remarkably well connected and informed, which prepared them for higher positions and more important assignments after their Grand Secretariat career. In this sense, the post of zhongshu not only offered aspirating degree-holders promising paths to climb the ladder of success but also trained them to be capable bureaucrats on behalf of the Qing empire.

  1. The “Great Disappearing Act of Success”: Technologies of Speculation in Contemporary Black Financial Fictions
    Deborah Thurman · pp. 1-25 · online 2026-06-22
    摘要

    This article examines how two contemporary works of Black speculative fiction imagine a financialized future, playing with racialized logics of prediction that position whiteness as the watchword for the ceaseless accumulation of value over time. Both Boots Riley’s Sorry to Bother You (2018) and Mateo Askaripour’s Black Buck (2021) depict salesmen on trajectories of individual upward mobility, prospering despite the racial and financial inequalities of their near-future dystopian worlds. Like the tech companies where they work, these characters generate profitable projections, fabricating visions of the future that solicit audience investment. For both protagonists, success involves the strategic performance of whiteness as a tool of financial causality that promises future happiness, security, and unfettered growth. Yet, even as they stage the spectacle of success, Sorry to Bother You and Black Buck formally sabotage the plausibility of their own growth narratives, using flimsy props, temporal acceleration, exaggerated plot twists, and situational irony to render their own storytelling fundamentally absurd. The result, I argue, is speculative fiction that undermines the act of speculation, in both narrative and financial forms. Moving beyond exposure, these texts explore how finance capitalism disciplines desire to foster affective attachments to incredible projections. They invite audiences to disinvest from prediction as the means to secure a happy future, turning instead toward strategic destabilization and radical narrative uncertainty.

  2. Postsentimental Horizons in Sui Sin Far’s “In the Land of the Free”
    Xavier Xin · pp. 26-49 · online 2026-06-23
    摘要

    This article explores the racial politics of sympathy in Sui Sin Far’s short story “In the Land of the Free” (1909). Widely celebrated as the “mother” of Asian American literature, Sui Sin Far dedicated much of her writing career to the advocacy of Chinese immigrant rights. Contrary to the common understanding that presumes the early Asian American writer’s appeal to white sympathy for Chinese immigrants as fundamental to her short stories, I reconsider Sui Sin Far as a trenchant critic of the dominant white sentimental politics of recognition who nonetheless experimented with sentimental tropes to provoke a more liberatory model of social justice that I call “postsentimental allyship.” Building on Lauren Berlant’s formulation of postsentimentalism and Xine Yao’s recent work on unfeeling, I honor this horizon of sociality and its affective reorganization of white-Chinese relations amid the stifling pressure to yield to the terms of white sympathetic recognition during the Chinese Exclusion Era. In analyzing the short story, I locate Sui Sin Far’s dissent from the sentimental politics of recognition through reading practices that attend to Sui Sin Far’s often-overlooked narrative experiments and the Chinese immigrant characters in the story, whose words and gestures express their demand for and enact the practice of alternative politics of advocacy. As sympathy has been normalized into the default affective mode in animating white activism, reading Sui Sin Far’s short story in this way helps us see that there are other possible ways to feel solidarity that do not reinscribe oppression but rather can begin rearranging race relations toward more just dynamics.

  3. Beyond “Saving” Life: Biopolitical Dynamics and Virus Narrative in Saving the World
    Tianran Chen · pp. 50-72 · online 2026-05-27
    摘要

    Julia Alvarez’s Saving the World (2006) employs virus narratives to weave two storylines into a shared account of the entanglement of life, medical intervention, and biopolitics. Reading the novel through the biopolitical transformations of the early nineteenth century, this article examines the 1803 Royal Spanish Smallpox Expedition and its reliance on live carriers to show how an ostensibly humanitarian project was structured by colonial power. It then situates the novel within the context of twenty-first-century globalization to trace the neo-imperial logic of US intervention in the Global South during the AIDS pandemic, particularly at the nexus of biomedical aid, neoliberal governance, and counterterrorism. The article further argues that Alvarez imagines forms of affiliation that exceed colonial and imperial containment through a negative affirmation that moves from immunized individuals to communal life. Saving the World thus reworks the immunitary paradigm by envisioning communities forged across racial, national, and territorial boundaries. In bringing a colonial history of smallpox into dialogue with a fictional AIDS narrative and linking both to questions of care, violence, and survival, the novel reframes biopolitical dynamics transnationally and expands the critical scope of multiethnic US literary study.

    Martha J Cutter · pp. 73-96 · online 2026-07-27
    摘要

    This article concerns medical racism and sexual trauma in Toni Morrison’s Paradise (1997), but also the innovative African Diasporic healing ceremonies the novel depicts, which are key to understanding the mysterious deaths and seeming rebirth of the women who reside in the Convent and are (in theory) massacred by the men from Ruby at the end of the novel. I argue that the healing figure at the center of this novel (Consolata Sosa) creates a unique boundary-melting ceremony that ties together fragments from three different traditions of Africanist healing to create a new ritual that enables physical and spiritual rebirth. Connie draws on Nigerian Òs∘un healing rituals involving water, Afro-Brazilian practices of repair originating in Candomblé, and a configuration of feminine agency and revivification present in the Gnostic and Egyptian-influenced Christian gospel “The Thunder, Perfect Mind” and its invocation of the Egyptian goddess Isis. This last topic, in particular— Morrison’s use of the Gnostic Gospel and the figure of Isis, who was thought to bring people back to life—is key to comprehension of how the novel creates an innovative ritual that facilitates (in Morrison’s own words) “a resurrection that is beyond death.” The healing ceremony at the heart of the novel engenders new psychic and corporeal restorations even after the “death” of the Convent women. The women can therefore return from death to repair the bonds of their communities and institute ongoing forms of reconciliation and reparative justice.

  5. “Playing Latinx” as Settler-Colonial Reenactment
    Sophia Martínez Abbud · pp. 97-113 · online 2026-05-28
    摘要

    This is an article about the “problem of the indio” in a transamerican context of migration, and about accounting for the political role of Indigeneity in contemporary Latinx and Latin American literature. The figure of “the Indian” has been a central concept for national literatures in the so-called Americas since the nineteenth century, and its role becomes further complicated when considering the convergence of Indigeneities across the United States and Mexico and their unique nationalist literary traditions. In considering the intersections of these literary traditions in the space of the US-Mexico borderlands, this article identifies the narrative act of “playing Latinx,” whereby texts about the US-Mexico borderlands perform the dual reenactment of mestizaje and settler-colonial history. Using a Critical Latinx Indigeneities framework to analyze Valeria Luiselli’s migration texts—Tell Me How It Ends: An Essay in Forty Questions (2017) and Lost Children Archive (2019), to which I refer jointly as the “Lost Children Project”—this article traces the related but distinct intellectual genealogies that reduce Indigeneity to a cultural trait rather than a political condition.

  6. Eva’s (In)visible Man: Reading Gayl Jones through the Lens of Black Male Vulnerability
    Tuula Kolehmainen · pp. 114-133 · online 2026-07-17
    摘要

    Despite its title, Gayl Jones’s novel Eva’s Man (1976) is not a story of a man. Instead, it is a disturbing account of the experiences of an abused woman, Eva Medina Canada, who grotesquely murders Davis Carter, a man she had met a few days prior. While exploring Eva’s Man from the perspective of Black women’s victimization is relevant and necessary, in this article, I read beyond a victim/perpetrator binary and focus attention on the male victim and female perpetrators that are seldom addressed in critical readings of this novel or in scholarship more generally. Drawing on Tommy J. Curry’s theorization of Black male vulnerability (Man-Not), I examine the (in)visibility of Black men as victims and women as perpetrators across the spectrum of intergenerational and interpersonal violence reproduced in society and reflected in the novel. I argue that reading the male character as not only a metonym for masculine aggression against women but also as a victim allows us to understand the novel more deeply. Not only does Davis stand for and remind Eva of her previous abusers but also he is a victim of the same cycle of violence in which Eva is victimized and in which all the characters, men and women, are somehow involved. Rereading the novel through the lens of Black male vulnerability enables us to see beyond racialized gender stereotypes and binaries and focus instead on the spectrum of violence itself to better understand its psychological, social, and political functions and ramifications.

  7. “The Logic Is Built Right into the Architecture”: Speculative Architecture in Contemporary Queer-of-Color Science Fiction
    Kathryn Harlan-Gran · pp. 134-157 · online 2026-07-17
    摘要

    This article studies Rivers Solomon’s An Unkindness of Ghosts (2017) and Larissa Lai’s Salt Fish Girl (2002) to explore a concept that I term speculative architecture, which describes speculative, humanmade spaces and structures onto which authors layer social meaning. I argue that authors such as Solomon and Lai leverage the generic characteristics of speculative fiction to write social ideologies into the physical constructs of the world, posing a challenge to forms of oppression that rely on our understandings of such spaces, and their structuring logics, as natural and innate. In An Unkindness of Ghosts, Solomon transcribes histories of the Middle Passage onto the futuristic spaceship, challenging certain sciencefiction traditions that treat interstellar colonization as an idealized future for humanity without acknowledging the circumstances necessary for such a future to come about. In Salt Fish Girl, Lai critiques the racialized and gendered histories of inclusion and exclusion written into sub/urban borders and the mechanisms of control necessary to maintain those borders. Interestingly, both novels suggest gardens as potentially revolutionary interstitial spaces, in which the protagonists explore possibilities not prescribed by the material structures of oppression that otherwise dictate their lives. Thus, attention to speculative architectures highlights various possibilities for navigating narrative and material spaces, offering alternative epistemologies of both familiar and fantastical structures. Importantly, these characteristics are transferable across other works of speculative fiction, including not only sci-fi but also horror, fantasy, and magical realism, offering an interpretive lens that can be used to broadly articulate representations of spatiality, materiality, and sociality.

  8. Dirty Words: Lack and/of Innocence in Toni Morrison’s The Bluest Eye
    Rachel Windsor · pp. 158-177 · online 2026-06-12
    摘要

    Toni Morrison’s The Bluest Eye (1970) depicts a complex interplay of lack and fetishism. While many scholars read narrator Claudia and protagonist Pecola in opposition—emblematic of childhood survival and failure, respectively—this article argues that the novel links the girls insofar as both are excluded from an innocence primarily associated with white childhood. Both girls respond to the shameful sense of lack that emerges from their unfulfilled desire for innocence by fetishizing symbols of the ideal object. While innocence depends on negation, fetishization operates by substituting one love-object for another. As such, fetishization necessarily fails to “produce” innocence for either girl. Claudia, who fetishizes cleanliness and “good grammar,” recognizes the inadequacy of her substitution even as she maintains an attachment to it. She consequently exhibits what David Eng and Shinhee Han call “racial melancholia,” an orientation toward lack that permeates the formal elements of her narrative. Conversely Pecola, who fetishizes the titular blue eyes, uncritically adores her substitution. Enacting the process of incorporation theorized by Nicolas Abraham and Maria Torok allows Pecola to keep innocence “alive” within her unconscious but also requires she compulsively stage the fantasy of the object’s continued existence. Attending to the girls’ shared melancholia alongside the parallels between them ultimately enables a reparative reading that honors their position in Morrison’s lineage of complex girlhood friendships.

  9. Political Act and Poetic Act: An Interview with Kimiko Hahn

    This interview with renowned Asian American poet Kimiko Hahn, Chancellor of the Academy of American Poets and New York State Poet Laureate, 2025-27, includes biographical information about her life growing up with artistic parents in a mixed-ethnicity family, the blended influences of Japanese and European poetic forms on her work, her childhood love of language, activism as a young feminist in the 1960s and 70 s, the roles of unconscious processes and formal structures within the creative process, and the place of poetry in our social landscapes.

    摘要

    Melanie R. Hill’s Colored Women Sittin’ on High: Womanist Sermonic Practice in Literature and Music provides a useful interdisciplinary analysis of women’s public speech and performance as it is affiliated with theology and social justice. The book includes discussion of African American literary characters as well as actual women, ordained or not, who have preached and sung their way into local, regional, and national influence. Hill’s argument relies on insights drawn from literary theory, critical race theory, classic and contemporary theology, and musicology. Its coverage sweeps across twentieth- and twenty-first-century America with references to earlier periods. Given the disciplinary isolation within which many scholars work, nearly every reader will find much that is new here. In her introductory chapter, Hill links these disciplines through attention to “sermonic practice.” That is, while most of the figures Hill explores are not literal ministers preaching from a literal pulpit, they all engage with readers and listeners as a preacher might through “prayers, prophecy, and praise” (1). As specifically African American women often communicating with a primarily African American audience, they participate in the ministry of the Black church in America, which understands its call as liberatory. Hill interprets scenes from literature and musical performances as doing the work of sermons, but she also examines sermons—the texts and the delivery—as a literary genre. In this chapter, she devotes extensive space to contextualizing her argument and defining her terms, not only the specifically religious ones such as “sermonic practice” but also more theoretical ones such as “womanist,” a term used primarily within literary studies as an African American elaboration on, amplification of, and critique of feminism. She acknowledges the particularly patriarchal assumptions and practices embedded in many religious traditions, a fact that prompts her analysis and approach.

  1. Political notes of nauras : Emergence of an aesthetically embodied kingship practice in Adil Shahi Bijapur
    Namrata B. Kanchan · pp. 263-289 · online 2026-07-17
    摘要

    From late sixteenth century, Bijapur’s sultan, Ibrahim Adil Shah II (r. 1580–1627 ce ), used nauras —a polyvalent term used extensively within the Sanskrit aesthetic realm—on his kingdom’s cultural artefacts as well as political and administrative insignia. An avid music lover, he is renowned for his Dakani work on music titled Kitāb-i Nauras ( circa 1580s). Portrayed by previous scholars as religiously unorthodox, Ibrahim Adil II and nauras are located chiefly within narratives of Bijapur’s political instability and the sultan’s indulgence in leisure over statecraft. Recent scholarship has challenged such notions but no study focuses on the reasons for nauras ’ crossover to the political domain or its appearance on state insignia. This article offers new insights by locating the sultan within a matrix of Indic, Turco-Mongol, and Islamicate sovereignty practices. In doing so, it argues that Ibrahim Adil II strategically employed the corporeal, religious, aesthetic, and polyvalent dimensions of nauras to forge a uniquely personalized embodied cosmic kingship practice to govern a multicultural populace. In particular, this article elucidates that the realms of art, aesthetics, and kingship were not mutually exclusive in the Indic or Islamicate worlds and that nauras was a rational manoeuvre to elevate the ruler above courtly factions and religious differences.

  2. Whose women and whose honour? A fragile imperial discourse on the Baluch-Punjab frontier, late nineteenth century
    Gagan Kumar · pp. 290-322 · online 2026-07-06
    摘要

    This article focuses on the Punjab-Baluch borderland region during the last decade of the nineteenth century. It shows how this region was a conflict zone, not only between local communities across borders but also between the two colonial frontier governments of Punjab and Baluchistan. The article explores the nature of these conflicts by examining a cross-border dispute involving women. It analyses how different competing legal systems—Shariat, customs, and colonial law—operated on the ground and were used by the disputants to resolve the conflict. Additionally, it discusses how, during this process, the colonial state documented women’s presence and used their voices and actions to serve the objectives of state-making. Through this case study, the article demonstrates that in local feuds involving women, colonial authorities emerged chiefly as disputants rather than just arbitrators. By claiming to be the legitimate custodians of the ‘abducted’ women, the two frontier governments competed against each other to fulfil the aspirations of the tribal communities they represented. This intra-tribal and intra-colonial dispute reveals deep fissures in colonial understanding of questions of state intervention, sovereignty, and colonial subjecthood—rendering the imperial project inconsistent, fragile, and contradictory in the Punjab-Baluch borderlands.

  3. Typhoid, milk, and the military: India’s first dairying revolution, 1880–1925
    David Arnold · pp. 323-346 · online 2026-09-04
    摘要

    Government alarm over the extent of enteric fever (typhoid) among British troops in India in the late nineteenth century focused concern on adulterated milk as a likely medium for the transmission of disease and incentivized the creation of cantonment dairies, of which there were more than 30 by 1914. Aided by the introduction of modern milking techniques and butter-making equipment, military farms and government-sponsored dairies helped create a new market for dairy products in India, fostered the growth of privately run dairies, and encouraged the idea of milk consumption as an aid to health. The new dairies, with their intensive cattle-breeding programmes, were further seen as model institutions and centres for the dissemination of scientific dairying across India. The cantonment dairies drew in part on India’s own cattle culture and anticipated the ‘white revolution’ of the 1970s; but the uniqueness of the cantonment environment, the high costs of intensive dairying, and the reliance on specialized breeding inhibited the wider application of the military dairy model while intensifying Hindu opposition to cantonments as cow-killing sites.

  4. Borderland extraterritoriality: The Yunnan-Burma frontier meetings (1902–1949)
    Li Wan · pp. 347-372 · online 2026-09-22
    摘要

    Britain exercised a distinctive form of extraterritorial jurisdiction around the Yunnan-Burma border before 1949. In 1902, Chinese and British officials established a joint trial system under the 1902 Manai Agreement. From then on, Chinese, British, and Burmese officials convened temporary frontier meetings each winter in border areas, including in Manai, Nawngma, and Sima. These meetings adjudicated disputes involving theft, injuries, and trans-frontier cultivation pursuant to tribal customary law. The frontier meetings normally issued four distinct types of judgments and awarded a uniform remedy in the form of damages. This system served the practical needs of border tribes by delivering swift justice to prevent blood feuds and maintain law and order. These meetings developed a case law for resolving borderland cases that diverged from the national laws of both China and Britain. This system was jointly administered by Chinese, British, and Burmese officials under ostensibly reciprocal terms, though Britain’s exercise of extraterritorial jurisdiction in China ultimately placed a heavier burden on the Chinese side. The joint trial system came to an end after Burma officially gained independence in 1948. British extraterritorial jurisdiction in China was not absolute but operated through distinct jurisdictional systems in the interior and in the borderlands.

  5. The brokerage of order in Karachi
    Adeem Suhail · pp. 373-392 · online 2026-08-05
    摘要

    This article reframes Lyari’s gangs in Karachi as brokers of political order rather than merely criminal entities. Drawing on five years of ethnographic and archival research, it argues that the figure of the ‘gangster’ functioned as a political intermediary, stabilizing contradictions between military regimes, capital accumulation, and working-class urban life. Through portraits of three interlocutors—a tragic and unlikely ‘gangster’, a gang underboss who mediated between state projects and the denizens of his neighbourhood, and a socialist activist targeted for elimination by the gangs on behalf of the state—the article demonstrates how state, civil society, and scholarly discourses have unwittingly colluded to produce ‘Lyari-as-gangland’ without attending to what the gangs actually did in Lyari apart from the violence that overdetermines their era of dominance. It argues that coding brokerage as criminological masks the gang’s everyday functions in projects of public health, housing, and bureaucratic mediation. Furthermore, the rise of gangs to this role is historically situated in the conjuncture of the role of Pakistan’s military dictatorship in the global war on terror, where violent non-state actors were instrumentalized to produce a highly unequal order in the city.

  6. Waves of feeling: Emotions, media, and the Chinese Communist Revolution
    Dayton Lekner · pp. 393-415 · online 2026-08-11
    摘要

    How did the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) foster emotional engagement with its revolution? How did the advent of new media transform this engagement? Building on research that has noted the importance of emotions in the CCP’s revolution, this article explores these questions through a study of CCP radio and the person of the announcer. Using broadcast circulars and directives, memoirs, and diaries, it explores how broadcasters found an appropriate emotional tone for political texts, and how individual broadcasters functioned as nodes in the diffusion of emotions over an expanding network of radio stations. I make three arguments: first, that along with the well-documented normative forces of Party organization, announcers relied on reason and introspection to find their own emotional expression of a text and, with that, an emotional engagement with the revolution; second, that announcers were not anomalous in their reasoned engagement, but represent a consistent strain of community-building emotional practice within the ranks of the CCP; and third, that the advent of radio empowered the CCP to scale up its subject-oriented emotion work, developed at Yan’an but locally bound, to the regional and, eventually, the national scale. In this scaling up, extant CCP work-practice interacted with the promises and limits of the new media to create a distinct broadcasting culture that would shape the use of radio throughout the Mao era.

  7. Managing culture: The role of music in state-led cultural reproduction in post-colonial Pakistan
    Ghulam Ali Shair · pp. 416-448 · online 2026-09-17
    摘要

    If music’s place remains ideologically contested in the national cultural formation of post-colonial Pakistan, what are the terms, if any, by which the state engages with this art form? Answering this question, along with others, this article advances the term ‘logic of managing culture’ to explore the Pakistani state’s relationship with music. Through contesting India-centric scholarship on music and cultural politics in the South Asian context and relying on an eclectic array of empirical evidence, I argue that the post-colonial state’s engagement with music is marked by a set of priorities that entails a logic of managing music rather than reproducing it. This orchestration plays out at two major levels: the international, involving strategically projecting selected elements of Pakistan’s musical-cultural identity internationally, and the national, relying on language (Urdu) and religion (Islam) for national integration, while bypassing the role of music. I suggest that this amounts to a logic of cultural management, wherein the state, through a set of cultural institutions, ‘conducts’ music and its practitioners while presupposing the ideologically contested place of this art form in the national cultural formation of Pakistan.

    Prashant Iyengar · pp. 449-518 · online 2026-07-06

    This article presents conclusions from a study of 1,400 criminal trials in cases involving anti-caste and tribe violence, filed in the trial court of Aurangabad District (Sambhajinagar) in western India. Employing computational analysis upon the metadata and text of decisions filed under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) (POA) Act 1989 during a 20-year period (2002–2023), I offer an exploratory socio-legal analysis of hate-crime adjudication in India. This article sheds light on hitherto unexplored questions about criminal adjudication in India such as: Which cases are most likely to result in acquittals and convictions? What kind of evidence does the court consider and in what manner is evidence read? How frequently are cases dismissed due to witnesses turning hostile? What kinds of punishments do Indian courts hand out? How long do criminal trials typically last? What kind of charges are most commonly brought against the accused in these cases? How easy is it to get bail and what conditions do courts typically impose? How long do POA-accused spend in jail before they get bail?. In doing so, this article offers a first-of-its kind phenomenology of ‘hate-crime’ adjudication and, more broadly, of criminal adjudication in India.

  9. The dynamics and ambiguities of ‘Chineseness’: Interethnic marriage practices in the Dutch Batavia before 1850
    Victoria S. Zhou, Tak-Wai Hung · pp. 519-544 · online 2026-09-16
    摘要

    This article explores how interethnic marriage produces and governs ambiguous identities within legally pluralist port-city settings. Taking the construction of ‘Chineseness’ in the Dutch Batavia before 1850 as a case study, this article analyses how identity was contested, negotiated, and reconfigured in a colonial legal landscape. Drawing on archival records from the Batavia Kong Koan (the Chinese Council), this article argues that normative orders from the homeland, such as Confucian ethical distinctions between the ‘civilized’ and the ‘uncivilized’ and gendered prescriptions governing family life and female conduct, were not merely adapted to local conditions but were frequently disrupted by diasporic realities. Through case studies of interethnic marriages and female-initiated divorces, the article highlights how female agency within the Kong Koan’s hybrid legal regime fractured the ideological coherence of the Confucian moral order and exposed the instability of ‘Chineseness’ under colonial rule. Situated at the intersection of claimed Chinese custom, Dutch colonial statutes, and the everyday realities of interethnic co-residence, the Kong Koan did not preserve tradition so much as mediate and fragment it. Rather than reinforcing a fixed notion of identity, the institution became a mechanism for its continuous remaking. By locating identity within everyday social practice and the institutional logics of colonial governance, this article challenges essentialist conceptions of diaspora. It offers a historically grounded account of how an ethnic identity like ‘Chineseness’ was continuously unmade and remade at the intersection of multiple legal and cultural systems within colonial jurisdictions.

  10. Inscribing chölkha : Census, election, and the making of modern Tibetan diaspora identity
    Ugyan Choedup · pp. 545-584 · online 2026-09-21
    摘要

    This article examines the historical formation of modern chölkha identity, a cornerstone of contemporary Tibetan nationalist thought. Rather than a direct continuation of medieval Tibetan identity categories, this article argues that modern chölkha identity is a contingent product of the Tibetan encounter with colonial modernity, especially in exile. By analysing the introduction of the modern census and electoral representation in exile, this article demonstrates how institutional logics of governmentality reconstituted once-fluid, elite-defined spatial categories into standardized, mutually exclusive popular identities. This is not to suggest that chölkha identity was invented ex nihilo by exiled Tibetan nationalist elites. On the contrary, and well known among scholars, the chölkha , as a spatial category among the literate class, has existed since the thirteenth century. Yet, as this article argues, its form, scope, and semantic load were different from those of its modern counterpart. Drawing on this history, the article proposes a ‘sequential thesis’ as a way of reframing Benedict Anderson’s concept of seriality. This article argues that ‘unbound’ and ‘bound’ serialities are best understood not as opposing types but as historical sequences, a process wherein fluid imaginaries are contingently captured by the state’s institutional grid, generating the rigid collective subjectivities that define the modern world.

  11. Hybridity, glocalization, and the negotiation of contemporary Chineseness in guoman (national animation): White Snake: Afloat (2024)
    Chenglong Zhou · pp. 585-612 · online 2026-09-22
    摘要

    This article examines Light Chaser’s animation White Snake: Afloat (2024) within the context of the revival of Chinese guoman 國漫 (national animation) since the 2010s. It reflects on a key gap in existing literature: a failure to analyse the dynamic interplay of state ideology, market demands, and animators’ agency in the construction of specific guoman texts. Drawing on an interdisciplinary framework comprising Homi Bhabha’s ‘hybridity’, Roland Robertson’s ‘glocalization’, and Weiyu Zhang’s ‘Chineseness as identity work’, this article explores how the tripartite negotiation leads to distinct forms of hybridity across three aspects of the film—techno-artistic, narrative, and structural—against the backdrop of media glocalization. The analysis also examines how the film’s hybrid forms embody competing versions of Chineseness. The overall argument is that the hybridity in Afloat is a product of the triad’s complex negotiation; it illuminates the contentious status quo of contemporary Chineseness as a globalized ‘identity work’—a dynamic, ongoing, and contested process of constructing identity, encompassing not only a subject’s self-identification but also how others identify that subject.

  12. Allies apart: China, Russia, and the limits of mnemonic friendship
    Vincent K. L. Chang, Eric S. Zhang · pp. 613-641 · online 2026-09-17
    摘要

    Addressing a gap in memory studies and international relations, this article examines the construction and limits of Sino-Russian mnemonic friendship through historical narratives of the Second World War. Drawing on extensive multilingual datasets of Chinese and Russian state-sponsored media output, supplemented by additional primary sources and fieldwork in China, it identifies a complex pattern of selective remembering and strategic forgetting across four key wartime themes: the wartime Kuomintang (KMT)–Chinese Communist Party (CCP) united front, early Soviet aid, bilateral tensions in Xinjiang, and the Soviet offensive in Manchuria. While Beijing and Moscow’s official discourses converge on the moral lessons of the war, alignment on historical events remains largely confined to strategic silences. There is little substantive narrative convergence, and personal wartime stories and Sino-Soviet cooperation remain largely untapped. This limited convergence is explained by domestic legitimation imperatives, ethnonationalist impulses, enduring mutual distrust, and divergent visions for regional and global order. The article argues that mnemonic alliances are inherently fragile, dependent on bottom-up engagement and broader social resonance, even in authoritarian contexts. Drawing attention to the mnemonic dimension of China–Russia relations illuminates the fragility of mutual trust and the long-term vulnerability of this relationship, as narrative silences can be easily undone.

  1. Experience, person, and myth: A socio-cultural history of the ‘oily man’ in post-colonial Malaysia and Singapore
    Esmond Chuah Meng Soh, Jin Rong Aw · pp. 1-29 · online 2026-10-26
    摘要

    Drawing on English, Chinese, and Malay newspapers, this article examines the ‘oily man’, a figure who shifted between sexual assailant, ghost, and intruder across twentieth-century Singapore and urban and semi-urban peninsular Malaya/Malaysia. It situates him not as a timeless ‘Malay’ entity but as an elastic label and repertoire, assembled and reassembled through rumours, retellings, and recurring events. Departing from most studies of Malay-world monsters, which reduce such figures to allegories or cinematic symbols of gender, modernity, or social change, this article demonstrates how the oily man’s historical force lay in intrusions, panics, and community responses—events mediated, disputed, and reworked across time and place. His history is framed through three registers: experience, person, and myth, which trace how this elastic label took shape through encounter, attribution, and retelling. Experience captures sightings, rumours, and assaults that animated fear; person traces how individuals were accused or apprehended as oily men; myth designates the narratives and repertoires that amplified these encounters in film, fiction, and folklore. Across these registers, the article shows how monsters emerge through lived circulations of testimony, attribution, and storytelling. It highlights the value of historical research that privileges experience and offers a framework for future scholarship: monsters as unstable, context-specific composites of encounter, narrative, and transmission that illuminate the entanglements of state, society, culture, and religion in post-colonial Malaysia and Singapore, with resonance for the study of rumour and monstrosity elsewhere in Asia.

  2. Where is Rama in Bengali folk songs? A case of devapolitik, mythopoetic dissonance, or performative abstention in bhakti federalism of Bengal
    Sayantan Thakur · pp. 1-16 · online 2026-10-26
    摘要

    This article examines the striking marginality of Lord Rama in Bengali-language folk songs and performance-based devotional repertoires, reading this absence not as a simple omission but as a culturally patterned silence shaped by regional aesthetics, vernacular religiosity, and historical power formations. Rather than presuming a uniform pan-Indian bhakti field, the article focuses on Hindu devotional song-worlds in Bengal—especially Vaishnava-inflected oral and performative contexts—where Krishna emerges as the dominant affective deity: intimate, plural, and theatrically adaptable. Rama, by contrast, appears as comparatively distant, associated with moral restraint and epic discipline that often resist the emotional grammar of folk performance. Drawing on folkloristics, performance theory, and critical approaches to discourse and cultural hegemony, the article argues that devotional absence can function as a mode of cultural agency: what is not sung may still carry ideological weight. Concepts such as devapolitik, mythopoetic dissonance, bhakti federalism, performative abstention, and scriptural decentring are deployed as interpretive tools to illuminate how regional devotional cultures selectively remember, transform, or sideline divine figures, thereby producing a distinctive devotional geography within Bengal’s plural religious landscape.

Vol. 52, No. 6 · 2026-11 · 4 篇 · SAGE · China · Peer-reviewed
  1. A Changing Legal World: Christianity and Extraterritoriality in a Sichuan Courtroom (1810–1911)
    Yuan Tian · pp. 639-674 · online 2026-07-30
    摘要

    This article examines the juridical interactions between Christian congregations and local communities in late Qing Sichuan by tracing how extraterritoriality operated in everyday judicial practice. Moving beyond accounts centered on anti-Christian violence, it analyzes how Chinese converts, non-Christian litigants, Western missionaries, and Qing officials navigated the uncertainties that imperial encroachment brought to local adjudication. Drawing on county-level judicial cases, imperial documents, local gazetteers, and missionary accounts, the study shows how Chinese Christians learned to mobilize missionary-backed extraterritorial leverage to circumvent routine barriers to legal access, while non-Christians and local elites developed strategic countermeasures to cope with foreign interference. Rather than treating extraterritoriality solely as a colonial imposition, the article argues that it became embedded as an additional, treaty-produced dimension of judicial operation in local society. By foregrounding the agency of multiple social actors, this study offers a nuanced account of how extraterritoriality reshaped late Qing local justice.

  2. Pulling Strings at the Margins: Blind Storytellers and the Politics of Survival in Socialist China, 1938–1977
    Yi Ren · pp. 675-705 · online 2026-08-04
    摘要

    This article examines the mobilization and governance of blind storytellers in Southeast Shanxi from 1938 to 1977, arguing that disabled bodies occupied a structurally ambivalent position within the Chinese Communist Party’s revolutionary project. Their mobility, endurance, and bodily labor enabled the extension of state power into rural society and were endowed with political value. However, these same qualities proved increasingly incompatible with socialist labor regimes organized around standardized productivity and administrative control. As a result, blind storytellers were progressively reclassified from effective propagandists into marginal or welfare-dependent subjects. Drawing on local archives and oral histories, this article shows how revolutionary inclusion did not resolve social difference but reorganized it, producing new forms of differentiated value and exclusion. The case of blind storytellers thus reveals a fundamental tension within socialist governance between incorporation and control.

  3. Hindered by Informal Property Relations: A Case Study of Developmental Strategies in Rural Industrialization in China
    Xinxing Duan · pp. 706-749 · online 2026-06-10
    摘要

    Why have existing developmental strategies failed to promote rural industrial development more effectively in many regions of China? This question cannot be fully answered by prevailing developmental state theory, which emphasizes the institutional conditions of embedded autonomy, market competition, and enterprise investment capacity, while overlooking the influence of informal property relations within industries. This article’s case study of an industrial township in northern China demonstrates that informal property relations, tied to entrepreneurs’ informal access to labor, land, and environmental resources, have been persistently maintained through socially embedded power interactions. These relations have contributed substantial profits to rural industries and greatly alleviated pressure on entrepreneurs, making them unwilling to reinvest profits into development activities. Instead, profits are allocated to simple industrial expansion or personal consumption. As a result, the developmental strategies fail to achieve their intended effects because of a lack of response from enterprises. Furthermore, this study examines two attempts by the government to formalize these property relations—the construction of industrial parks and more stringent environmental governance—and explains how their impact has been constrained. This research provides valuable insights for late-developing regions with lagging political and economic reforms and deepens our understanding of the substantive view of the economy.

  4. Public Opinion on Criminal Trial Proceedings in China: An Examination of a Capital Case
    Bin Liang, Jiaqi Yan, Ming Hu, Hua Zhong · pp. 750-785 · online 2026-08-26
    摘要

    Historically, opportunities for members of the public in China to observe criminal trials have been limited. Other than jurors and lay judges (“people’s assessors”), the public has rarely had opportunities to observe criminal trial proceedings in person. Along with China’s reform measures to increase judicial transparency, the move to broadcasting trials online via platforms like China Court Trial Online offers an invaluable opportunity for the public to observe trials. In this study, a fully recorded homicide trial in mainland China was shown to students enrolled in law majors (n=97) and non-law majors (n=86) from one Chinese university. Their evaluations of the trial proceedings were subsequently surveyed. This is the first known study that allows members of the public to watch a full-length trial and provide their assessments of criminal trial proceedings in China. The issues reported by students echo problems identified by scholars and shed significant light on potential lessons to be learned from public observation of Chinese criminal trials.

Modern Chinese Literature and Culture

  1. Note from the Editors
    Natascha Gentz, Christopher Rosenmeier · pp. v-vi
    摘要

    Several articles in this issue of Modern Chinese Literature and Culture examine physical disability and the boundaries of body and mind.As usual, the various studies cover a wide range of approaches and sources, but to the extent that a common thread runs through many of these pieces, it relates to fragmentation.Bodies, minds, texts, and identities are divided, split, and, at least occasionally, reassembled or reconstituted through technological means.Deleuze and Guattari feature in three studies, all in different ways, showing the breadth of their theoretical frameworks and their wide applicability.Jiahe Mei analyzes Guo Moruo's 1928 fairy tale "One Hand," examining how disability serves as a constituent of revolutionary literature.By linking the short story's industrial injuries to Guo's own hearing loss, the author explores ironic temporalities and the deaf phonograph metaphor to redefine revolutionary subjectivity.Physical disability is configured in a dramatically different way in 1960s-1970s Hong Kong popular culture, as shown in Liu Jinping's examination of Hong Kong martial arts films and science fiction.Liu uses the "dividual" concept to view the broken body as a site for technological assemblage.This dividual body allowed creators to negotiate the socio-historical pressures of war, industrialization, and postcolonial identity through a fluid, non-essentialist sense of self.Moving on to the fragmentation of the mind, Richard Letteri analyzes Zhang Yimou's celebrated 1991 film Raise the Red Lantern

  2. “One Hand” and the Deaf Ear: Disabled Futures in Guo Moruo’s Revolutionary Fairy Tale
    Jiahe Mei · pp. 1-29
    摘要

    This essay revisits the agenda of “revolutionary literature” through the lens of “disability,” focusing on two overlooked aspects of Guo Moruo’s life: his 1928 fairy tale “One Hand” (Yi zhi shou), which thematizes workplace injuries as a catalyst for proletarian revolution, and his own hearing loss that spurred his transition from medicine to literature. By analyzing the tale’s ambivalent portrayal of disabled characters alongside the revolutionary writer’s sensorial and experiential loss amid a revolutionary crisis, I reveal how the fairy tale destabilizes normative assumptions about temporality and communication in revolutionary literature. In particular, I argue that the tale features an “ironic” temporality that precludes disabled aspirants from their envisioned futures as well as a “loud” pedagogy that displaces conceptions of a transparent voice with a materialist, processual notion of sound. Foregrounding the twin paradoxes that revolutionary triumph was envisioned in the wake of actual failure and that the well-known phonograph metaphor was articulated when Guo was nearly deaf, this essay complicates the debates on revolutionary subjectivity and paves new paths for conceptualizing disability not as an exception to but as a constituent of revolutionary literature and revolutionary futures.

  3. More than Dismemberment: The Fragmented Body in 1960s–1970s Hong Kong Popular Culture
    Liu Jinping · pp. 30-59
    摘要

    Bodily fragmentation emerged as a significant topos in Hong Kong popular culture in the 1960s and 1970s, as it was produced, circulated, and proliferated across interconnected genres, such as martial arts novels, science fiction, and action films. Existing studies, informed by the notion of a stable and complete body, often interpret imagery such as the one-armed hero as a form of horrific dismemberment produced by violence. This article employs the concept of the “dividual” to capture the body's permeable, divisible, and reconfigurable nature, which is prominent in these works. From this perspective, the mutilation of the human body becomes an opportunity for relational and technological assemblages with nonhuman objects, as particularly exemplified in Chang Cheh's martial arts films and Ni Kuang's science fiction. Situated within a specific historical context shaped by the dynamics of war, industrialization, and postcolonialism, the representation of the fragmented body in 1960s and 1970s Hong Kong popular culture presents not only the dismembered body but also an attempt to negotiate and respond to it. This response involves constructing a dividual Hong Kong body that is constantly open to the process of heterogeneous assemblage and becoming.

  4. Deleuze and Guattari's Despotic and Capitalist Social Machines in Zhang Yimou's Raise the Red Lantern
    Richard Letteri · pp. 60-94
    摘要

    Chinese film scholars have long established the ways in which the Fifth Generation of filmmakers employ rural allegory to symbolize the patriarchal authoritarianism that has reigned over the Chinese people. However, focusing my analysis on Zhang Yimou's Raise the Red Lantern (Dahong denglong gaogao gua) from 1991, I suggest that to understand the struggles of Songlian, the film's female protagonist, it is necessary to address not only the repressive patriarchal forces of Confucian morality in combination with the authoritarian character of the Communist party-state but consider also the forces unleashed by liberalism and capitalism from the May Fourth Movement through Deng Xiaoping's policy of economic modernization. I develop my analysis of the film through Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari's understanding of the despotic and capitalist social machines. I show how these social machines release the forces of territorialization and deterritorialization in ways consistent with the polyvalent forces at play in twentieth-century China and explain how Songlian, who represents both the students who participated in the 1989 Democracy Movement and the Chinese people more generally, moves from a political state of paranoid neurosis to one of catatonic psychosis. This essay thus presents a “schizoanalytic” investigation of the conflicting forces of deterritorialization and reterritorialization and their effects on Chinese subjects caught between the despotic and capitalist social machines.

  5. The Rebellious Manchu Self in the Early Work of Liu Honglin (Xiao Jun)
    Martin Blahota · pp. 95-119
    摘要

    Liu Honglin, better known by his pen name Xiao Jun, is widely recognized as the author of one of the first novels to expose the situation in occupied Manchuria, Village in August (Bayue de xiangcun), whose publication in 1935 served to unite the Chinese nation in a time of crisis. However, a reading of Liu Honglin’s early self-referential work, published only a few years before the Japanese occupation, indicates that in the late 1920s, his vision of Manchuria’s attachment to China was highly complicated. This paper argues that the portrayal of the Manchu self in Liu’s stories and essays published mainly in 1929 strained the relationship with China represented in these writings. The paper places Liu Honglin’s early work in the context of the broader sociohistorical factors of the period to demonstrate that it narrates a fragmented borderland subjectivity informed by the marginal position of Manchus and Manchurian Chinese. Proposing to see Liu as an intellectual whose work challenged discrimination against minority groups within mainstream Han Chinese society, the paper opens up a space for a reassessment of Liu Honglin’s early work, highlighting a neglected and unexpected Manchu voice in the history of modern Chinese literature.

  6. Happy Together: The Socialist Utopia in a Shanghai Worker's Apartment
    Antonio Yijiao Guo · pp. 120-145
    摘要

    This paper analyzes the visual manifestation of happiness in the propaganda poster A Happy Life Given by Chairman Mao, designed by Xin Liliang and published in 1954 in Shanghai. Special attention is paid to how material abundance defines a utopian vision of socialism via the potlatch composition. The poster embodies a paradox: people can only understand socialism by celebrating and fetishizing an array of commodities such as foodstuffs, furniture, appliances, and the poster itself. At the same time, the symbolic contentment of materiality forges a “nostalgia” for a socialist utopia that is ambiguously defined in time and space. The poster consequently validates the policies regarding labor, production, and redistribution, which, in turn, are believed to bring about the envisioned contentment and happiness. Eventually, the individual pursuit of happiness is intertwined with a national metanarrative of the promised bright future, even though the tension between individuals and the state is ubiquitous and irreconcilable.

  7. Hsia Yü's Algorithmic Authorship: Reading Pink Noise as Computer-Generated Text
    Kate Costello · pp. 146-167
    摘要

    This article examines the work of Huang Qingqi (1956–), an enigmatic figure in the Taiwanese literary scene better known by her pen name Hsia Yü. Her 2007 landmark collection Pink Noise (Fenhongse zaoyin) is celebrated for its unique material form and creation process: translated pink lines on clear acetate pages, with text attributed to the Apple Sherlock software system. In laying claims to algorithmic authorship, Pink Noise is a computer-generated text, the product of an ambiguous collaboration between human and machine. Interrogating Hsia Yü's creative process, the paratextual proclamations about machine translation serve to obscure human agency and labor practices in the book's creation. The contested authorial status of the poetry demands attentiveness to textual detail. Reading Pink Noise as a computer-generated text in its full textual detail reveals unsettling grammatical slippages, its saccharine imagery veering toward the dystopian and the surreal. This article argues that Pink Noise merits a position alongside other works of algorithmic authorship; its fragile textuality deserves attentive reading and rereading.

  1. Localized Stone Forms and Local Agency: Satsuma Stupas and the Material Practice of Zen Buddhism in Kamakura Kyushu
    Soyeon Kim · pp. 1-31
    摘要

    This article examines the Satsuma stupas ( satsumatō ), a group of distinctive stone monuments produced in coastal Kyushu during the Kamakura period, as evidence of localized Buddhist material practice shaped through transregional contact. Rather than treating these monuments as anomalous derivatives of continental prototypes or as passive by-products of maritime trade, this study approaches them as material responses to changing religious and social conditions in thirteenth-century Japan. Through a comparative analysis of stone stupa forms from Southern Song coastal China and their selective reception in Kyushu, the article traces how Song-style visual idioms were transmitted, transformed, and redeployed without the wholesale transfer of their original doctrinal frameworks. Attention is given to the roles of Zen expansion, funerary practice, imported materials, and artisanal networks in shaping these monuments. Situating the Satsuma stupas within overlapping spheres of maritime exchange and local religious need, this study argues that they represent community-based, non-elite forms of Buddhist expression that illuminate how "ordinary" monuments mediated death, memory, and salvation at the margins of institutional orthodoxy in medieval Japan.

  2. The Breath of Nonduality: Genjū Zen, Buddhist Doctrines of Breathing, and Kōan Commentaries in Premodern Japan
    Marta Sanvido · pp. 33-71
    摘要

    This article examines the integration of discourses on respiration into kōan exegesis within the Genjū lineage of Rinzai Zen in medieval Japan. Drawing on missan (records of private face-to-face exchanges between masters and students on various kōan ) preserved at the Matsugaoka Bunko and presenting a selection of these as annotated translations, it argues that Genjū monks developed a distinctive interpretive framework within kōan discourse in which breath occupied a central role. This framework, however, can only be fully understood when situated within broader medieval Japanese Buddhist discourses on respiration, particularly those articulated within Shingon Buddhism (including the Tachikawa sublineage), Tendai's Genshi kimyōdan initiations, and Jōdo Shinshū's secret insights. Through a comparative analysis of these parallel traditions, the study demonstrates that Genjū monks understood respiration as both a physical practice and a conceptual manifestation of nonduality. Breath thus emerges as the locus where cosmology, embodiment, and realization converge in unity, forming the essential foundation of kōan practice. Ultimately, this study proposes that respiration offers a vital lens for rethinking the relationship between embodiment and exegesis in kōan practice and Buddhism more broadly.

  1. Sacralizing, Materializing, Normalizing China: Monarchy, Merchants, and Media in Contemporary Thailand
    Chaiyaporn Phayakhrut, Ying-Kit Chan · pp. 401-423 · online 2026-08-14
    摘要

    Thailand’s relations with China have expanded in recent decades through diplomacy, cultural exchange, and economic integration. Scholars have explained such expansion through economic interdependence and geopolitical alignment. This article suggests that the durability of Thailand-China relations also depends on mechanisms of social legitimation operating in Thai society; we conceptualize these mechanisms as a monarchy-merchant-media (3M) nexus. Royal diplomacy sacralizes bilateral ties through symbolic authority, corporate networks materialize them through investment and commercial integration, and popular media normalizes them through cultural representation and everyday consumption. Rather than operating sequentially, these forces interact to embed China’s presence in Thailand’s cultural landscape and political economy. While tensions surrounding Chinese influence periodically emerge in Thailand, the configuration of symbolic authority, capital networks, and cultural narratives helps stabilize bilateral relations. By highlighting these processes, the article contributes to debates on how asymmetrical regional power can be reproduced not only through state coercion but also through socially embedded forms of legitimacy.

  2. Differentiated Alliance Management: The Generative Logic of Institutional Divergence in “US-Japan+” Trilateral Security Cooperation
    Xingchuan Jiang · pp. 424-451 · online 2026-08-26
    摘要

    Since 2022, three trilateral mechanisms anchored on the US-Japan alliance have advanced in parallel: US-Japan-Australia, US-Japan-Republic of Korea (ROK), and US-Japan-Philippines. Yet they have diverged sharply across four dimensions: organization, process, capability, and network. The three share the same US-Japan axis and converge on the China challenge, so one might expect their institutional forms to converge as well. They have not. This divergence is the puzzle the article addresses. To explain it, the article proposes “differentiated alliance management.” Washington and Tokyo, the argument runs, do not apply a uniform template. They adjust commitment form, organization, capability integration, and network connectivity to fit each third party’s domestic-political, capability, and diplomatic-risk constraints. Process tracing across the three cases shows that the same axis, filtered through different constraints, produces three stable but distinct forms: a non-alliance yet steadily deepening high-level integration with Australia, a legally non-binding political commitment with the ROK, and a selectively activatable, capability-building arrangement with the Philippines. It argues that Washington and Tokyo have not applied a uniform template when building trilateral cooperation with third parties; rather, they have calibrated the institutional configuration of each mechanism according to the domestic political, capability-structural, and diplomatic-risk constraints that each partner faces.

  3. Beyond Hedging: A Dynamic Model of Equidistant Diplomacy in Indonesia
    Shuqi Wang · pp. 452-472 · online 2026-08-11
    摘要

    Research on middle-power strategy often subsumes diverse practices under hedging, obscuring how governments operationalize neutrality over time. Equidistant diplomacy specifies three perception-management tools—paralleling, downplaying, and broadcasting—but existing accounts treat them as a static menu and say less about when and why states reweight them. This article reconceptualizes equidistant diplomacy as a stage-based process consisting of three core phases—initiation, navigation, and recalibration—and one cross-cutting mode of episodic adjustment triggered by shocks. It argues that tool choice and phase movement reflect the interaction between external pressures and domestic political factors, especially leadership change and electoral incentives. The framework is applied to Indonesia’s management of US–China rivalry from 2014 to 2025. Under Joko Widodo, Indonesia established a neutral baseline through the Global Maritime Fulcrum and symbolic paralleling, then institutionalized equidistance by pairing deeper economic engagement with China with diversification toward the United States and its partners. Natuna maritime frictions, the 2019 election, and COVID-19 prompted adjustment episodes dominated by downplaying and defensive broadcasting. Prabowo Subianto’s early diplomacy is interpreted as recalibration, combining paired high-level diplomacy, new security dialogues, and intensified broadcasting to reset neutrality in a more assertive form. The article adds temporal structure and mechanism-based specificity to equidistant diplomacy, clarifying an operational question often left underspecified in hedging: how sequenced, domain-specific signalling can help preserve autonomy while managing perceptions of alignment as great power competition intensifies.

  4. Institutional Decay and Electoral Upheaval: Party System Fragility and Nepal’s 2026 Political Transformation
    Suvexa Pradhan Tuladhar · pp. 473-486 · online 2026-06-22
    摘要

    When the 2025 Gen Z movement toppled the incumbent government and dissolved the House of Representatives, Nepal’s democracy appeared on the brink. Yet six months later Nepal successfully conducted a midterm election. The result was a near supermajority for four-year-old Rastriya Swatantriya Party (RSP), which secured 182 of 275 parliamentary seats, delivering a historic defeat to Nepal’s long-dominant establishment parties. Prevailing explanations attribute these outcomes to the Gen Z movement and the populist appeal of RSP’s prime ministerial candidate, Balendra Shah. While these factors contributed to the transformation, they do not fully explain it. Drawing on Mainwaring and Scully’s Party System Institutionalization theory, I contend that both the protest movement and RSP’s breakthrough are best understood as the culmination of a structural party system crisis decades in the making. Analysis of electoral volatility data, public trust surveys, and party organizational patterns reveals a system characterized by unstable competition, eroding party-voter linkages, persistent legitimacy deficits, and weak internal party democracy. Yet RSP’s rise reproduces the same personality-driven, weakly institutionalized pattern it sought to dismantle. Its durability will depend on whether it can achieve what Nepal’s party system has historically failed to deliver: institutionalized, programmatically grounded, and organizationally coherent party politics.

  5. Neither Democratic Breakthrough nor Conservative Consolidation: Thailand’s 2026 General Election in a Contested Political Order
    Prajak Kongkirati · pp. 487-498 · online 2026-08-05
    摘要

    Thailand’s general election of February 8, 2026 produced a fragmented outcome that did not satisfy expectations for either decisive reform or for outright conservative restoration. Bhumjaithai (BJT) emerged as the largest party with 192 seats, yet its victory rested not on ideological appeal so much as on an extraordinary convergence of provincial patronage networks, bureaucratic resources, and elite endorsement. This article analyzes the principal dynamics at play in the election, examining BJT’s rise, the continued decline of military-backed parties, and the setbacks suffered by both the reformist People’s Party and the Thaksin-aligned Pheu Thai. Drawing on electoral data and qualitative evidence, it argues that Thai electoral politics remains more competitive and institutionally complex than conventional accounts suggest, even as informal power structures continue to shape its outcomes.

  6. “One Step Forward, Two Steps Back”: Unpacking Pakistan’s Post-9/11 Policies of Madrassah Reforms
    Abdur Rehman Shah · pp. 499-510 · online 2026-06-02
    摘要

    Despite numerous initiatives by the Pakistani government to reform religious seminaries, or madrassahs, results have been constrained by institutional resistance and flawed state policies. Drawing on madrassah literature, as well as interviews with government officials, madrassah administrators, and analysts, this article offers a fresh perspective on post-9/11 reform efforts. It argues that the reform process has been hampered by policy inconsistency, lack of a compelling narrative, and counterproductive securitization of a complex socioeconomic issue. This article advocates for a transition away from the current situation of ambitious, holistic strategies towards a more nuanced, long-term approach focused on incremental goals. The article argues that in addition to adopting this strategy of refinement, the state must also desecuritize the agenda of madrassah reform. This shift from reactive securitization to a consistent and comprehensive agenda offers a more viable path for reform in Pakistani madrassahs.

  1. Hidden Representation in Bicameralism: Petitions, Second Chambers, and Complementary Representation in the Japanese Diet
    Ken Kinoshita · pp. 1-30 · online 2026-10-30
    摘要

    This article examines petitions as channels of complementary representation under bicameralism. Complementary representation refers to cross-chamber differentiation in the institutional pathways through which citizens’ and groups’ demands are connected to parliament, formally recognized, and processed without necessarily producing policy change. Using 15,674 petitions submitted to the Japanese Diet between 2001 and 2025, the article compares petition adoption and functions in the House of Representatives (H.R.) and the House of Councillors (H.C.). Although raw adoption rates differ little, the full-period controlled model yields average predicted adoption probabilities of 5.9 percent for H.C. petitions and 3.2 percent for H.R. petitions. The negative H.R. coefficient remains significant in several full-period specifications, including a title-only analysis, but is smaller under title-only classification. The adoption difference is concentrated before the 210th Diet, while functional differences are sensitive to textual comparability. The findings extend bicameralism research beyond inter-chamber bargaining by showing that second chambers can provide distinct institutional pathways through which social demands become visible and formally recognized. They also identify the production and availability of parliamentary records as an important measurement condition for comparative research on representative functions.

  4. Altercasting China as a Partner: Vietnam and Cambodia's Divergent Foreign Policy Responses
    Vu Quy Son, Nguyen Cong Tung, Hoan Quang Truong · pp. 1-27 · online 2026-10-13
    摘要

    How do small states interpret and respond to China's rise? This article employs altercasting in role theory to compare Vietnam's and Cambodia's foreign policy responses towards China. It argues that despite both maintaining comprehensive strategic cooperative partnerships with China, the two smaller states have developed different China policies due to divergent expectations of China's roles. Rather than reflecting material asymmetry alone, this divergence stems from contrasting altercastings of China's behaviour under the same institutional framework. While both view China as an important cooperative partner, Vietnam frequently perceives China as failing to enact the role of a trusted partner, particularly in security and trade, where Chinese actions are seen as contradicting stated commitments. By contrast, Cambodia views China's behaviour as consistent with its expectations. The argument is developed through a paired comparison across two case studies: South China Sea disputes and the Belt and Road Initiative.

  6. When Do Chinese Workers’ Protests Survive? Conditions and Causes for the Backlash of Repression
    Yongsu Cho, Kyung Suk Lee · pp. 1-22 · online 2026-10-12
    摘要

    Under what conditions does state repression of workers’ protests backfire rather than suppress? Chinese authorities quell many labour protests swiftly, yet others persist and escalate despite coercion, and the sources of this variation remain unclear. Through process-tracing of four critical cases, the Yue Yuen Strike, the Jasic Incident, the Ansteel Lianzhong Protest, and the Quang Viet Protest, this article argues that repression outcomes are shaped before the state resorts to force. Two pre-repression conditions together generate what we term institutional cooptation failure: the absence of a channel binding workers to the All-China Federation of Trade Unions (ACFTU), and leadership by migrant workers. The two interlock, since migrant-led protests are rarely absorbed by a union whose organizational routines are anchored in locally registered workers. By relocating the determinants of protest outcomes from the aftermath of repression to the institutional terrain that precedes it, the study shows how cooptation failure can paradoxically sustain the mobilization of excluded workers and blunt repression under authoritarian rule.

    The potential for simultaneous conflicts in the Taiwan Strait and on the Korean Peninsula has emerged as one of the most critical security challenges in East Asia. While analysts have primarily focused on how North Korea might respond to a Taiwan contingency, less attention has been paid to the reverse scenario: how China might react in the Taiwan Strait if North Korea attacks South Korea. For a more balanced analysis, this article compares the structural and political variables shaping the likelihood of conflict in both regions. I argue that, beyond intentional attacks at the strategic level, we must also consider the unintentional consequences of low-level aggression at the tactical level.   25. Chinese and Australian Aid in the Pacific: Which is More Effective at Developing Influence?
    Oliver Sinclair · pp. 1-13 · online 2026-09-24
    摘要

    In 2022, China and Solomon Islands signed a security deal allowing for the Chinese navy to potentially use Honiara’s ports. In that same year, Beijing attempted to author a region-wide security pact with ten Pacific Island Countries. These moves signalled a new strategic reality in the Pacific—China had arrived as a power with intent to shape international cooperation in the region. Those same moves reflected another reality—Australia’s place in the Pacific as the security partner of choice was now contested. This paper examines aid as a theatre of contest in the Pacific, and compares the approaches of China and Australia for developing influence in Pacific Island Countries. I argue that China’s focus on infrastructure has achieved significant soft power gains and resulted in regional alignment with Beijing’s strategic goals. I also suggest that Australia’s multi-modal aid practice is struggling to secure its strategic aims and a recalibration of Australian aid funding is needed to meet the needs of Pacific Island Countries. Using population surveys conducted throughout the Pacific, this paper reveals the extent of awareness and affability towards Chinese aid in the Pacific. The results contain timely lessons for Australia if it wishes to remain the region’s partner of choice.

  26. Gradual, Cumulative, Consequential: Monetization and the Rise of Private Domestic Demand in North Korea
    Ruediger Frank · pp. 1-21 · online 2026-09-22
    摘要

    North Korea's economy has undergone a fundamental transformation over the past three decades, yet its significance remains underappreciated. This article advances a monetization thesis: the restoration of money's core functions—not marketization per se—is the analytically decisive process driving that change. After the collapse of state distribution in the mid-1990s, money again served as medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value, setting off a causal chain from private wealth accumulation to demand formation to structural pressure on the state. Drawing on development economics, Kornai's analysis of shortage economies, and a range of North Korean and third-country sources, the article traces the expansion of private consumption from basic necessities to higher-order goods and services. The channels through which private wealth might leave the country remain closed, so purchasing power accumulates at home, frustrating a middle class with limited opportunities to spend it and generating inflation that falls hardest on those who earn in won. The resulting pressure narrows the state's options to repression or selective liberalization. Should the latter prevail, North Korea would converge—unevenly and incompletely—toward a developmental dictatorship, rendering it more responsive to both sanctions and engagement.
