Pacific Historical Review

Vol. 95, No. 4 · 2026-11-01 · 12 篇 · U California Press · Pacific / Asian American history · Peer-reviewed
  1. In Search of the Mer de l’Ouest
    Owen Stanwood · pp. 373-402
    摘要

    From the seventeenth century onward French explorers and mapmakers theorized the existence of the “Mer de l’Ouest,” an inland sea in the northwestern part of North America. Connected to the Pacific and convenient for trade with Asia, the sea was home to “civilized” people, who built cities and sailing ships and who could be either trading partners or targets for conquest. The French heard about the sea from numerous reports from their Native allies and, in the eighteenth century, sought very hard to reach it, even sponsoring the creation of backcountry forts and encouraging expeditions to the Far West. Of course, they were unsuccessful, as the Western Sea was, as one scholar described it, more a “mirage” than a real place. Nonetheless, these stories should be taken seriously. While not completely accurate, Indigenous intelligence of the Mer de l’Ouest was also not entirely wrong. There was a vast inland body of saltwater in the Northwest, now known as the Salish Sea, and the French speculations about the far northwest clearly gave a correct if incomplete portrait of a densely populated region that was a center of Indigenous settlement and trade. Thus, in French stories of the Western Sea, we see early glimpses of the Pacific Northwest and can understand how that region was connected both to the rest of Native North America and to the French imperial imagination.

  2. From Naval Platform to Commercial Hub of New Spain
    Guadalupe Pinzón Ríos · pp. 403-428
    摘要

    This article considers how and why the Naval Department of San Blas, beyond its maritime purposes, also functioned as a commercial port in western New Spain and became a hub as maritime shifts took place in the Pacific World. For a better understanding of San Blas’s significance, and above all its function as a maritime hub, it is necessary to analyze how trade networks developed at San Blas, ultimately forcing the Naval Department to also serve as a commercial port. In the context of the period’s eighteenth-century mercantile transformation, population growth and economic change swept the territory of New Spain. These transformations were part of the politicization of the Pacific coast and the need to protect Spain’s lucrative transpacific routes.

  3. Channeling Expertise
    Yuan Yan · pp. 429-458
    摘要

    This study examines how academic expertise on China influenced U.S. policymaking through multiple channels in the late 1960s. The phrase “containment without isolation,” widely associated with the Lyndon B. Johnson administration, in fact originated among Sinologists and was incorporated into the government’s China agenda after mid-1966. By contributing to the State Department’s China Advisory Panels, engaging with the National Security Council staff and President Johnson, and participating in the task force for Democratic candidate Hubert H. Humphrey’s presidential campaign, centrist Sinologists sought to guide U.S.-China policy toward greater flexibility. By highlighting how ideas ascended through bureaucratic channels and crossed partisan boundaries, this study underscores the role of non-state actors in shaping diplomatic history and deepens our understanding of the origins of rapprochement.

Past & Present

Vol. 272, No. 1 · 2026-08-01 · 8 篇 · Oxford UP · History (general) · Peer-reviewed
  1. Slavery, Prosperity, and Inequality in Roman Pompeii
    Seth Bernard · pp. 3-50 · online 2025-03-18
    摘要

    Historians of premodern economies, in contrast to modern ones, have only infrequently contemplated the economic contribution of slavery. Here, I suggest that quantitative and statistical tools allow us to evaluate the place of slavery in an early economy, using Roman Pompeii as a case study. At the time of its destruction in 79 ce, Pompeii appears prosperous, having benefitted from the economic development thought to have characterized the Roman world. Recent discoveries, meanwhile, shed new light on the conditions of working classes and slaves throughout the city. These narratives can be seen to form two sides to the same coin, as Pompeii’s prosperity was created in large part thanks to slave labour. The connection is supported by constructing a probabilistic model, which suggests some 6 million sesterces (HS) flowed every year to Pompeii’s masters through their exploitation of slaves. Slave owning probably formed the largest single income source for the urban economy. This scale of income is shown to be consistent with recent reconstructions of wealth and income inequality in the city. The results not only speak to slavery’s profound importance to Pompeii’s prosperity, but they encourage a recentring of labour and slavery in Roman economic history.

  2. Reckoning and Economic Life in Late Medieval England
    Tom Johnson · pp. 52-86 · online 2025-04-23
    摘要

    This article explores the practice of ‘reckoning’, a means of reciprocal accounting that becomes prominent in late-medieval England. Despite its critical importance to everyday exchange in this period, the practice has not received much attention from historians. The article argues that reckoning should be understood as a kind of economic infrastructure, one that performed some of the same functions as formal markets; and that as a concept, it was critical to the way that contemporaries delineated different forms of economic exchange. I proceed by tracing the emergence of reckoning from a convergence of institutional accounting, increasing technical literacy, and the proliferation of written accounts from the thirteenth century onwards. I go on to argue that as a tool of economic exchange, reckoning was particularly well-suited to the straitened economic conditions of the fifteenth century, in particular the shortage of coin, the retrenchment of formal markets, and the pervasive use of credit. I then examine three case studies in which reckoning went ‘wrong’, in order to explore the ideals of exchange relations on which it drew. In conclusion, I suggest that reckoning can help us to frame some of the broader transformations in economic culture in post-plague England.

  3. The making and unmaking of religious toleration in Spanish Manila, 1571–1755
    Adrian Masters · pp. 87-125 · online 2025-08-05
    摘要

    This article traces the rise and collapse of religious toleration of non-Christian Chinese merchants in Spanish Manila between 1571 and 1755, offering a case study in early modern global commerce and interfaith governance in European Asia. It demonstrates that Manila became the most religiously diverse and tolerant city in the Spanish Empire — and perhaps in the entire early modern Latin West — despite many hardline authorities’ and jurists’ insistence upon maintaining the widespread imperial practice of persecution of non-Christian ritual and belief. This deviation owed largely to coordinated efforts of non-Catholic Chinese merchants and sympathetic authorities — especially the Spanish governors and municipal aldermen. Jurists responded by formulating a theory of toleration rooted in scholastic contractualism, natural law, and voluntarism. Manila thus became a pioneer of the de facto and de jure toleration that underpinned Christian Asia — and whose arrangements resemble later developments in Dutch Batavia and French Pondichéry. Yet while Manila’s practices later became mainstream in many European-dominated entrepots, the risk of war between Manila and the Zheng maritime power in the early 1660s shattered the city’s tolerant alliance, setting the stage for a slow dismemberment of non-Christian institutions culminating in the 1755 expulsion of non-Catholics. As other regional European powers adopted toleration, the regional trailblazer thus abandoned it. Manila toleration’s unique trajectory compels a partial re-evaluation of the Spanish Empire’s reputation for religious intolerance, underscores the critical importance of toleration in the emergence of commerce and governance in Christian Asia, and provides further evidence against the widespread liberal narrative in which toleration emerges exclusively in Northern Europe among a handful of eminent Protestant and deist freethinkers.

  4. Making sugar out of opium: A narco-plantation regime in early modern Southeast Asia
    Guanmian Xu, Shohei Okubo · pp. 126-158 · online 2025-06-05
    摘要

    In the early modern period, while slavery became firmly entrenched in the Atlantic’s sugar economies, Southeast Asia witnessed the rise of distinct plantation regimes. Unlike their Atlantic counterparts, these Asian plantation regimes relied not on enslavement but on addiction — particularly to opium smoking — as a means to control and exploit plantation labour. Existing research has highlighted how such opium-driven regimes, along with Asian ‘coolie’ labour, proliferated globally in the nineteenth century following the abolitionist movement. Yet, their early modern origins in Southeast Asia remain largely unexplored. As a result, a deep plantation labour history outside the Atlantic World is still lacking, and researchers often continue to essentialize early modern plantation capitalism as inherently tied to slavery, while overlooking other, often more insidious, forms of plantation labour control that existed beyond the Atlantic. This article seeks to address this gap by examining the emergence and development of a narco-plantation regime on the sugar frontier of rural Batavia (Jakarta) from the late seventeenth to the early nineteenth centuries.

  5. Fossil Energy and The Ecology of Everyday Life in The Low Countries During The Long Eighteenth Century
    Wout Saelens · pp. 159-196 · online 2025-08-12
    摘要

    Why did early modern households bring the polluting energy of fossil fuels into their homes? For a long time, peat and coal were considered inferior to firewood due to their smoky nature. And yet, by the late eighteenth century, these ‘dirty’ fuels had become not just acceptable but even desirable — precisely as consumer ideals of domestic cleanliness and private health were gaining in prominence. How can we explain this paradox? This article shifts the focus in energy history from the ‘outdoor’ to the ‘indoor’ by exploring the ecology of everyday life. Using household manuals, medical advice books, autobiographical documents, and other narrative sources, it examines how discussions of heating and air quality grappled with the tension between smoky warmth and clean, fresh air at home. It argues that the early modern energy transition involved an important eco-cultural transformation, in which domestic consumers increasingly detached themselves from the ‘dark’ side of fossil fuels, only to emphasize their ‘bright’ side. By the dawn of the modern consumer society, peat and coal were seen no longer as sources of smoke nuisance but as essential elements of a warm, cosy, and clean home.

  6. The purposeful workhouse of England’s Old Poor Law
    Susannah Ottaway · pp. 197-241 · online 2025-07-09
    摘要

    It has long been recognized that the English workhouses of the Old Poor Law era (1601-1834) were important precursors to institutions of the modern social services, but what kind of places were they? Characterized by eighteenth-century humanitarians as ‘pauper prisons’, and by early nineteenth-century political economists as ‘pauper palaces’, workhouses were undoubtedly varied institutions with hybrid regimes that included both care and work, nurture and discipline. Integrating recent work that has revealed much about material conditions and the agency of workhouse inmates, this article reassesses work in Old Poor Law workhouses, focusing especially on houses of industry in the county of Norfolk. We find a new perspective on these poor law institutions by recognizing their serious and sustained efforts to keep inmates working productively. Simply put, workhouses worked in the long eighteenth century. To house the infirm, embed work habits in the young, provide temporary shelter and confinement for the able-bodied or unsettled poor, parishes poured time and resources into their local and regional workhouses. In their multifaceted nature, workhouses most resembled not the prisons or hospitals to which they are sometimes compared, but rather the institution of the household-family that was the bedrock of society in the long eighteenth century.

  7. Housing and the Peripheralization of Race Politics in Britain, 1948–1977
    Christopher Hilliard · pp. 242-278 · online 2025-08-05
    摘要

    The idea that there was a ratio of people of colour to white people that, if exceeded, would prompt a white backlash was a tenet of folk sociology in Britain. This belief was the basis of strategies of ‘dispersal’. In the 1940s and 1950s, officials counted on the labour market to spread people from the Caribbean, South Asia, and Africa around the country. However, the housing market had the opposite effect. It ‘concentrated’ Black and Asian people in run-down parts of British cities. Later, as urban authorities began to demolish these neighbourhoods and to integrate public housing, some (most notably Birmingham) introduced formal dispersal programmes with racial quotas. Dispersal in particular and housing policy in general illustrate the way central government devolved contentious matters involving race to local councils. Examining this process of ‘peripheralization’ brings two distinct concerns in the historiography — national policy on immigration and local social processes — into the same frame. City and regional authorities in France and West Germany pursued dispersal in parallel ways, despite the differences in the three countries’ migration histories and citizenship regimes. The similarities in the project of dispersal and its failure point to a common European history of the origins of multiculturalism.

  8. Air Travel, Statelessness, and the Rights Claims of Ugandan Asians, c. 1973
    Ria Kapoor · pp. 279-315 · online 2025-10-09
    摘要

    In the aftermath of Idi Amin’s expulsion of Uganda’s South Asians in 1972, some of those made technically stateless arrived in India unsupported by the United Nations or any national government. Eleven of them attempted to fly on via Sri Lanka, without the required paperwork, to join their families in the United Kingdom. As large colonial empires gave way to postcolonial nation states, and as the international community and the former colonial metropole shed responsibilities towards their former subjects, the various destinations to which such stateless persons were considered for deportation reflect the uneasy status of diasporic communities. Using what official records saw as the ‘problem’ of this international flight, this article explores how the sealed realm of air travel became a locus for the articulation of their rights as these peoples of the postcolonial world used the devices of deportation and ‘shuttlecocking’ against national and international actors to challenge the inequitable application of notionally universal principles to deny material assistance and recognition of their rights as refugees and stateless persons. In this way, individuals and non-state actors were able to use air travel to intervene bodily to influence national and supranational discourses designed to exclude them.

Online first（尚未編入期別）· 8
  1. The Irrational Computer: Randomness and Unreason in the History of Artificial Intelligence
    Benjamin Lindquist · online 2026-10-19
    摘要

    How did the computer, a machine built for logic and calculation, come to model the messy human mind? To answer that, ‘The Irrational Computer’ breaks with a familiar narrative of rationalization and quantification that stretches from the Enlightenment to the Cold War. Against this story of rational mastery, this project shows how influential British and American engineers came in the middle of the last century to see controlled chaos as essential to machine intelligence. They intentionally injected randomness into otherwise deterministic systems to achieve their desired result: ‘a slight error of reasoning’. Archival records, technical reports, internal memos, and popular coverage reveal the appeal and controversy of randomness in the history of AI. Rooted in theories of invention, modernist art, and wartime mathematics, notions of randomness allowed engineers to mechanize and materialize murky conceptions of creativity, intuition, and the unconscious. The evidence is abundant, but the argument is simple: today’s AI emerged from the conviction that replicating original thought required modelling not only logic but something deeply human, in other words, the irrational.

  2. The Transition to Wage Labour, in Stone, in North Wales, in Jamaica
    Siân Davies · online 2026-10-14
    摘要

    Completed around 1821, a monument commemorating the enslaver and industrialist Richard Pennant and his wife, Anne Susannah Warburton, elides any mention of the family’s sugar plantations in Jamaica and instead celebrates the Pennants as benevolent modernizers who transformed their Welsh estate and tenants. A material artefact of national history writing, the monument severs this local story from imperial concerns. Yet a comparative study of the transition to wage labour on the family’s properties in North Wales and Jamaica reveals the work the Pennant memorial’s story was doing for both Britain’s local and its imperial labour projects. In North Wales, estate managers confronted labourers’ independence; in post-emancipation Jamaica, plantation authorities similarly faced freed people’s efforts to defend their autonomy. Racial ideology reconciled these parallel histories by constructing Black labourers as uniquely idle, thereby legitimizing restrictive post-emancipation labour regimes while masking coercion within Britain itself. By tracing the circulation of labour ideologies, moral vocabularies, and managerial practices across North Wales and Jamaica, this article challenges historical narratives that separate industrial Britain from slave and post-slave colonies, a tendency epitomized in the Pennant monument, and instead exposes the joint construction of national mythology and imperial rationality.

  3. Daughters of the First Empire: Inherited wealth, surveillance, and Napoleon’s contested imperial power
    Netta Green · online 2026-10-08
    摘要

    Young daughters occupy an anomalous position in the legal landscape of Napoleonic France. While the Civil Code of 1804 reduced wives to legal dependents, it guaranteed daughters equal inheritance rights alongside their brothers, a striking exception within an otherwise conservative family law. This article suggests that the anomaly was not incidental: rather than reflecting principled commitment, Napoleon’s retention of egalitarian inheritance may have derived from his recognition that a growing market of wealthy heiresses could serve as instruments of political consolidation. By orchestrating marriages between these women and loyal officers, his government hoped to fuse old noble families with the new imperial notables. To identify suitable candidates, Savary, the minister of police, secretly ordered prefects to compile detailed lists on young women across the empire. Two surviving tables, from the departments of Vienne and the annexed Simplon (today Valais, Switzerland), illustrate how this project unfolded on the ground, and why it largely failed. Though Napoleon’s matchmaking schemes yielded meagre results, the tables themselves document a significant moment in the history of state bureaucratic science and surveillance: the incorporation of young women’s bodies, fortunes, and futures into the administrative machinery of imperial power.

  4. Gandhi’s Voice, Mass Politics, and the Arrival of Public Address Technology in India, 1927–1931
    Kama Maclean · online 2026-10-01
    摘要

    Historians often draw on texts of public speeches in an effort to understand the politics of the past, while seldom pausing to consider if they were audible at the time. This is particularly relevant to the case of anti-colonialism in South Asia between the two world wars, when political speeches were typically delivered to mass open-air audiences and audibility must have been a considerable challenge. Historians have assumed that the arrival of public address systems in India overcame this problem, but a focus on the phase of its implementation, as both speakers and audiences gradually became acculturated to the ways in which microphones and loudspeakers mediated public speaking, shows how unreliable they were, introducing new dynamics and challenges to the processes of both speaking and listening. Adopting an intermedial, multisensory approach and focusing on speeches by M. K. Gandhi, who sought to dominate inter-war anti-colonialism in British India, this article looks for ways of understanding how political messaging operated in contexts where being able to hear a speech was not a given.

  5. The Politics of Energy in Colonial Suriname
    Chelsea Schields · online 2026-09-04
    摘要

    In colonial Suriname, a society shaped by slavery and indenture, the infrastructure and technologies of energy arrived as extensions of a colonial order that had long concentrated resources among elites. Drawing on colonial and company archives, this article shows how working-class Surinamese women and men engaged with gas and electricity, destroying street lamps one day while demanding connection the next. During the tumultuous 1930s, these communities protested against unequal access to power, exploitative labour practices at energy plants, and the racialized logics of privatization. As a monopoly in a small colonial society eager to expand its customer base, the European energy utility was compelled to respond to these demands. Yet even as energy use crossed from public into private space, working-class households continued to thwart colonial expectations that it would appease them, instead adapting these technologies to the survival of their own social worlds. Whether on the street or in the home, working-class engagement with energy revealed an ambivalence towards colonial modernity that challenged the terms of its imposition. This examination of how energy became a site of conflict shaped by a Caribbean plantation context thus extends energy history beyond its usual focus of the Global North.

  6. Microhistory and Women’s Time Use
    Jane Humphries · online 2026-09-03
    摘要

    Gender historians have pioneered attention to ‘doing words’ to identify otherwise invisible women’s work. Searches in court records for verbs with female subjects have documented women’s widespread participation in economic activity, often directing and managing, while playing down their unpaid care for family members. This article turns to a microhistorical source, diaries written by Peter Walkden, a farmer and Nonconformist minister living in eighteenth-century Lancashire. Walkden’s account of his farming routine and interactions with family and community incidentally describes the activities of his wife, Catherine. Evidence of her ‘doings’ identifies Catherine’s repertoire of tasks but is extended here to identify work and labour relations by the ownership of equipment, production for use or sale, and the need for occasional stand-ins when Catherine was indisposed or unavailable. Additional circumstantial evidence and other historical and modern sources enable the estimation of the frequency and duration of tasks, so providing the first breakdown of an early modern woman’s working day. Findings confirm the extent of women’s work but reinstate unpaid care as vital to the functioning of Walkden’s household, and by inference to social reproduction generally. Significantly, when Walkden himself had to provide care or pay for an understudy, it was understood as work and its value recognized.

  7. Black-on-Black Makeup and the History of Blackface
    Ezequiel Adamovsky · online 2026-08-14
    摘要

    This article contributes to transnational perspectives on blackface by examining evidence of Black individuals and communities employing darkening make-up or black masks on both sides of the Atlantic. It challenges the assumption that all such practices derive from, or are analogous to, black minstrelsy in the United States. Drawing on historical and ethnographic sources, the article situates these performances within local and transnational festive traditions, particularly those rooted in Afro-Iberian cultural practices, with many pre-dating US minstrelsy. In some instances, black-on-black blackface reproduces racist stereotypes or engages with the codes of White blackface minstrelsy; in others, it functions as a racially affirmative practice unrelated to US traditions. Cases from across the world reveal multiple meanings, ranging from resistance to stereotypes to the symbolic restoration of ancestral blackness and affirmation of racial pride. Taken together, the evidence makes plain the need to interpret black-on-black blackface within its specific historical and cultural contexts. Furthermore, it calls attention to the transnational circulation of Afro-Iberian traditions of racial impersonation, largely overlooked in scholarship, alongside the diffusion of US minstrelsy. By foregrounding these alternative genealogies, the article contributes to a more nuanced and globally informed understanding of blackface and ethnic impersonation in the Atlantic world.

  8. Food Security, Nitrates Capitalism, and the Haber–Bosch Revolution
    Patricia Clavin · online 2026-08-06
    摘要

    This article reinterprets the early history of the Haber–Bosch process of ammonia synthesis through the transnational development of synthetic nitrogen production at Ludwigshafen am Rhein and Billingham-on-Tees, County Durham. It argues that the nitrates revolution in the early twentieth century was not simply a technological breakthrough but a contested project linking industrial strategy, state power, and food security. Tracing the British government’s wartime construction and subsequent privatization of the Billingham plant, it shows how economic orthodoxy constrained efforts to sustain state-led industrial co-ordination, even as private firms pursued cartelized forms of governance. It situates the British and German chemical industries within a shared political economy, and reframes fertilizer production as central to the emergence of modern food politics and the international political economy, anticipating later debates over sovereignty, inequality, and environmental limits. Recovering these histories reveals food security as a foundational problem of industrial modernity, with nitrates capitalism shaped by decisions about the governance of national resources, scientific expertise, and global markets.

  2. Esperanto on the Radio: Broadcasting Infrastructure and the Politics of Universal Speech in the Japanese Empire
    Edwin Michielsen, Derek Kramer · pp. 357-381 · online 2026-08-01
    摘要

    This article explores the interface between Esperanto and the radio in the Japanese Empire. Viewing radio as more than simply a mode of conveyance, it examines the tensions that emerged when a universalizing language met a universalizing medium. The following sections explore how new communication infrastructure enabled Esperantists’ claims to political salience. Radio in the Japanese empire helped articulate powerful forecasts of political solidarity, liberated from the restraints of space or state. However, Esperanto on the radio also appeared in ways that deepened the borders of colonial relations and linguistic hierarchies. The article first discusses the history of radio infrastructure in the Japanese Empire and its role in shaping linguistic topography of the 1920s and 1930s. It then turns to a case study of the 1928 “Esperanto Evening” broadcast from colonial Taiwan by Japanese Esperantists. As one of the few surviving examples of when universalizing language and media met, the transcript of this broadcast reveals the limits of Esperanto’s emancipatory reach.

  3. Self-Rescue in Media Networks: De-Blackboxing, Shanzhai Cyborgs, and Survival Among Workers with Pneumoconiosis in China
    Chu Wang · pp. 383-409 · online 2026-08-01
    摘要

    This article examines media networks as both the central object and method of analysis for understanding how Chinese workers with pneumoconiosis navigate survival in a postsocialist risk society where many are systematically denied compensation. Rather than emphasizing overt collective resistance, the study focuses on two forms of media-enabled self-rescue. First, it explores the “de-blackboxing strategy,” whereby workers use and rely on news reports and various social media platforms to give the slow violence of occupational disease public visibility and pursue justice. Second, it investigates the rise of “shanzhai cyborgs,” in which workers draw on technical knowledge shared within grassroots communities to construct life-sustaining homemade oxygen machines. The article contends that these fragile and improvisational modes of survival are neither isolated acts of heroism nor conventional political protest, but instead emerge through ongoing interaction and circulation within decentralized media networks. It argues that the effectiveness of self-rescue often depends on chains of mediation that translate, amplify, and mobilize private experiences into public events capable of driving tangible change. By dissecting these mediated practices, the article offers a new perspective on what resistance and survival mean for pneumoconiosis workers who are rendered disposable in contemporary China.

  4. Entering the Realm of Huan : Rethinking Immersion Through Early Modern Chinese Accounts of the Strange
    Jiayi Chen · pp. 411-436 · online 2026-08-01
    摘要

    This essay explores how immersion—its generative mechanisms, specific experiences, and cultural implications—was imagined and conceptualized in early modern accounts of the strange (yi 異). Rather than locating historical precursors to modern immersive technologies such as virtual reality (VR), it isolates immersion as an experiential mode from technologically driven paradigms that foreground presence within computer-simulated worlds. Drawing on sixteenth- and seventeenth-century accounts of the strange, particularly Pu Songling’s 蒲松齡 (1640–1715) Strange Tales from Liaozhai, this essay demonstrates that immersive experience emerges not from make-believe or technological sophistication but through multisensory engagement with liminal spaces where reality and illusion intermingle. Central to these tales is the rendering of huan 幻—not as abstract illusion but a deeply felt condition of absorption, triggered by techniques such as huanxi 幻戲 (illusion performance) and media like murals and narrative writing. These stories depict immersion as arising when everyday environments shift into the extraordinary and when multisensory experiences challenge established perceptual frameworks. They reveal a phenomenological understanding of the interplay between embodied sensory cognition and mediated environments. By approaching immersion from within these historical narratives and the reading experience they afford, this essay highlights the critical potential of accounts of the strange to illuminate a culturally specific, pluralistic understanding of immersion that technology-centered discourses frequently overlook.

  5. The Neighborhood as Refuge: Dignity, Inclusiveness, and Compassion in Takeda Rintarō’s “Kamagasaki” (1933)
    Ran Wei · pp. 437-461 · online 2026-08-01
    摘要

    Kamagasaki, an urban enclave in Osaka, maintains a long history of marginalization that can be traced to the late 1890s. This article examines the representation of Kamagasaki in Osaka writer Takeda Rintarō’s novella “Kamagasaki.” Published in 1933, shortly after the economically prosperous “Greater Osaka” (“Dai Osaka”) period had ended, the story features the underclass and working-class people in the neighborhood of Kamagasaki, revealing how Osaka’s development has concealed issues, including economic exploitation and social division. This article introduces the concepts of “a compassionate participant” instead of adopting existing tropes of observers of city life, such as the flâneur and the “curiosity hunter” (ryōkisha). Through the perspective of such an observer, Takeda represents the issues of poverty, segregation, and homelessness in a humanistic manner. Simultaneously, by constructing various voices for fictional characters in the novella, Takeda highlights the importance of the “internal gaze” and voices from Kamagasaki. This article argues that by emphasizing how the locals value dignity and interpersonal bonds, Takeda’s representations of Kamagasaki subvert the stereotype of urban margins as morally degenerate. Through his conscious resistance to the social stigma imposed on Kamagasaki by dominant national discourse, which reduces Kamagasaki to a place of degeneration and danger, Takeda depicts a neighborhood characterized by shared attachment and resilience.

  6. Nakai Masakazu and the Revolutionary Potential of Consumption: From Bi-hihyō to the “Logic of the Committee” and Kyoto’s “Housing Problem” in 1930s Japan
    Kyle Peters · pp. 463-494 · online 2026-08-01
    摘要

    This article focuses on the prewar theoretical and print activities of Kyoto school philosopher Nakai Masakazu. It spotlights Nakai’s efforts to confront alienation under finance capitalism and inspire a new “critical” and “cooperative” form of mass subjectivity in consumers. The article contributes to extant scholarship in two ways. First, it develops Nakai’s novel interpretation of Marxism and consumer struggle in connection with his mid-1930s article “Logic of the Committee” (“Iinkai no ronri”) and his work on the tabloid-format newspaper Doyōbi (Saturday). Second, it provides a broader picture of Nakai’s philosophical development by showing how these ideas trace back to his involvement with an understudied set of coterie journals from the early 1930s: Bi-hihyō (Aesthetics/Criticism) and Sekai bunka (World Culture). The article divides into three parts, each of which moves across theory and praxis. Part 1 focuses on Nakai’s work on Bi-hihyō and Sekai bunka. It traces the historical development of Nakai’s early philosophy of collectivity, media technology, and specialization and massification in connection with the “crisis” conditions of early 1930s Japan. Part 2 focuses on Nakai’s attempts to develop and consolidate these concepts in the context of finance capitalism in his seminal “Logic of the Committee.” In particular, it shows how Nakai reinterpreted these early philosophical concepts in terms of consumer alienation. Part 3 then focuses on Nakai’s response to this condition of consumer alienation in his tabloid newspaper Doyōbi. It reveals how these sustained engagements in philosophy and print developed into a novel interpretation of Marxism from the standpoint of consumer struggle, and it shows how this connected with the so-called “housing problem” (jūtaku mondai) or “housing crisis” that peppered the pages of Doyōbi before its censorship. It ends by briefly considering how Nakai’s philosophy offers a novel contribution to twentieth-century Western Marxism.

  3. Flattening and Unflattening Space: Photography and the 1975 Okinawa International Ocean Exposition
    Daniel Abbe
    摘要

    Through an analysis of photographs produced in and around the 1975 Okinawa International Ocean Exposition, this essay develops the concepts of flattening and unflattening in material and visual registers. In line with the construction championed by Prime Minister Tanaka Kakuei, the Ocean Expo demonstrates that the Japanese state took post-reversion Okinawa as a space to be flattened into the mainland. Drawing on a phenomenological approach to space, the essay explores photographs published in Ocean Expo News, an official publication of the Ocean Expo. These promotional photographs visually flattened out the land around the expo site. In this way, they oriented Okinawa within cartographic space, ready for assimilation. The essay also examines a series of photographs taken on the Amami Islands that the mainland photographer Nakahira Takuma made in response to the Ocean Expo. Through consistently disorienting photographic space itself, they suggest a mode of unflattening. Photographs taken by Okinawan activist Ahagon Shōkō of land on Iejima also warp the cartographic space of the state and the US military, as if pushing through the second dimension into the third. Taken together, these three groups of photographs suggest that an unflattening of space might happen through the body.

  4. From “Crawling Grids” to “Processing Words”: “Stylus” Transition and Computer Writing in the 1990s Chinese Cultural Marketization
    Zihan Feng
    摘要

    This essay examines the understudied role of personal computers in China’s literary transformation, focusing on the shift from handwriting to computer writing led by established literary elites circa the 1990s. It first contextualizes writers’ switch to computer writing within early-reform China’s information craze, exposing the purported efficiency of computer writing that allured writers and engineers alike as a constructed technophilic myth. It then contends that the adoption of personal computers has reconfigured literary composition into “processing words,” which manifests in three aspects: compartmentalized and human-machine entangled workflows, reinterpretation of the Chinese language stimulated by input methods, and writers’ negotiation with their new “processor” roles within the burgeoning and diversifying Chinese cultural market. Particularly, this essay closely analyzes Chen Cun 陈村 and his computer-written novel Fresh Flowers And 鲜花和 (1997) as an epitome of established writers’ shared navigation of the computerized creative environment. Writers grapple with the paradoxical effect of literary creation becoming “processing,” which unleashes new textual and paratextual expressive possibilities for literary experimentation but simultaneously desanctifies literary elites in the increasingly streamlined cultural production mechanism. This essay thus also identifies the nation’s pursuit of information modernity as a crucial catalyst of the cultural commodification witnessed in 1990s China.

  5. Father Jiggs in Shanghai: The Rise and Fall of Comic Strips in Republican China in Transnational Context
    Eike Exner
    摘要

    This article traces the popularization of modern comic strips in Republican-era Shanghai via such strips serialized in the English-language newspaper The China Press. Consumed by both foreign and Chinese readers, these comics were some of The China Press’s most attractive features, especially George McManus’s strip Bringing Up Father, which appears to have been nearly universally known in Shanghai. From around 1920, the characters, form, and visual vocabulary of comics such as Bringing Up Father increasingly permeated Shanghai media and society, with significant overlap between English- and Chinese-language publications and audiences. The use of comics for advertising purposes played an especially large role in familiarizing Shanghai readers with comics, culminating in the appearance of the first major serialized Chinese-language comics in 1928. A central factor in this local establishment of comics as a transnational narrative technology of modernity appears to have been their contemporaneous embrace by periodicals published in Japan, which were widely available in Shanghai. Japanese military aggression during the 1930s conversely would preempt the continued development of Republican Chinese comics.

  6. Continuously Leaving the Closet: A Queer/Crip Approximation to Kondō Ginga’s Artworks
    Aliwen
    摘要

    This essay examines the intermedial practice of Japanese artist Kondō Ginga, situating her work within the historical and theoretical contexts of postwar disability activism, queer/crip discourse, and feminist interventions in Japan. Through close readings of her works The Notifications (2021), Queer Street (2021), Separated (2022), Continuously Leaving the Closet (2022), and Prides in Streets (2024), the essay proposes that Kondō’ oeuvre renegotiates the intersections of digital and physical space, public and private visibility, and queer and disabled subjectivities. Kondō’s practice is analyzed along three dimensions: (a) the dissolution of the digital-physical divide; (b) small-scale, affective forms of reworlding and activism; and (c) sustained self-articulation across mediated and relational contexts. Historical case studies, from Ueno Park’ 1948 queer resistance to figures such as Yokota Hiroshi, Yonezu Tomoko, Asaka Yūho, and Hanada Minoru, contextualize her interventions, revealing continuities in gendered/queer and disabled visibility, exclusion, and resistance. The essay argues that Kondō transforms embodied limitation, chronic illness, and digital mediation into a politics of intimacy and care, redefining activism beyond public protest. Her work enacts “crip world-building,” demonstrating that survival, relationality, and aesthetic intervention constitute simultaneous, iterative forms of queer/disabled presence, challenging conventional notions of liberation, pride, and collective identities.

  7. Guo Moruo, André Malraux: Impaired Revolutionaries and the Gramophone in Early Twentieth-Century Anti-Colonial China
    Yu Wang
    摘要

    This article brings together science and technology studies, sound studies, postcolonial history, and critical disability studies by examining how the intellectuals André Malraux (1901–1976) and Guo Moruo (1892–1978), with speaking or hearing impairments, conceptualized sound reproduction technologies during the peak of imperialism. It focuses on how their ideas were entangled with and articulated through bodily experiences during the anti-colonial revolution and the global expansion of technological innovations. By analyzing their writings on the gramophone, this study highlights how bodily impairment influences cultural imagination and challenges the conventional narratives that are inattentive to the social experience of disability. It first investigates how Guo articulated his view of the gramophone against the backdrop of an ableist revolutionary culture, thereby adapting a distinctive sonic imagination to align with anti-colonial movements. It then supplements this with the works of Malraux to evaluate the potential of a disability-mediated view of revolution in the greater anti-colonial world. In so doing, this article assesses how the intellectuals’ impaired bodies, as sites of engagements with revolution and sound technologies like the gramophone, provide a valuable lens for contesting ableist assumptions and a critical understanding of the historical dynamics of auditory culture.

Prism: Theory and Modern Chinese Literature

  1. Transwriting as Method
    Ursula Deser Friedman · pp. 223-245 · online 2025-09-01
    摘要

    This article takes up the recent discovery of an unpublished draft of Eileen Chang's short story “She Said Smiling.” The thirty-one-year period, from 1952 until 1983, in which Chang translated this story into Chinese as “Xiangjian huan” (1978) coincided with her own double exile to Hong Kong (1952) and the United States (1955). In writing back and forth between English and Chinese, Chang harnessed transwriting as an extended textual performance. When Chang's bilingual personae converged, a third—a transwritten voice—emerged from the multilingual cacophony. The article first compares the bare-bones English-language source text with the embellished Chinese-language translated version, tracing changes in characterization, temporality, plot, and narration. Chang's process of creative retelling concretizes wartime trauma and invites readers to serve as collective memory repositories. Next, the article decodes the queer subtext embedded in the subversive smiles exchanged between the story's pair of estranged female cousins. While the matter-of-fact English-language narrator overtly queers the smiling cousins’ relationship, the Chinese-language narrator leaves their ambiguous desires up to readers’ interpretation by showing rather than telling. Finally, the article examines the intertextual resonance between Katherine Mansfield's homoerotic short story “Bliss” and “She Said Smiling” as a window into Chang's attempts to write herself into the World Republic of Letters.

  2. Feminist Politics in Du Pan Fangge's Translingual Poetics
    Jiaxin Yan · pp. 246-269 · online 2025-09-01
    摘要

    This article reevaluates Taiwanese Hakka poet Du Pan Fangge's 杜潘芳格 (1927–2016) contributions to postwar Taiwan poetry to shed light on the underlying connections between translingual practices and gendered forms of (in)visibility. Considered one of the leading figures in “the translingual generation,” Du Pan has long been both politically and theoretically neglected despite the rich complexity of her identity and poetic interventions. Probing into her personal trajectories and the multilingual interspecies tropes she creates, the article takes a feminist approach to bring the issue of gender into conversation with her translingual poetic practices. It traces the creative interplay between minor languages and gender and destabilizes analytical frameworks that cast and undervalue certain writers as minoritarian in Taiwan literature studies. Du Pan depicts three inherently fluid imageries that straddle land and water: nonfish, groundwater veins, and whale potatoes. Her works inspire a practice of intertextual reading that not only takes into account the precarious existence of Taiwan between competing empires, but allows feminist potentials to thrive in moments of extreme precarity. Her translingual poetics conjures up a liberating space, an inherently multivocal, trans-affective habitat outside of domestic and national enclosure.

  3. Toward an Archive Fever around the Last Monarch
    Chang-Yen Lo · pp. 270-290 · online 2025-09-01
    摘要

    This article examines how three distinct twentieth-century works, Pu Yi's From Emperor to Citizen, Bernardo Bertolucci's The Last Emperor, and Su Tong's My Life as an Emperor, not only offer varied literary and artistic representations of the last monarch but also interrogate the concepts of history and the archive. By interweaving these works with Jacques Derrida's Mal d'archive (Archive Fever), the article also seeks to elucidate how an archive fever around the last monarch emerges, and how the ontologically fragmented and violent processes of archiving historical figures are challenged, deconstructed, and reconfigured within these texts. In these works, the past is either acknowledged and harnessed in pursuit of truth, or questioned and reconfigured to unearth suppressed narratives, or entirely fabricated and toyed with to disrupt the conventional link between history and the archive. Through the examination of these three works, I argue that the archive around the last monarch undergoes an endless process of self-deconstruction and reconstruction. This process invites readers to actively engage in reevaluating and challenging historical accounts and narratives, thereby contributing to the de-archiving and re-archiving of the very concept of the last monarch.

  5. The Jiang'an Years of the National Academy of Drama
    Xiaomei Chen · pp. 296-325 · online 2025-09-01
    摘要

    This essay examines The National Academy of Drama (1936–49), which had trained around a thousand theater, film, opera artists, and leaders in the PRC. During the Sino-Japanese War period, the drama school moved five times and gave rise to the drama school's most productive years with its highest achievements. This essay examines the school's multicultural traditions stemmed from its faculty's American and European training in theater and the hybrid style of Western plays and traditional Chinese theater that nurtured a generation of new theater students. In all aspects of theater, such as theater building, management, advertising, stage design, lighting, custom, make-up, the drama school laid the foundations for the future theater development that culminated in the PRC period. This essay asks how one of the most productive periods of a drama institution could occur in the most challenging years of war-torn China—a time of campus relocations, artist migrations, poverty, and lack of resources. In the larger scheme of things, this essay weaves institutional history, theater formation, repertory building, war and regional cultures, economic conditions, and aesthetic movements both in and out of China for a more complex history of theater art across ideological and political boundaries.

  6. Chinese Socialist Discourse of Theatrical Performativity
    Tam Kwok-kan · pp. 326-348 · online 2025-09-01
    摘要

    A 1956 stage production of Ibsen's A Doll's House by the China Youth Art Theater offers an excellent example for the study of Chinese socialist theater performativity. The staging had sophisticated scenographic designs and acting details aimed at producing ideological messages, combined with visual effects intended to provoke the audiences and lead them to action. The performance had lasting impact in China, with another production of A Doll's House in 1962 by the Shanghai Theater Academy following similar scenic designs. It also served to substantiate Chinese socialist theory of drama with a practical example of theater performativity, which impacted subsequent theater theory and practice in the People's Republic. This cross-cultural experiment in theater performance illustrates artists’ effort to elevate art as art under stringent political conditions in observance of Mao's doctrine defining art as service to the Communist cause, which he put forth in his 1942 speech in the Yan'an Talks.

  7. Black Liberation on the Chinese Stage
    Emily Wilcox · pp. 349-370 · online 2025-09-01
    摘要

    In 1963, in response to a request from US Black radicals Mabel and Robert F. Williams, Mao Zedong issued a declaration announcing China's support for the African American struggle against racial discrimination and US imperialism. This marked the beginning of a nearly decade-long dialogue between Chinese leaders and the Williamses that shaped the Black power movement in the United States and beyond. The Chinese military dance drama Fires of Fury Are Burning (Nuhuo zai ranshao 怒火在燃燒), premiered in Beijing in 1964, used dance choreography to promote Mao's statement, as well as the Williamses’ philosophy and practice of armed self-defense for African Americans. With Chinese dancers portraying Black and white characters in the dance, Fires of Fury Are Burning built upon a tradition in twentieth-century China of employing racial impersonation to promote interracial solidarity, which differs in form and content from US blackface minstrelsy. Though dealing with similar themes, Fires of Fury Are Burning differed from African American dancer Katherine Dunham's Southland and Cuban filmmaker Santiago Álvarez's newsreel Now! because it offered an embodiment of Black empowerment and a vision of the future in which the struggle for racial justice emerged victorious, by directly combating anti-Black police brutality and KKK violence.

  8. Introduction
    Carlos Rojas · pp. 371-380 · online 2025-09-01
    摘要

    Introducing a set of three essays commissioned for a Theory Forum on digital labor, this essay begins by summarizing some questions raised by recent developments in advanced AI, which mirror a larger set of issues raised by the emergence of digital technologies since the mid-twentieth century—including technologies that enable practices of computation, communication, recording, and data storage that would have been difficult or impossible with analog technologies. The essay then reflects more specifically on how digital technologies not only have the potential to make some forms of labor more efficient, but they also create a new category of what is called digital labor. The essay proceeds to outlines several different ways of understanding the concept of digital labor, and some of the specific ways in which this category is relevant to economies, technologies, and cultures associated with East Asia.

    Viren Murthy · pp. 381-395 · online 2025-09-01

  11. Asianness in an Animated World
    Zachary Gottesman · pp. 420-437 · online 2025-09-01
    摘要

    Nickelodeon's Avatar: The Last Airbender (2005–2008) has endured as a beloved series across decades and spawned a massive media franchise. Though cocreated by two white Americans, a fantasy Asianness is an essential element of the setting, the characters, the martial arts, and a sense of authenticity. The show was also animated in a specific Asian country, South Korea, which served as both a source of cultural Asianness and a source of cheap animation labor. Empowered by the fallout from a live action film version of the story, which cast white actors in roles that had been coded by fans as Asian in the animated show, the original creators returned to create a sequel for an older audience, The Legend of Korra (2012–14) and encouraged its Korean animators to contribute creatively to the show. Investigating the failed effort to use Japanese anime studio Pierrot for outsourcing labor in season 2, the backlash that followed created awareness of the previously invisible Korean elements of the show's success. This coincided with the greatest Korean cultural input into the show itself, with Korean background art, historical and political references in the plot, and a highly stylized two-part special in an East Asian art style. Korra, which evoked East Asian modernity to critique the political limitations of Avatar, brought an American multicultural vision of Asianness into conflict with the Asianness of Koreans themselves rooted in nationalism and historical conflict. This essay analyzes the contradiction between these two forms of Asianness, their manifestation at the level of Korra's production and plot, and failed attempts at resolution. Ultimately, Korra reveals the limits of Korean cultural input in the global hierarchy of animation production.

  1. Matters of Cultivated Leisure: Humility of Things, Rabindranath Tagore and Yogāyog (1929)
    Sagar Das · pp. 861-880 · online 2026-06-05
    摘要

    Rabindranath Tagore’s (1861–1941) critique of the political and urban civilisation of the West as opposed to the spiritually oriented civilisation of the East consolidated the materiality/spirituality binary in the Manichean world of colonial Bengal. This dichotomy is codified in Tagore’s commentary on cultivated leisure, establishing the nebulous idea of taste through negating the ‘thingness’ of subject-object relations. Complicating such absolute discursive divisions, this paper proposes materiality as a method to read Tagore’s 1929 novel, Relationships (originally published in Bengali in 1929 as Yogāyog). Contextualising the ambiguities of ‘thing theory’ within the colonial context of Bengal, this paper examines Tagore’s navigation of modernity and its conflictual materialities beyond an overdetermined rejection of the corporeal. Informed by Tagore’s writings on material culture, it locates interruptions in the novel’s metaphysical mode, disturbing the ‘humility of things’ to reveal implicit materialities that mark the leisured spaces of retreat from the colonial praxis.

  2. The Dark Ecology of Flash Floods and Hydropower Dams in Sikkim
    Prajwal Pakhrin · pp. 881-900 · online 2026-07-16
    摘要

    This article proposes a dark ecology approach to address the ecological crisis compounded by hydropower dams in Sikkim. It argues that the Teesta flash floods magnified the visibility of the ecological mesh, i.e. a network of ecological beings or ‘strange strangers’ composed of human and non-human forms. The flash floods appeared like a strange stranger and problematised riverine communities, state and non-state agencies on multiple scales. The proliferation of hydropower dams and the 2023 flash floods have resulted in an ecological rupture that corresponds to ecognosis, a riddle to the local community, experienced through the changing climate, thereby resulting in changing traditional agrarian patterns. I conclude with the forgotten narrative of the 1968 flash floods and landslide in the region and ruminate whether the end of nature might be closer than expected, unless alternative plural indigenous ecological knowledge systems are acknowledged and practised on a planetary scale.

  3. Bridging the Worlds: Exploring Dialogues, Differences and Perceptions About ‘Others’ in the Upaniṣadic Tradition with a Spotlight on Brahman
    Rohit Kumar · pp. 901-918 · online 2026-07-07
    摘要

    India has a long-standing tradition of engaging with diversity through public discourse and intellectual debates. This openness has been upheld by strong arguments that celebrate variation and emphasise mutual respect through dialogue. This paper explores this dimension of early Indian literary tradition by analysing three significant dialogues, particularly with their pūrvapakṣa–uttarapakṣa dimension, from distinct Upaniṣadic texts: the dialogue between Gārgya Bālāki and King Ajātaśatru in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad; the interaction between Indra, Virocana and Prajāpati in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad; and the discourse involving Prajāpati devas and a yakṣa in the Kena Upaniṣad. The first two dialogues highlight differences, particularly in terms of philosophical traditions and social identities, while illustrating how these encounters transcend rigid boundaries without reaching definitive conclusions. The third dialogue sheds light on the accommodative spirit underlying these discussions. This paper argues that debate, difference and the accommodation of diversity are enduring themes in early Indian literary traditions, reflecting a deeply rooted ethos of intellectual plurality.

  4. ‘Poetry Is a Flavourful Ball’: Sinhala Poetic Prescriptions in Munidasa Cumaratunga’s Kavi Śikṣāva ( Poetics ), 1939
    Garrett Field · pp. 919-940 · online 2026-07-12
    摘要

    In twentieth century Sri Lanka, one of the most influential philologists of Sinhala literature was Munidasa Cumaratunga (1887–1944). In 1939, he published Kavi Śikṣāva (Poetics) to explain how to appreciate and compose metred Sinhala poetry. But he did so through a fictional dialogue between a groom-to-be and his future bride. In this article, I argue that Cumaratunga wrote these dialogues to reformulate Sinhala poetics according to his prescriptions that both challenged and sustained ties with premodern poetic conventions. Cumaratunga’s poetic prescriptions offer scholars of South Asian literary cultures a window into an understudied aesthetic paradigm that flourished prior to the emergence of Sinhala free verse in the 1950s. It was a literary sensibility that celebrated recited poetry that engaged listeners in a challenging but pleasurable task to decode double meanings.

  5. Ezhava Reform and Hindu Sanghadana in 1930s–40s Travancore
    Mukulika Radhakrishnan · pp. 941-961 · online 2026-07-07

    This article examines the intersections between subaltern anti-caste reform and ‘Hindu unity’ in early twentieth century South India, focusing on the princely state of Travancore. Centring the Ezhava reform movement and drawing on underexplored archival sources, the article argues that while some Ezhava elites resisted conservative assimilation, others pursued it, engaging with organisations such as the Travancore Hindu Mahasabha to negotiate status and social mobility. The article introduces a neglected archival document suggesting the existence of a Sree Narayana Dharma Samrakshana Yogam, distinct from the well-known SNDP Yogam, pointing to a more complex range of engagements with Hindu consolidationist projects. Situating these developments within wider anxieties over Christian conversions, princely state politics, and the growing influence of national Hindu organisations in the 1930s and 1940s, the article argues that Ezhava reform encompassed greater ideological heterogeneity than previously acknowledged.

  6. Laughing at Brahmanical Orthodoxy: Dube ji ki Chitthi and the Satirical Hindi Public Letter in Colonial India
    Charu Gupta · pp. 962-983 · online 2026-05-26

    This article examines Dube ji ki Chitthi (1924–44), a satirical epistolary column by Vishwambharnath Sharma ‘Kaushik’, to explore the political power of vernacular humour in colonial Hindi print culture. Written in the guise of a rotund, bhang-loving Brahman, Dube ji’s public letters deployed conversational rhythm, earthy idioms and performative satire to critique the rigidities of Sanatani Hinduism and Brahmanical pretensions. These letters blurred the boundaries between entertainment and dissent, offering a form of civic pedagogy rooted in folk logic and cultural embeddedness. At once conservative and progressive, complicit and critical, they reflected the ambivalences of inter-War Hindi literati and their limited radicalism. This essay argues that Kaushik’s use of satire forged a vernacular ethics of dissent, where laughter became a mode of survival and critique within an increasingly censored and polarised public sphere.

  7. Debating Islam, Nation and Belonging: Nigār Magazine and Muslim Publics in Late Colonial India
    Aaqib Javid · pp. 984-1004 · online 2026-06-05
    摘要

    This article examines Islamic modernism in colonial South Asia through the lens of Urdu print culture, focusing on the magazine Nigār (1922–63), edited by Niyaz Fatehpuri. Situating Nigār within the expansion of Urdu print in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the article analyses how Fatehpuri used the magazine as a platform to articulate a rationalist reinterpretation of Islam grounded in ethical reform and naturalist reasoning. Drawing on close readings of editorials, polemical essays, and reader correspondence published in Nigār during the 1930s and 1940s, the article reconstructs debates over religious authority, reason and public life within an emerging Muslim vernacular public sphere. Rather than treating Nigār as a neutral forum, the article argues that the magazine functioned as an editor-driven intervention that actively shaped intellectual contestation and forms of Muslim public reasoning in late colonial North India.

  8. ‘Ours Is a Species Adapted to Life on Water’: Land, Livelihood and the Peculiar Geography of Kuttanad, Kerala
    Mohit Mandal · pp. 1005-1025 · online 2026-06-16
    摘要

    Through a historical and ethnographic approach grounded in the rice-growing, low-lying region of Kuttanad in Kerala, this article traces threads of continuity between reclamation projects initiated in the British colonial period and the postcolonial construction of the Thanneermukkom bund in 1974. I argue that ideologies of agrarian settlement and technocratic intervention, set into motion under colonial capitalism, continue to confine the geography and ecology of Kuttanad’s water-saturated landscape, even as farmers and fisherfolk rely upon small-scale, collectivist techniques that emerge from the bottom up. When the history of agrarian cultivation and the flow of rivers is understood as mobile and dynamic rather than permanently settled or fixed, then solutions for climate adaptation in riverine ecosystems may seek to embrace principles of flexibility over control, aligning with—rather than seeking to master—the recurrence of seasons and cycles, such as the necessarily overflowing floods of the annual monsoons.

  9. Reading the Representation of Queerness in the Pakistani Film Joyland (2022)
    Sourav Saha, Shyamkiran Kaur · pp. 1026-1047 · online 2026-07-01
    摘要

    Through a close reading of the acclaimed Pakistani film, Joyland (2022), the article argues for a shift in South Asian queer cinema studies away from frameworks of identity, visibility and narrative resolution, and towards an examination grounded in the three interlinked registers of subjectivity, relationality and aesthetics. Situating the film within the Pakistani and South Asian broader context, the article contends that queerness in Joyland is constructed not as a singular identity or as emancipatory, but as a lived condition shaped by stringent family dynamics, patrilineal societal norms and adherence to normative gender roles. The paper posits Joyland as a unique South Asian cinematic intervention that situates queerness through failures of masculinity, transgressive desires, and traversing normative gender and sexual roles.

  10. Development Citizenship in the Age of Terror: The Pashtun Tahafuz Movement in Pakistan
    Naheem Jabbar, Usman Ali · pp. 1048-1069 · online 2026-06-22
    摘要

    Many lessons might be learnt about the borderland as a transnational place in the Global South in our era of paranoid hyper-nationalism. Gramsci’s insights teach us that the rehabilitation of a dissident population as a preventative measure by militaries is no different when it comes to combating the ‘first elements’ of insurgency. This article examines the response to these measures by a single social movement that has been borrowing development and human rights norms from the international setting to expose the failures of the new regime, post-pacification, for nearly two decades. Our participants, selected by the PTM (Pashtun Tahafuz Movement or Pashtun Protection Movement) itself for their experience of conflict in Waziristan, ultimately show us how ‘an unprecedented concentration of hegemony’ is required for the task of rehabilitating populations in the historically liminal places between Afghanistan and Pakistan.

  11. Exploring Gift Exchange Practices in Swat State (1917–69): Insights from the Era of the Walis
    Jalal Uddin · pp. 1070-1090 · online 2026-06-22
    摘要

    This study examines the practices of gifting in the princely state of Swat under the rule of Miangul Abdul Wadud (1917–49) and his successor, Miangul Abdul Haq Jahanzeb (1949–69), highlighting the interplay between personal generosity, political strategy and cultural patronage. Gifts, fines, allowances and material rewards functioned not merely as symbolic gestures of benevolence but as deliberate instruments for cultivating loyalty, securing alliances and reinforcing hierarchical structures within the governance framework. Regular stipends operated as structured quasi-gifts, consolidating authority both within the state and in relations with external actors. Beyond political utility, the Walis’ gifting practices encompassed cultural, educational and recreational domains, including the distribution of books, patronage of literary gatherings and the sharing of hunted game. This study demonstrates that in Swat state, gifting was integral to governance, operating at the intersection of authority, diplomacy and social obligation, thereby illuminating the broader significance of material culture.

  12. ‘We Do Not Want a Farmer Husband’: Analysing the Marriage Drought in Rural Western India
    Akshay Sawant · pp. 1091-1109 · online 2026-07-07
    摘要

    Based on a year’s ethnographic fieldwork in a village in the drought-prone Beed district of Maharashtra, this article explores the emerging ‘marriage drought’ phenomenon among Marathas, a dominant landholding caste. The crisis, popularly voiced as ‘shetkari navra nako (we do not want a farmer husband)’, reflects a broader socio-economic transformation in which agriculture has lost its prestige, and rural masculinity is being redefined through urban aspirations, consumerism and non-agricultural employment. This article analyses the strategies Marathas adopt to negotiate this crisis, including seeking brides beyond traditional caste and regional boundaries and challenging caste endogamy norms. While existing scholarship has linked this phenomenon to gender imbalances, demographic shifts and agrarian distress, this article extends the conversation by exploring a less examined dimension: the impact of the marriage drought on intercommunity relationships, particularly those across caste and religious lines, offering insight into shifting social boundaries in a transforming rural landscape.

  13. Urban Imageries and Educational Aspirations: Perspectives from Delhi’s Margins
    Sriti Ganguly · pp. 1110-1128 · online 2026-07-12
    摘要

    This paper explores the aspirations and negotiations of residents in a forty-year-old multigenerational slum for socio-spatial mobility, escape from stigmatised identifications and the centrality of urban education in this pursuit. In doing so, the paper situates itself at the crucial but often neglected intersection of urban sociology and sociology of education to examine the meanings and significance they attribute to urban education. With the neoliberal turn and its accompanying urban transformations, Delhi’s educational landscape has also undergone change. Using Edward Soja’s critical spatial perspective, the paper analyses articulations among the acutely stigmatised slum residents for a better future and attempts to overcome their marginalisation through the pursuit of urban education and its associated notions of sophistication and civility. Further, if much of the existing literature provides planners, elites and dominant middle classes’ desires and perspectives of urbanity and exclusivity, this paper highlights urban imageries from/at the margins.

  1. Pogson’s Tomb: Three Narratives of Life and Death in Banaras
    Michael S. Dodson · pp. 1-21 · online 2026-10-25
    摘要

    This essay examines the life of Lieutenant-Colonel W.R. Pogson (1787–1843), a middle-ranking officer in the East India Company’s army, as well as the socio-cultural significance of his death in contemporary Banaras (Varanasi). Pogson was also a noted orientalist who wrote at length about India’s history and military cultures. His monumental grave, located in a poor neighbourhood of Banaras, now acts as a shrine for local residents, and they consider Pogson himself to be a wish-granting spirit. The tomb thus serves as an alternative religious space in this largely Hindu city. Three different versions of Pogson’s life and death are recounted here as a way of illustrating the different meanings one can ascribe to Pogson’s historical and contemporary significance. This essay also argues that Pogson’s continued relevance to the life of Banaras’ poor highlights the failures of recent attempts to rebrand the city as an aspirational modern Hindu space.

  2. Visual Grammar of Viraha in the Paintings of Select Partition Artists
    Kamayani Kumar · pp. 1-20 · online 2026-10-25
    摘要

    Decades have passed, yet South Asia continues to grapple with cartographic anxieties invoked by the Partition of the Indian subcontinent. This paper addresses Partition as an unresolved cultural trauma, examining how its post-memories have been transgenerationally transmitted. Partition translated into a violent ‘unhoming’ for millions and, in the process, caused a deep sense of viraha—longing for the unruptured past. Art and literature from the subcontinent have represented this viraha—as a persistent longing for the lost home and culture. This paper, with its focus on the work of artists such as S.L. Parasher, Satish Gujral, Zarina Hashmi and Krupa Makhija, explores how artists have represented the memories, post memories and prosthetic memories of Partition trauma. In the process of collective mourning, art serves as a tool for ‘aesthetic wit(h)nessing’.Footnote1 While official historiography has provides ‘systemic’ truths about Partition, artistic discourses translate the profound sense of loss of home.
